text: Begin the morning by saying to yourself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
context: Written by a Roman emperor in a private notebook. Not cynicism but preparation: he goes on to say such people act from ignorance, and that he cannot be harmed by them or angry with his own kin.
about:
Marcus Aurelius, born in Rome in 121, became Roman emperor and kept a private notebook, the Meditations: twelve short books written for his own use. A note at the end of Book I says it was written on campaign among the Quadi. Book II opens with this morning exercise.

It sounds gloomy: today I will meet the meddler, the ungrateful, the arrogant. But Marcus goes on at once. They act this way because they do not know good from bad, and they are his kin, made to work together with him. So none of them can really harm him, and he cannot hate them. Expecting difficult people is not cynicism. It is preparation, so that their behaviour doesn't catch us off guard.
prompt: Who might test your patience today, and how do you want to meet them?

text: The best way of avenging yourself is not to become like the wrong-doer.
context: One of the shortest entries in the Meditations. Being wronged offers a choice: to copy the wrong, or to remain who you are.
about:
The Meditations is the private notebook of Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor born in 121. This entry is one of its shortest: a single line between longer notes on change and on the mind.

When someone wrongs us, revenge feels natural: hurt them back. Marcus suggests a better kind of revenge: don't become like them. If they were unfair, stay fair. If they were cruel, stay kind. That way the wrong ends with them, instead of being copied by us. It is also the only revenge fully in our power. We can't control what others did, but we decide whether their behaviour becomes ours.
prompt: Whose behaviour has been quietly changing yours?

text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and you too are wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in your power whenever you choose to retire into yourself.
context: Marcus reminds himself that the quiet he longs for in the countryside is always available within. The retreat is a practice, not a place.
about:
Rich Romans escaped to country houses and seaside villas, and Marcus Aurelius admits in his private notebook, the Meditations, that he longs for such places too. He was ruling an empire at the time.

But, he tells himself, you can retire into yourself whenever you choose, and there is no quieter place. The retreat we crave is not only a place but a practice: a few moments of turning inward, reminding ourselves of what matters, then going back to work. He ends the entry with a short summary for such moments: the universe is change, and life is opinion. A holiday rests the body; this kind of retreat rests the mind.
prompt: Where in yourself can you retreat to, right now, for a minute?

text: Do not act as if you were going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you live, while it is in your power, be good.
context: The Stoics kept death in mind not to frighten themselves but to focus. Marcus, ruling an empire, tells himself the same: the time to be good is not later, but now.
about:
Book IV of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations keeps returning to how short life is. Just before this entry, he pictures grains of incense on one altar: one falls sooner, one later, and it makes no difference.

Then the reminder: don't act as if you had ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you live, while you can, be good. The Stoics kept death in mind not to frighten themselves, but to focus. Most of us postpone kindness, honesty or courage to a later that may never come. Marcus, with an empire to run, tells himself that the time to be good is now.
prompt: What good thing have you been postponing as if you had endless time?

text: Occupy yourself with few things, says the philosopher, if you would be tranquil.
context: Marcus quotes Democritus, then refines the advice: do what is necessary, and you gain the calm of doing few things and doing them well.
about:
In this entry of his Meditations, Marcus Aurelius quotes an older philosopher's advice: if you want to be tranquil, occupy yourself with few things.

Then he improves it. Rather than doing few things, do what is necessary, what our nature as social beings requires. That brings two kinds of calm: from doing things well, and from doing few things. Most of what we say and do, he adds, is unnecessary; drop it, and we gain time and peace. It is a useful question for a crowded day: which of these things actually needs doing?
prompt: What could you stop doing to make room for what matters?

text: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.
context: An image of steadiness. The waves do not stop coming; the rock simply does not move, and the water around it grows calm.
about:
Marcus Aurelius wrote this image in Book IV of his Meditations, just after picturing the end of life as an olive that falls when it is ripe, thanking the tree it grew on.

Be like the headland, he writes: waves keep breaking on it, but it stands firm and calms the water around it. Then he turns it on himself. Am I unhappy because this has happened to me? No: I am happy, though it has happened, because I am still free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor afraid of the future. The waves don't stop. What changes is whether they knock us over.
prompt: What keeps breaking against you, and how could you stand more firmly?

text: Such as are your habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of your mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
context: Just as cloth takes on the colour it soaks in, the mind takes on the colour of what it repeatedly thinks.
about:
The image in this entry from Marcus Aurelius' Meditations comes from cloth-dyeing: fabric takes on the colour of the dye it soaks in.

So, he says, our habitual thoughts colour the mind. Then he offers a thought worth soaking in: wherever a person can live, they can also live well, even in a palace. The idea is practical. We become what we repeatedly think. Worry, resentment and comparison stain slowly; so do gratitude and patience. Choosing our thoughts, again and again, is how a character is dyed.
prompt: Which thoughts do you return to most often, and what colour are they giving your mind?

text: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if you will ever dig.
context: Marcus pictures goodness as a spring inside us. It does not arrive from outside; it has to be uncovered again and again, by paying attention to what we already are.
about:
In Book VII of his Meditations, Marcus Aurelius sets down this short note right after a reminder to attend to himself and resolve to be good in every act.

Look within, he writes: there is a fountain of good, and it will always bubble up if you keep digging. Goodness here is not something we fetch from outside, from praise or good circumstances. It is a spring we already have, though it gets covered over. The digging is the daily work of attention: noticing what matters, choosing well, and coming back to our principles when we drift.
prompt: What good in you needs digging out today?

text: If you are pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs you, but your own judgment about it. And it is in your power to wipe out this judgment now.
context: One of the clearest statements of Stoic freedom: the judgment is ours, so we can revise it, not someday but now.
about:
One of the central ideas of Stoicism fits into a few lines of Book VIII of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations. Just before, he reminds himself that nature brings nothing a person cannot bear.

If something outside you causes pain, he writes, it is not the thing that disturbs you but your judgment about it, and you can wipe out that judgment now. The Stoics did not deny real pain. They noticed how much of our suffering comes from the story we add: this is unfair, this is a disaster, this should not happen. Change the story, and much of the pain changes with it.
prompt: Which judgment about your situation could you revise right now?

text: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
context: Marcus, tired of his own philosophising, tells himself to stop describing virtue and start living it.
about:
Late in his Meditations, in Book X, among reminders that little of his life remains, Marcus Aurelius writes himself this blunt instruction.

No longer talk about what a good person should be like; be one. It reads like a rebuke to himself, perhaps after years of writing philosophy in his notebook. Discussing virtue can become a way of avoiding it. We can read, plan and talk about patience or kindness for years. Marcus cuts through all that: at some point, the only thing left to do is to act.
prompt: What ideal have you been discussing that you could simply live today?

text: When you are offended with any man's shameless conduct, immediately ask yourself, Is it possible, then, that shameless men should not be in the world? It is not possible. Do not, then, require what is impossible.
context: Expecting a world without difficult people only guarantees frustration. Marcus asks himself to expect them, and so to meet them calmly.
about:
Marcus Aurelius gives himself a test, in Book IX of his Meditations, for the moment he is offended by someone's shameless behaviour.

Ask yourself: is it possible that there should be no shameless people in the world? It is not. Then don't demand the impossible; this person is simply one of them. The question changes how we meet difficult people. Much of our anger comes from feeling that something shouldn't be happening. Accepting that rude and dishonest people exist doesn't excuse them. It lets us deal with them calmly, instead of being outraged each time.
prompt: What are you demanding of others that is simply impossible?

text: In the morning when you rise unwillingly, let this thought be present,—I am rising to the work of a human being.
context: Even an emperor struggled to get out of bed. His answer was to remember what he was for.
about:
Book V of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations opens with this note about getting out of bed. Even a Roman emperor, it seems, sometimes rose unwillingly.

His answer is to remember what he is for: I am rising to the work of a human being. Then he argues with himself. Was I made to lie under the covers and keep warm? It is more pleasant. But was I born for pleasure, or for action? The scene is funny and very human. On hard mornings, remembering why our work matters can do more than any alarm.
prompt: What work, worthy of a human being, is waiting for you today?

text: When you wish to delight yourself, think of the virtues of those who live with you; for instance, the activity of one, and the modesty of another, and the liberality of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth.
context: A Roman emperor's simple exercise in gratitude: when you need cheering up, think of the particular good qualities of the people around you, one by one.
about:
Marcus Aurelius had a simple way to lift his mood, and he noted it in Book VI of his Meditations.

When you want to cheer yourself up, think of the good qualities of the people around you: the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third. Nothing delights so much, he says, as seeing virtues in those we live with. It is an early gratitude exercise, and a useful one. We tend to notice people's faults first. Naming their good qualities, one person at a time, changes how we feel about them, and about our day.
prompt: Name one good quality in each of three people close to you.

text: How much trouble he avoids who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he does himself.
context: Marcus noticed how much of his unrest came from watching what others said and did. Turning attention back to our own conduct removes a surprising amount of trouble.
about:
Marcus Aurelius wrote this in Book IV of his Meditations, right after reminding himself not to act as if he would live ten thousand years.

How much trouble we avoid, he writes, if we don't watch what our neighbour says, does or thinks, but only what we do ourselves, that it may be just and pure. Then he quotes a poet: don't look around at others' bad morals, but run straight along your own line. Comparing and judging take up a surprising amount of our attention. Turning it back to our own conduct is calmer, and far more useful.
prompt: Whose life have you been watching instead of tending your own?

text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
context: The opening line of Epictetus' handbook. Everything else in Stoic practice follows from sorting life into what we can govern (our judgments, intentions, actions) and what we cannot (other people, reputation, outcomes).
about:
Epictetus was a slave in Rome, later freed, who spent his life teaching philosophy. He wrote nothing himself: his teaching was written down by Arrian, including the short Manual, or Enchiridion, which opens with this line.

Some things are in our power, and some are not. In our power, Epictetus says, are our opinions, impulses, desires and aversions: in a word, our own acts. Not in our power are our body, property, reputation and position. Everything else in his teaching follows from this sorting. We suffer when we treat what isn't ours to control as if it were, and neglect what is. Freedom begins with knowing which is which.
prompt: What are you carrying today that was never yours to control?

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.
context: Epictetus, born a slave, taught that suffering often lives in our interpretation of events rather than in the events themselves. Change the judgment and the disturbance changes with it.
about:
Epictetus, born a slave and lame from an early age, knew hardship well. His Manual, a short handbook of his teaching, puts this idea at its centre.

People are disturbed not by what happens, he says, but by their opinions about it. Death, for example, is not terrible, or it would have seemed so to Socrates; the opinion that it is terrible is the terrible thing. So when we are upset, we should blame not others but our own opinions. This is not a denial of real loss. It is a way of finding the part of our distress that we can change.
prompt: What story are you telling yourself about something that upset you recently?

text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
context: Epictetus does not ask us to stop caring, but to stop demanding that reality match our wishes.
about:
Epictetus' Manual sets down this short rule just after a picture of life as a voyage: when the ship's captain calls, run back aboard and leave everything behind.

Don't wish for things to happen as you want; wish for them to happen as they do, and your life will flow calmly. It sounds like giving up, but it isn't. Epictetus still expects us to act and to care. What he asks us to drop is the demand that reality obey our wishes. Much frustration comes from that demand. Meeting events as they are leaves more energy for dealing with them well.
prompt: What would you accept today if you stopped arguing with it?

text: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
context: Everything we hold is on loan. Speaking of 'returning' rather than 'losing' changes how we hold what we have while we have it.
about:
The examples Epictetus gives in this part of his Manual are hard ones: a child dies, a wife dies, an estate is taken away.

Never say I have lost something, he writes; say I have given it back. Everything we have is on loan, to be cared for while it is ours, as travellers care for an inn. That can sound cold in grief. But the idea is not to love less. It is to remember, while we have people and things, that they are not ours forever, and so to value them more while they are here.
prompt: What do you hold that you could hold more lightly, and more gratefully?

text: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it.
context: Life passes things around like dishes at a dinner. Take your share with grace; don't grab, and don't cling to what moves on.
about:
Epictetus, the former slave who became a teacher of philosophy, offers this image in his Manual.

Behave in life as at a banquet. When a dish is passed to you, take a fair portion politely. When it passes you by, don't hold it back. When it hasn't reached you yet, don't stretch your desire towards it; wait. He applies this to children, a spouse, high office and wealth. Good things come and go around the table. We can enjoy them without grabbing, clinging, or staring at what others have.
prompt: What is passing by you that you are trying to hold onto?

text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you.
context: Insults wound only when we agree with them inwardly. Epictetus hands the power back to the one being insulted.
about:
One of the boldest claims in Epictetus' Manual comes from a man who had been a slave, with little power over how others treated him.

It is not the person who abuses or hits you who insults you, he says, but your own opinion that this is insulting. So when someone irritates you, it is your opinion that has irritated you. His advice is not to be carried away at first: gain time, and you will master yourself more easily. Insults can still sting. But they wound most when part of us agrees with them, and that part is ours to examine.
prompt: Whose words have you allowed to irritate you, and could you take that permission back?

text: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of the act by that handle wherein he acts unjustly, for this is the handle which cannot be borne; but lay hold of the other, that he is your brother.
context: Every situation can be picked up in a way that can be carried or a way that cannot. We choose the handle.
about:
Near the end of his Manual, the short handbook of his teaching, Epictetus offers this image of two handles.

Everything has two handles: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it can't. If your brother wrongs you, don't pick it up by the handle that he acted unjustly; that one can't be carried. Pick it up by the other: he is your brother, raised with you. The facts stay the same. What changes is which part of them we choose to hold, and whether we can carry it.
prompt: Which handle are you holding a difficult relationship by?

text: If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write.
context: From a discourse on how habits are formed: every capacity is strengthened by its corresponding action, and weakened by neglect.
about:
Epictetus taught for many years at Nicopolis, in Greece, and Arrian wrote down his talks as the Discourses. This one is about how habits grow.

Every habit, he says, is kept up and strengthened by its matching actions: walking by walking, running by running. If you want to be a good reader, read; if a writer, write. Stop for thirty days and you will see the result, as legs grow weak after ten days in bed. The same holds for patience, anger or kindness: each grows with use. So it is worth noticing which ones we are practising.
prompt: What do you want to become, and did you practise it today?

text: What is the first business of him who philosophizes? To throw away self-conceit. For it is impossible for a man to begin to learn that which he thinks that he knows.
context: Learning begins with humility. Whatever we think we already understand, we stop examining.
about:
A talk in Epictetus' Discourses on applying our general ideas, of good and bad, to real situations opens with this question.

The first task of anyone who takes up philosophy, he says, is to throw away self-conceit, because no one can begin to learn what they think they already know. We all talk about good and bad, fair and unfair, as if we understood them. That confidence is exactly what stops us examining them. Humility here is not low self-esteem. It is the open door that learning needs.
prompt: What do you think you already know that might be worth relearning?

text: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it … we do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one, and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1
context: Seneca wrote this essay to his friend Paulinus. Life, he argues, is long enough if we know how to use it; it only feels short because we give so much of it away.
about:
Seneca, the Roman Stoic, addressed his essay On the Shortness of Life to Paulinus. It opens with a common complaint: life is too short, and runs away just as we are getting ready to live.

Seneca disagrees. We are not given a short life, he says; we make it short, by letting so much of it run to waste through luxury and carelessness. Life is long enough for great things, if we arrange it well. It is a bracing thought. The question shifts from how much time we have to how we spend it, and that question we can answer every day.
prompt: Where did your time go recently, and was it given or taken?

text: You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3
context: Seneca names a strange contradiction: we are anxious because we are mortal, yet we behave as if we had all the time in the world.
about:
In On the Shortness of Life, Seneca looks at how people spend their time: as if they had an endless supply, though any day they give away might be their last.

You fear everything like mortals, he says, and want everything like immortals. We are anxious because we know we can lose things, and greedy as though we will never die. Both habits waste the present. The contradiction is uncomfortable because it fits so many of us. Remembering that we are mortal could make us both braver and less grasping.
prompt: Which of your desires assumes you will live forever?

text: How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it!
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3
context: Said of people who plan to start living once they retire. Seneca's point: there is no later version of life waiting for you.
about:
Seneca quotes, in On the Shortness of Life, the plans people make: after my fiftieth year I will give myself to leisure; my sixtieth will be my last year of public office.

What guarantee, he asks, that you will live that long? How late it is to begin life just when we have to leave it! He is not against work or plans. He is against postponing the life we actually want to an age that few of us reach. Retirement, holidays, someday: Seneca's point is that the time to live wisely, rest and think is woven into now, not saved for later.
prompt: What have you been saving for 'someday'?

text: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it: if it delays, it will come to an end.
context: Seneca's treatise on anger is a manual for a calmer life. His first remedy is the simplest: wait.
about:
Seneca wrote his long essay On Anger for Novatus, who had asked him how anger can be calmed. Just before this remedy, he notes that most people are angry not with wrongs, but with wrongdoers.

The greatest remedy for anger, he says, is delay: ask anger for time, not so that it will forgive, but so that it can judge rightly. If it waits, it will pass. Don't try to crush it all at once, because its first impulses are strong. It is simple, and it works. A pause between feeling and acting lets the heat fade and judgment return. Many regrets are made in the first few minutes.
prompt: When did waiting before you reacted last save you from regret?

text: So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose IV
context: Boethius wrote this book in prison, around 524, while awaiting execution. Philosophy, appearing to him as a woman, reminds him that how we judge our situation shapes how we live it. Shakespeare's Hamlet later says something very similar.
about:
Boethius was a Roman nobleman and scholar who rose to the highest honours under Theodoric, the Ostrogoth king of Italy. Within a year he was a prisoner at Pavia, facing death. There he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, in which Philosophy visits him as a woman.

Here she argues that his place of exile is someone else's home, and that many would feel rich with a scrap of his lost fortune. Nothing is wretched, she says, unless thinking makes it so, and any lot is happy if borne calmly. It echoes the Stoics: much of our misery lies in judgment. That does not make his prison pleasant. It shows where his remaining freedom lies.
prompt: Which of your troubles is mostly made of the way you think about it?

text: For truly in adverse fortune the worst sting of misery is to have been happy.
source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose IV
context: Boethius had been one of the most powerful men in Rome. Losing it all hurt more because he remembered what he had. Philosophy's reply: happiness that can be taken away was never fully yours.
about:
Boethius fell from the highest honours to a prison cell at Pavia, and wrote The Consolation of Philosophy there. In the book, Philosophy visits him as a wise woman, and he argues with her.

Here he says what anyone who has lost a good life feels: the worst sting of misery is to have been happy. Philosophy doesn't brush this aside. She asks what kind of happiness it was. If it depended on fortune, it was never truly his, and losing it shows what it was. The memory of good times can hurt. It can also teach us to look for a happiness that can't be taken away.
prompt: When a good time ends, do you hold its memory as a loss or as something you still have?

text: Why, then, you children of mortality, do you seek from without that happiness whose seat is only within us?
source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose IV
context: Wealth, rank, and fame can all be lost. Philosophy points Boethius to the one place no one can take from him.
about:
Writing as a prisoner awaiting death, Boethius imagines Philosophy arguing that the happiness fortune gives can never last, nor fully satisfy.

So why, she asks, do mortals seek outside the happiness that lives only within? Then she points to the hinge of it all: is anything more precious to you than yourself? If you are master of yourself, you have something no fortune can take. The thought was written in a prison cell, which gives it weight. Wealth and rank can be removed; self-possession cannot.
prompt: Where are you looking outside for something only you can give yourself?

text: What! are you really striving to stop the swing of the revolving wheel? Oh, stupidest of mortals, if it takes to standing still, it ceases to be the wheel of Fortune.
source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose I
context: The Wheel of Fortune, a favourite image of the Middle Ages, owes much to this book. The wheel's whole nature is to turn; expecting it to stop is the real mistake.
about:
Boethius, rich and honoured one year and a prisoner the next, complains in The Consolation of Philosophy about the cruelty of Fortune. Philosophy replies that Fortune has simply behaved as Fortune does.

If you hand yourself over to Fortune, she says, you must accept her moods. Would you stop the turning wheel? Foolish mortal: if it stood still, it would no longer be Fortune's wheel. The image is plain and memorable. Expecting luck to stay is the real mistake, because changing is what luck is. Knowing that, we can enjoy good times without counting on them, and meet bad times without feeling cheated.
prompt: What good thing in your life are you trying to make permanent?

text: For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. To act against one another, then, is contrary to nature.
context: Marcus reminds himself, on a day full of difficult people, that humans are built to work together like parts of one body. Fighting each other goes against what we are.
about:
Marcus Aurelius' morning note in Book II of the Meditations begins with a list of the difficult people he will meet today: the meddler, the ungrateful, the arrogant. This is how it ends.

Why shouldn't he be angry with them? Because, he says, we are made for co-operation, like feet, hands and eyelids, like the upper and lower rows of teeth. To act against one another goes against nature, and being vexed and turning away is already acting against them. The image is physical and memorable. Teeth that fought each other couldn't eat. People who work against each other can't live well either.
prompt: Who are you working against who is really part of the same body?

text: The universe is transformation: life is opinion.
context: Six words that sum up Stoic practice. Everything around us is changing, and how we experience it depends on the view we take.
about:
Marcus Aurelius ends a long entry in his Meditations, about finding a retreat within oneself, with two thoughts to keep at hand.

First, things outside don't touch the soul; our disturbances come from the opinions within. Second, everything we see changes and will soon be gone. Then the summary: the universe is transformation, life is opinion. Everything is moving, and how we experience it depends largely on the view we take. Neither half is gloomy. Together they suggest that if the world keeps changing, our view of it can change too.
prompt: Which change are you resisting only because of how you see it?

text: Time is like a river made up of the events which happen, and a violent stream …
context: Marcus goes on to say that as soon as one thing appears it is swept away, and another takes its place. Nothing stays long enough to cling to.
about:
This image belongs to a run of short notes about change in Book IV of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations.

Time is a river of events, a violent stream: as soon as something appears it is swept away, something else takes its place, and that too will be swept away. The image is not meant to make us anxious. Just before, Marcus writes that change is no evil. Seeing time as a river helps us hold things more loosely, enjoy them while they pass, and not be surprised when they go.
prompt: What are you holding onto that the river has already carried away?

text: Love the art, poor as it may be, which you have learned, and be content with it …
context: Whatever your craft or job, Marcus suggests taking pride in doing it well rather than wishing for someone else's.
about:
In Book IV of his Meditations, Marcus Aurelius describes philosophers so poor that one has no tunic and another no book, yet both stay true to reason. Then he turns to himself.

Love the art you have learned, however modest, he writes, and be content with it, and go through the rest of life neither tyrant nor slave of anyone. Whatever we do, a trade, a job, a skill, there is dignity in doing it well. Envying other people's work rarely improves our own. Marcus asks for pride in the craft we have, and freedom from both bossing and grovelling.
prompt: What would change if you loved the work you already do?

text: Let no act be done without a purpose, nor otherwise than according to the perfect principles of art.
context: Every action, even a small one, can be done on purpose and with skill. Drifting through the day is the opposite of living well.
about:
Early in Book IV of his Meditations, just before his famous note on retreating into oneself, Marcus Aurelius sets down this rule.

Let no act be done without a purpose, he writes, nor otherwise than by the best principles of the art. Art here means craft: doing something with skill. It is a rule for small things as much as big ones: a meal, a letter, a conversation. Much of a day can pass on autopilot. Marcus suggests treating each action as worth doing properly, which turns ordinary hours into practice.
prompt: What did you do today without really meaning to?

text: Constantly regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul …
context: The Stoics saw the cosmos as a single living whole, with each of us a small part of it. Seeing it this way puts personal worries in proportion.
about:
Like other Stoics, Marcus Aurelius thought of the universe as one ordered whole, in which every part is connected. He reminds himself of it in Book IV of his Meditations.

Always think of the universe as one living being, he writes, with one substance and one soul, where everything acts together and everything helps cause what happens. It is a cosmic picture, but its effect is personal. If we are each a small part of a great, connected whole, our worries shrink to their real size, and what happens to us looks less like a private disaster and more like part of a larger story.
prompt: How do your worries look from the scale of the whole universe?

text: Nothing happens to any man which he is not formed by nature to bear.
context: A Stoic encouragement for hard times: we are stronger than we think, and most of what we fear is bearable.
about:
Marcus Aurelius wrote this among the notes in Book V of his Meditations that he used to steady himself.

Nothing happens to anyone that they are not formed by nature to bear. Then he adds: the same things happen to others, and they stay firm, either because they don't notice, or because they want to look brave. It would be a shame, he says, if ignorance and vanity were stronger than wisdom. The point is encouragement. We are often stronger than we fear, and many people have carried what we now face.
prompt: What hard thing have you already carried that you once thought you couldn't?

text: The intelligence of the universe is social.
context: For Marcus, reason itself points us toward community. A wise mind looks after the common good, not only its own.
about:
An entry in Book V of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations opens with this line. Just before it, he describes his choice to live as a rational and social being.

The intelligence of the universe is social, he writes: it has made things for one another, and fitted the higher beings to each other. For Marcus, reason doesn't isolate us; it ties us together. A clear mind sees that our good is bound up with other people's. That changes how we use our intelligence. It is not only for getting ahead, but for living well together.
prompt: Where does your thinking stop at yourself instead of reaching others?

text: Nothing great, said Epictetus, is produced suddenly, since not even the grape or the fig is.
context: Epictetus goes on: if you want a fig, he says, first let it blossom, then bear fruit, then ripen. Growth in character takes the same patience.
about:
In this talk from Epictetus' Discourses, a man asks how he can stay calm even if his angry brother never makes peace with him.

Nothing great, Epictetus answers, comes about suddenly, not even a grape or a fig. If you want a fig, it needs time: let it blossom, then bear fruit, then ripen. If a fig isn't ready in an hour, he asks, would you have the fruit of a human mind so quickly and so easily? Changing ourselves, or our relationships, is slow work. Patience isn't a delay to progress. It is how progress happens.
prompt: What are you expecting to ripen faster than it can?

text: Do not admire your clothes, and then you will not be angry with the thief.
context: Our anger is tied to what we value. The less we prize possessions, the less power their loss has over us.
about:
Why do we get so angry with people who wrong us? Epictetus asks this in one of his Discourses: is it because we value so much what they take from us?

Don't admire your clothes, he says, and you won't be angry with the thief. The thief is simply mistaken about what is good: he thinks it lies in fine clothes, just as you do. Our anger is tied to what we prize. The less our happiness depends on possessions, the less power their loss has over us. That doesn't mean letting thieves off. It means not letting them rule our mood.
prompt: Which of your possessions owns a piece of your peace of mind?

text: Is freedom anything else than the power of living as we choose?
context: Epictetus, who was born enslaved, spent a whole discourse on true freedom. It isn't status but being free from fears and cravings that rule us.
about:
This question opens a long talk on freedom in Epictetus' Discourses. Epictetus had been a slave himself, so he spoke about freedom from experience.

Freedom, he says, is nothing else than the power of living as we choose. Then he asks: do you want to live in error, in fear, in sorrow? No one does. So no one who lives that way is free. It is a surprising turn. Many people with full legal freedom are ruled by fears and cravings, while someone in chains can be free inside. For Epictetus, the deepest freedom is inner.
prompt: What, if anything, stops you from living as you choose?

text: I must be present like the hour, and past like the hour.
context: We are here for a time and then we pass, like any hour of the day. Epictetus accepts both parts calmly.
about:
Epictetus imagines, in one of his Discourses, a ship sinking. What can he do? Only the one thing he can: not drown full of fear, screaming and blaming.

Because, he says, I am not immortal but a man, a part of the whole, as an hour is part of the day. I must be present like the hour, and pass like the hour. The image is calm, almost gentle. An hour doesn't resent ending; that is what hours do. Seeing our lives this way doesn't make death welcome, but it can make it less frightening, and the present more worth being present in.
prompt: How would you live this hour if you accepted that it will pass?

text: Know you not how small a part you are compared with the whole.
context: Remembering our size in the universe is not meant to crush us but to free us from taking ourselves too seriously.
about:
Epictetus' Discourses often remind his students of their place in the larger order of things. Here he asks why they should be discontented with how the world is arranged.

Don't you know how small a part you are compared with the whole? Then he adds a crucial line: he means in body. In mind, he says, you are not inferior, for intelligence is measured not by length or height but by thoughts. So the reminder cuts both ways. Physically, we are tiny and passing. In what we think and choose, we have a greatness that size cannot measure.
prompt: When did feeling small last make you feel lighter?

text: Things themselves (materials) are indifferent; but the use of them is not indifferent.
context: Money, time, and talent are neither good nor bad in themselves. What matters is what we do with them.
about:
A talk in Epictetus' Discourses on how to be careful without being anxious begins with this line.

Things themselves are indifferent, he says; what we do with them is not. His example is a game of dice: the counters don't matter, but how we play does. Money, time, health and talent work the same way. They are neither good nor bad in themselves. The skill is to take the game seriously, playing well with whatever we are dealt, without staking our peace of mind on the counters.
prompt: What resource do you have that you could use better?

text: But so long as you do not show him the truth, do not ridicule him, but rather feel your own incapacity.
context: When someone doesn't understand you, Epictetus suggests looking at your own way of explaining before mocking them.
about:
Philosophers, Epictetus complains in this talk from his Discourses, learn the rules of argument but have little practice using them with ordinary people.

Give one of us an uneducated person to talk with, he says, and if the man answers off the point, we abuse or mock him and give up. But a guide who finds someone lost leads them back to the road; he doesn't mock them and leave. Show them the truth, and they will follow. Until you do, don't ridicule them; feel your own failure. Before blaming the listener, it is worth asking how well we explained.
prompt: When someone disagrees with you, how often do you question your own explanation?

text: It does not matter what you bear, but how you bear it.
context: Seneca's short essay asks why good people suffer. His answer: we can't always choose our troubles, but we can choose how we carry them.
about:
Seneca's short essay On Providence answers a question from Lucilius: why do so many misfortunes fall on good people? He compares them to athletes, whose strength droops without an opponent.

Good people, he says, should not fear hardship or lament their fate, but take what comes and turn it to good. It does not matter what you bear, but how you bear it. That moves the question from what happens to us, which we can't always choose, to how we respond, which we can. Two people can face the same loss: one is broken, the other grows. The difference lies in the bearing.
prompt: How are you carrying the weight you have right now?

text: Fire tries gold, misfortune tries brave men.
context: Just as fire tests the purity of gold, hardship shows what a person is made of.
about:
The life worth writing about, Seneca says in On Providence, is not a straight road but a voyage through rough water, up and down, against fortune.

Fire tests gold, he writes; misfortune tests brave people. Then he quotes a poet describing the steep road of the sun's chariot: virtue has no safe, level path. The image explains why hard times matter. They show what we are made of, to others and to ourselves. Gold isn't made in the fire, but it is proven there.
prompt: What has a hard time revealed about you?

text: Unbroken prosperity cannot bear a single blow.
context: Those who have never struggled are the most fragile when trouble finally comes. Small difficulties prepare us for large ones.
about:
Seneca's On Providence compares hardship to the training a strict parent gives a child: tasks begun early, no idleness even on holidays, exercise until they sweat.

Those spoiled by ease, he says, break down under effort, even under their own weight. Unbroken prosperity cannot bear a single blow. But someone who has wrestled with misfortune grows a thicker skin, yields to nothing, and even when they fall, fights on from their knees. Small difficulties prepare us for big ones. A life protected from every hardship can leave us fragile.
prompt: What small discomfort could you welcome as training?

text: Do you not blush to spend so long a time in dreading what takes so short a time to do?
context: We often spend more energy fearing something than the thing itself would take. Seneca's question applies to death, and to many smaller tasks.
about:
On Providence, Seneca's essay on why good people suffer, ends with a speech about death, and how quickly it comes, whatever its form.

The moment the breath leaves the body is too short even to measure. Do you not blush, the speech asks, to spend so long dreading what takes so short a time to happen? It is a bracing question, and it reaches beyond death. We often spend weeks fearing a difficult conversation, an exam or a task that, when it comes, takes minutes. Much of our suffering lies in the waiting.
prompt: What have you been dreading longer than it would take to do?

text: …by degrees men find pleasure in doing what they were first driven to do by necessity.
context: What starts as a hard duty can, with time, become something we enjoy. Habit changes how effort feels.
about:
Seneca describes, in On Providence, the peoples beyond the Roman frontier on the Danube: endless winter, poor soil, shelters of leaves and thatch, food they must hunt for themselves.

Are they unhappy? No, he says: there is no unhappiness in what habit has made part of one's nature. By degrees, people find pleasure in what necessity first forced them to do. It is a hopeful observation. Hard routines, early starts, practice and frugality can become part of us, even enjoyed. What first feels like a burden can, with time, become a strength.
prompt: What started as an obligation and became a pleasure for you?

text: The invulnerable is not that which is never struck, but that which is never wounded.
source: Seneca, On the Firmness of the Wise Man
context: Strength is not avoiding every blow, but not letting blows damage who we are.
about:
Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher. In On the Firmness of the Wise Man he sets out to show that a wise person cannot truly be injured or insulted. That sounds impossible, so he explains what he means.

Being invulnerable doesn't mean never being hit; people will still be rude, unfair or cruel. It means the blow doesn't reach who we are. Seneca says an injury takes something from us: our dignity, our body, or things outside us. But the wise person's real good is their character, which fortune never gave and so cannot take away. Firm strength shows itself under attack. The goal is not a life without blows, but a self that stays whole through them.
prompt: What criticism or setback could you take without being wounded by it?

text: …fortune can take nothing away save what she gave.
source: Seneca, On the Firmness of the Wise Man
context: Luck can take back money, status, and comfort, because luck gave them. Character, which we built ourselves, is out of its reach.
about:
Seneca's On the Firmness of the Wise Man, addressed to Serenus, argues that a wise person cannot truly be injured. The reason: the wise have invested everything in themselves, and entrusted nothing to fortune.

Their only real good is virtue, which neither grows nor shrinks with luck. Fortune can take nothing away except what she gave, and she does not give virtue. Money, status and comfort come from fortune, and she can take them back. Character we build ourselves. It is an old comfort, and a sturdy one: what we make of ourselves is the one possession luck cannot reach.
prompt: What do you have that no bad luck could take from you?

text: Mankind is born for mutual assistance, anger for mutual ruin: the former loves society, the latter estrangement.
context: Seneca argues that anger goes against human nature, which is built for helping one another.
about:
Novatus had asked Seneca how anger can be calmed, and Seneca answered with a long essay, On Anger. In its first book he asks whether anger is natural to human beings.

His answer is no. What is gentler than a human being in a healthy state, he asks, and what is crueller than anger? Mankind is born to help one another; anger, to ruin one another. One draws us together, the other drives us apart. Seneca's point is that anger is not a part of us to express freely, but a betrayal of our deeper nature, which is made for helping others.
prompt: Whom has your anger pushed away?

text: Cease, then, to seek the wealth you have lost, since in true friends you have found the most precious of all riches.
source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose VIII
context: After losing his wealth and position, Boethius discovers who his real friends are. Philosophy tells him this is the better treasure.
about:
Having lost his wealth, honours and liberty, Boethius imagines Philosophy pointing out, in The Consolation of Philosophy, one good thing his misfortune has done.

Good fortune, she says, hid from him which friends were true and which were false. Bad fortune, leaving, took her own friends with her, and left him his. What would he not have paid to know that when he was prosperous? So stop seeking the wealth you have lost, she says, since in true friends you have found the most precious riches. Hard times are a painful but reliable test of friendship.
prompt: Who has stayed with you through a loss?

text: Nature is content with few things, and with a very little of these.
source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose V
context: Our real needs are small. Most of what we chase is extra, and losing it costs less than we fear.
about:
Can riches ever really belong to us? Boethius imagines Philosophy putting the question to him in The Consolation of Philosophy, as he mourns the wealth he has lost.

If you are content to meet your needs as far as nature asks, she says, you have no need of fortune's gifts. Nature is content with few things, and with very little of those. Force extra on her, and it becomes unpleasant or harmful. Most of what we chase is beyond need. Seeing that doesn't require poverty. It simply makes us freer, because losing the extras costs less than we feared.
prompt: What do you really need, as opposed to want?

text: Why, what amplitude or magnificence has glory when confined to such narrow and petty limits?
source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose VII
context: In prison, Boethius imagines Philosophy as a wise woman visiting him. She points out that even great fame reaches only a small corner of a small planet, and fades within a few generations.
about:
In The Consolation of Philosophy, Boethius imagines Philosophy putting fame in perspective. The earth, she says, is a mere point in the heavens, and only a narrow part of it is lived on.

So what grandeur can glory have, confined to such narrow limits? Even in that small space, many peoples with different languages and customs will never hear of us. Fame looks huge from inside, and tiny from far away. Boethius had been famous and powerful, so this is not sour grapes. It is a sober look at what reputation is really worth, next to what we are.
prompt: How much of your effort goes to being known, and by whom?

text: Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.
context: Epicurus lived with his friends in a community called the Garden. For him, friendship was not an extra in a good life but its foundation.
about:
Epicurus (about 341–270 BCE) taught in a community of friends just outside Athens, known simply as the Garden. His Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings, sum up his teaching; they survive because Diogenes Laertius copied them into his Lives of Eminent Philosophers.

Of everything wisdom provides for a happy life, this one says, by far the most important is friendship. The next doctrine adds that nothing makes us feel safer in our uncertain lives. For Epicurus, friends are not a pleasant extra on top of a good life; they are its foundation. Money, success and comfort all help, but without people to share them with, they protect us less than we think.
prompt: Which friendship deserves more of your attention than it has been getting?

text: Death, therefore, the most awful of evils, is nothing to us, seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not.
context: Epicurus saw the fear of death as poisoning ordinary life. His argument is simple: death is the end of all experience, so there is no one left to suffer it.
about:
Epicurus summed up his ethics in a letter to Menoeceus, which Diogenes Laertius copied into his Lives of Eminent Philosophers. Just before this line, he notes that whatever causes no pain when present causes only groundless pain when we dread it.

Death, then, is nothing to us. When we exist, death is not here; when death is here, we no longer exist. It is a short argument with a large aim: to free us from a fear that spoils ordinary life. Epicurus is not saying that losing others doesn't hurt, or that life is cheap. He is saying that our own death is not something we will ever experience, so dreading it only steals from the life we have.
prompt: If fear of an ending were set aside, how would you spend this day?

text: Let no one be slow to seek wisdom when he is young nor weary in the search thereof when he is grown old. For no age is too early or too late for the health of the soul.
context: The opening of Epicurus' letter summarising his ethics. Philosophy, for him, was a lifelong practice of caring for the soul, never too early and never too late.
about:
These are the opening words of Epicurus' Letter to Menoeceus, a short summary of his ethics. Epicurus taught around 300 BCE in the Garden, his community of friends outside Athens.

No one should be too young to seek wisdom, or too old to keep seeking it, because no age is too early or too late for the health of the soul. Saying the time for philosophy has not come yet, or has passed, is like saying the time for happiness has not come or has gone. Philosophy here is not a subject for experts. It is a way of looking after ourselves, and it is never too late to start.
prompt: What are you still curious to learn about how to live?

text: Nature’s wealth at once has its bounds and is easy to procure; but the wealth of vain fancies recedes to an infinite distance.
context: What we really need is limited and easy to get, but wants born of imagination keep moving further away, however much we gain. Epicurus thought most unhappiness comes from chasing the second kind.
about:
Epicurus taught in the Garden outside Athens around 300 BCE, and his Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings, keep his ideas in their most compact form. Several of them are about what we really need.

What nature needs, says this one, has limits and is easy to get: food, water, shelter, friends. But the wealth of empty fancies recedes to an infinite distance: however much we gain, it moves further away. That is why chasing it never satisfies. The fault lies not in our efforts but in the goal, which has no end. Knowing which needs are real, and which are imagined, is the beginning of contentment.
prompt: Which of your wants keeps receding the closer you get?

text: And even as men choose of food not merely and simply the larger portion, but the more pleasant, so the wise seek to enjoy the time which is most pleasant and not merely that which is longest.
context: Just as we choose food for taste rather than size, a wise person wants the most enjoyable life, not simply the longest one. Quality of time matters more than quantity.
about:
The wise, Epicurus writes in his Letter to Menoeceus, neither scorn life nor fear its end. Then he explains what kind of life they want.

We don't choose food simply by its size, but by how good it is. In the same way, the wise want not the longest life, but the most pleasant. Quality matters more than quantity. It is a calming thought for anyone who worries about time running out. A shorter life, well lived, among friends and free from fear, can be richer than a long one spent anxious or bored.
prompt: How could you make today sweeter rather than longer?

text: We must remember that the future is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours, so that neither must we count upon it as quite certain to come nor despair of it as quite certain not to come.
context: Epicurus warns against two opposite mistakes: planning as if tomorrow were guaranteed, and giving up as if it will never come. A calm mind holds the future lightly.
about:
Epicurus' Letter to Menoeceus is a short summary of his ethics. After discussing death, it turns to the future.

The future, he writes, is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours. So we should neither count on it as certain, nor despair of it as if it will never come. Both mistakes are common. Some people plan as if tomorrow were guaranteed; others give up because nothing is certain. Epicurus suggests a middle path: prepare sensibly, hope reasonably, and keep our happiness rooted in the present we actually have.
prompt: What are you either counting on or despairing of too much?

text: For the end of all our actions is to be free from pain and fear, and, when once we have attained all this, the tempest of the soul is laid.
context: Epicurus' aim was ataraxia, a calm, untroubled mind. Once it is reached, there is nothing more to chase.
about:
Epicurus' Letter to Menoeceus sorts our desires into natural and empty ones, and the natural ones into necessary and not. Then it names what all of this is for: health of body and tranquillity of mind.

The end of all our actions, he says, is to be free from pain and fear, and once we reach that, the storm in the soul dies down. It is a modest-sounding goal, and a deep one. Epicurus didn't promise constant thrills. He promised calm: a body without pain, a mind without fear. Once there, he suggests, we can stop chasing, because there is nothing left that we lack.
prompt: What is stirring a tempest in your soul right now?

text: We do not choose every pleasure whatsoever, but often pass over many pleasures when a greater annoyance ensues from them. And often we consider pains superior to pleasures when submission to the pains for a long time brings us as a consequence a greater pleasure.
context: We don't take every pleasure on offer, because some bring bigger troubles later; and we sometimes accept pain because it leads to greater good. Epicurus was not a pleasure-seeker but a careful weigher of costs.
about:
Epicurus called pleasure the starting point and goal of a happy life, which made him famous, and often misunderstood. His Letter to Menoeceus explains what he meant.

Because pleasure is our natural good, he says, we don't choose every pleasure whatsoever, but often pass over many when greater trouble follows from them. And we often prefer pains, when bearing them brings a greater pleasure later. So pleasure, for Epicurus, needs judgment. A good evening that ruins a week isn't worth it; a hard task that brings lasting ease is. Wise pleasure is a kind of long-term thinking.
prompt: Which pleasure costs you more than it gives?

text: Plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet, when once the pain of want has been removed, while bread and water confer the highest possible pleasure when they are brought to hungry lips.
context: Epicurus' own diet was famously simple. Bread and water, eaten when truly hungry, give the deepest pleasure.
about:
Simple living, for Epicurus, was not a sacrifice but a source of real pleasure. His Letter to Menoeceus explains why.

Plain food, he says, gives as much pleasure as a costly feast once hunger is gone, and bread and water give the highest pleasure to someone who is truly hungry. Getting used to simple fare keeps us healthy, makes us ready for life's demands, lets us enjoy the occasional feast more, and makes us fearless of bad luck. Needing little is a kind of freedom. If we can be happy with bread, fortune has less to take.
prompt: When did a simple thing last give you real pleasure?

text: When we say, then, that pleasure is the end and aim, we do not mean the pleasures of the prodigal or the pleasures of sensuality, as we are understood to do by some through ignorance, prejudice, or wilful misrepresentation. By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul.
context: By 'pleasure' Epicurus did not mean partying or luxury, as his critics claimed, but simply having no pain in the body and no worry in the mind.
about:
Epicurus' critics accused him of teaching a life of indulgence, and his Letter to Menoeceus answers them directly.

When we say pleasure is the goal, he writes, we don't mean the pleasures of the wasteful or of sensuality, as some claim through ignorance or ill will. By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul. It is not drinking-bouts and revelry, he goes on, that make life pleasant, but sober reasoning. Epicurean pleasure is much closer to peace than to partying.
prompt: What would bring a little more peace to your body and soul today?

text: The magnitude of pleasure reaches its limit in the removal of all pain.
context: Epicurus believed pleasure has a ceiling. Once pain and worry are gone, adding more luxury does not make life better, which frees us from chasing endless increase.
about:
Epicurus' Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings that sum up his teaching, put his ideas in their most compact form. The doctrine just before this one says that death is nothing to us.

Here he gives pleasure a ceiling: it reaches its limit when all pain is gone. As long as pleasure lasts uninterrupted, there is no pain of body or of mind. It is an unusual idea. We often imagine happiness as something we can always add to: more comfort, more fun, more things. Epicurus says that once pain and worry are gone, adding more doesn't raise the ceiling. It only changes the decoration.
prompt: Where are you chasing 'more' past the point of enough?

text: It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly.
context: Epicurus is often mistaken for a pleasure-seeker. Here he argues the opposite: a reckless or unfair life brings fear and trouble, so real pleasure needs wisdom and justice.
about:
Epicurus is often imagined as a pleasure-seeker. Epicurus' Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings that sum up his teaching, show a different picture.

You cannot live pleasantly, this one says, without living wisely, well and justly, and you cannot live wisely, well and justly without living pleasantly. Pleasure and goodness, for him, are tied together. A dishonest or reckless life brings fear, conflict and regret, which destroy calm. A good life brings the peace that real pleasure needs. It is a practical argument for virtue: it is the surest route to a pleasant life.
prompt: Which of the three is weakest in your life right now?

text: No pleasure is in itself evil, but the things which produce certain pleasures entail annoyances many times greater than the pleasures themselves.
context: Epicurus judges pleasures by what they lead to. An evening of excess is not evil in itself; the trouble is the cost that follows it.
about:
Among Epicurus' Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings that sum up his teaching, is this careful view of pleasure.

No pleasure is bad in itself, he says, but the things that produce certain pleasures bring troubles many times greater than the pleasures. So he judges pleasures by what they lead to. A glass of wine isn't evil; a habit that wrecks health and friendships is costly. This is neither prudish nor careless. It asks us to look at the whole price of a pleasure, including the part we pay later, before we buy it.
prompt: Which pleasure costs you more afterwards than it gives?

text: The just man enjoys the greatest peace of mind, while the unjust is full of the utmost disquietude.
context: For Epicurus, justice is valuable partly because it lets us sleep at night.
about:
The Principal Doctrines are 40 short sayings that sum up Epicurus' teaching. For him, the aim of life was “health of body and tranquillity of mind”: to be free from pain and fear. This saying applies that test to justice.

Epicurus did not see justice as an absolute law built into the world, but as an agreement between people not to harm one another or be harmed. Whoever breaks that agreement, even in secret, can never be sure they won't be found out, and that fear wears away their calm. So for Epicurus, being just is not only right but wise: it is part of living without fear.
prompt: What on your conscience is disturbing your peace?

text: Of our desires some are natural and necessary; others are natural, but not necessary; others, again, are neither natural nor necessary, but are due to illusory opinion.
context: Epicurus' famous threefold sorting of desires. An ancient commentator gives examples: drink when thirsty; fine food; crowns and statues in one's honour.
about:
This is one of Epicurus' Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings that sum up his teaching. An ancient note in the text gives examples: drink when thirsty is natural and necessary; costly food, natural but not necessary; crowns and statues in one's honour, neither.

Desires come in three kinds: natural and necessary, natural but not necessary, and neither, which come from empty opinion. It is a simple tool for a cluttered life. Hunger and thirst must be met. Fine food is fine to enjoy, but we can live without it. Fame, status and honours are desires we pick up from others, and they never end. Sorting our wants this way shows where peace is easy to find.
prompt: Sort three of your current desires into these three kinds.

text: On this blissful day, which is also the last of my life, I write this to you. My continual sufferings from strangury and dysentery are so great that nothing could augment them; but over against them all I set gladness of mind at the remembrance of our past conversations.
context: Written by Epicurus on the day he died, in great pain. Memories of friendship and conversation outweighed everything else.
about:
Epicurus wrote this letter to Idomeneus on the day he died, in great pain from illness. Diogenes Laertius preserved it in his life of Epicurus, just after Epicurus' will, in which he frees several of his slaves.

My sufferings, he writes, are so great that nothing could add to them. But against them all I set the gladness of my mind at the memory of our past conversations. It is a remarkable letter, calling his last day blissful. Epicurus taught that friendship and good memories can outweigh pain, and here he puts it to the hardest test. This is not denial of the pain. It is choosing, in the middle of it, what to hold on to.
prompt: Which conversations would you want to remember at the end?

text:
The nations wax, the nations wane away;
In a brief space the generations pass,
And like to runners hand the lamp of life
One to another.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: The Roman poet Lucretius pictures the generations as relay runners, each handing the torch of life to the next. No one carries it forever, and no one carries it alone.
about:
Lucretius was a Roman poet who, around 50 BCE, set out the philosophy of Epicurus in a long Latin poem in six books, On the Nature of Things. William Ellery Leonard put it into English verse in 1916.

Here he describes how the world renews itself: tiny particles leave one thing and join another, so some things wither while others flower. Nations grow and fade; generations pass quickly, and like runners in a relay they hand the lamp of life from one to the next. No one carries it forever. The image is humbling, and also warm. Our part is to carry the light well for a while, then pass it on.
prompt: What are you carrying that you hope to hand on?

text:
Why not,
Even like a banqueter, depart the halls,
Laden with life? why not with mind content
Take now, you fool, your unafflicted rest?
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Nature asks someone afraid of dying, 'Why not leave life like a guest leaving a good dinner, full and content?' Lucretius thought a well-lived life can end without bitterness.
about:
In the third book of On the Nature of Things, the Roman poet Lucretius imagines Nature herself speaking to someone who weeps at the thought of death.

If your life has been good, she asks, and its pleasures didn't all run through you like water through a sieve, why not leave like a guest leaving a banquet, full of life, and take your rest with a contented mind? And if it has not been good, why want more of the same? Lucretius isn't mocking grief. He offers the image of a satisfied guest, who leaves the table not cheated, but full.
prompt: What would let you leave today like a guest who has eaten well?

text:
Since from amid the well-spring of delights
Bubbles some drop of bitter to torment
Among the very flowers…
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things IV
context: Even in the middle of our pleasures, a drop of bitterness appears, such as guilt, worry, or the thought that it will end.
about:
Lucretius describes, in the fourth book of On the Nature of Things, a life spent chasing desire: fortunes spent on fine clothes, rich banquets, games of chance, perfumes and garlands.

All in vain, he says: from the very fountain of delights a drop of bitterness bubbles up, even among the flowers. Perhaps the mind is gnawed by regret for wasted years, or by doubt about a lover's word. The point is not that pleasure is bad. It is that pleasures chased without wisdom carry their own poison: worry, guilt, and the knowledge that they won't last. For an Epicurean, calm is the better pleasure.
prompt: What bitterness rises in you even amid good things?

text: You don't control tomorrow, yet you postpone joy.
context: The Vatican Sayings are short maxims of Epicurus and his followers, found in a manuscript in the Vatican Library in 1888. This one asks why we keep delaying happiness for a future we can't count on.
about:
The Vatican Sayings are short sayings of Epicurus and his followers, rediscovered in 1888 in a fourteenth-century manuscript in the Vatican Library. Peter Saint-Andre's translation of 2010 is dedicated to the public domain.

This one begins: we are born once, and cannot be born twice. Then the sharp line: you don't control tomorrow, yet you postpone joy. It ends: life is ruined by putting things off, and each of us dies without truly living. We often wait to enjoy life until the work is done, the house is ready, the year is over. Epicurus asks why we wait for a future we cannot command.
prompt: What joy are you postponing until 'later'?

text: It is not the young man who is most happy, but the old man who has lived beautifully …
context: Youth is often seen as the best time of life. Epicurus disagrees: a life well lived gives a happiness that only time can bring.
about:
Youth is often called the best time of life. One of the Vatican Sayings, short sayings of Epicurus and his followers, found in a medieval manuscript in the Vatican Library, disagrees.

It is not the young who are happiest, but the old who have lived well. The young, at their peak, are tossed about by fortune, it goes on, while the old have settled into age as into a harbour, secure in gratitude for good things they were once unsure of. Youth has energy and chances, but also confusion. A life well lived gives a calm that only the years can bring.
prompt: What would it mean for you to grow old having lived beautifully?

text: He who forgets the good things he had yesterday becomes an old man today.
context: Gratitude for the past keeps us young. Forgetting what was good leaves us feeling poor and tired.
about:
Epicurus valued gratitude for the past as a real source of happiness, and the Vatican Sayings, short sayings of Epicurus and his followers, include this line about memory.

Whoever forgets the good things they had yesterday becomes old today. Good days, friendships and conversations don't vanish when they end; remembering them keeps them working for us. Forgetting them leaves us poorer and wearier than we need be. The saying invites a small habit: to keep yesterday's good things in mind, and let them warm today.
prompt: What good thing from the past few days have you already forgotten?

text: Friendship dances around the world, announcing to each of us that we must awaken to happiness.
context: One of the most joyful lines in ancient philosophy. For Epicurus, friendship is not just pleasant but a wake-up call to live well.
about:
Some of the warmest lines in ancient philosophy are found in the Vatican Sayings, short sayings of Epicurus and his followers. This one is about friendship.

Friendship, it says, dances around the world, announcing to each of us that we must wake up to happiness. The picture is joyful: friendship as a messenger, calling everyone to a good life. For Epicurus, friends were the heart of happiness, and his own community lived together in the Garden. The saying suggests that friendship doesn't only make us happy. It reminds us that happiness is possible, and worth waking up for.
prompt: Which friendship reminds you to be happy?

text: Nature must be persuaded, not forced.
context: Working with our nature, rather than against it, is the gentle Epicurean way, whether in health, habits, or desires.
about:
Epicurus preferred gentle methods to harsh ones, and this saying, from the Vatican Sayings, short sayings of Epicurus and his followers, puts it in a single line.

Nature must be persuaded, not forced. It goes on: we persuade her by meeting our necessary desires, and our natural ones too if they cause no harm, while firmly refusing the harmful ones. We often try to force ourselves: strict diets, harsh routines, willpower alone. Epicurus suggests working with our nature instead, meeting real needs kindly, so that it stops fighting us.
prompt: Where are you forcing yourself when you could persuade?

text: Nothing is enough to one for whom enough is very little.
context: If we think 'enough' is not much, no amount will ever satisfy us. Contentment depends on how we define enough.
about:
Contentment is a theme Epicurus returns to again and again, and this short line from the Vatican Sayings, short sayings of Epicurus and his followers, turns it into a riddle.

Nothing is enough for someone to whom enough seems too little. If we always feel that what we have is small, no amount will satisfy us, because the feeling moves with us. Contentment, then, is less about how much we have than about how we judge it. Epicurus doesn't ask us to own nothing. He asks us to notice when we already have enough, which is often sooner than we think.
prompt: What would 'enough' look like for you?

text: The wise man does not deprecate life nor does he fear the cessation of life.
context: Epicurus' balanced view of mortality: neither complaining about life nor dreading its end.
about:
People sometimes run from death as the worst of evils, Epicurus writes in his Letter to Menoeceus, and sometimes wish for it as a rest from life's troubles.

The wise, he says, do neither: they don't complain about life, and don't fear its end. Life is no burden to them, and its ending is not an evil. It is a balanced view that avoids two opposite fears. Some people dread dying; others feel life is not worth it. Epicurus suggests a third way: to enjoy the life we have, without clinging to it or wishing it away.
prompt: Do you lean more toward complaining about life or fearing its end?

text: Natural justice is a contract of expediency, to prevent one man from harming or being harmed by another.
context: For Epicurus, justice is not a law from the heavens but an agreement people make so they can live together without harming one another.
about:
Epicurus' Principal Doctrines end with a group of sayings on justice. The one before this warns that some natural desires, pursued with great effort, come only from empty opinion.

Natural justice, this one says, is an agreement about what is useful: a pact that we will neither harm one another nor be harmed. Justice, for Epicurus, grows from a practical need: living together safely. That makes it something we create and keep together. It also shows why breaking it is foolish. Whoever harms others has left the very pact that protects them too.
prompt: What unwritten agreements make your community work?

text: There never was an absolute justice, but only a convention made in mutual intercourse, in whatever region, from time to time, providing against the infliction or suffering of harm.
context: Epicurus says justice is not a law written into nature but an agreement people make not to harm each other. Its rules change with time and place; its purpose stays the same.
about:
Among the doctrines on justice that close Epicurus' Principal Doctrines, the one just before this notes that animals and tribes unable to agree not to harm each other have neither justice nor injustice.

There never was an absolute justice, Epicurus says, only an agreement made between people, in one place or another, at one time or another, against doing or suffering harm. Justice, for him, is not one fixed rule for all times, but something people work out together. That is why laws differ between places and change over time. What they share is their purpose: keeping people safe from harm.
prompt: Which of today's rules do you think will look wrong in a hundred years?

text: The flesh assumes the limits of pleasure to be infinite, and only infinite time would satisfy it.
context: Epicurus says the body never decides on its own that it has had enough; it always wants more. Only the mind can see that pleasure has a natural limit, and stop there.
about:
Epicurus' Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings that sum up his teaching, include several on the limits of pleasure. The one before this says that, measured by reason, endless time holds no more pleasure than limited time.

The flesh, he says, assumes pleasure has no limits, and only infinite time would satisfy it. But the mind, understanding the body's limits and setting aside fears of the future, makes a complete life possible, with no need for infinite time. The body always wants more. Only reflection can see that enough is enough, and that a full life doesn't have to be endless.
prompt: Which appetite in your life never seems satisfied?

text: Nothing from nothing ever yet was born.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things I
context: Lucretius' first principle: everything comes from something. There is no magic in nature, only causes we have not yet understood.
about:
Early in On the Nature of Things, the Roman poet Lucretius sets out the first principle of his Epicurean view of the world. Only an understanding of nature, he says, can drive away the darkness of fear.

Nothing comes from nothing: everything has causes, even when we can't see them. People are afraid, he goes on, because they see so much in land and sky whose causes they don't understand. Once we grasp that nothing arises from nothing, we can start looking for the real causes. The line holds the root of a scientific attitude: patient curiosity about how things work, instead of fear of the unknown.
prompt: What in your life seems to come from nowhere, but has a cause?

text: Nothing returns to naught; but all return / At their collapse to primal forms of stuff.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things I
context: Things don't vanish when they end; they break down into the material that will form new things. It is an early version of a modern scientific idea.
about:
Lucretius pairs his first principle, that nothing comes from nothing, with its partner in the first book of On the Nature of Things: nothing goes back to nothing.
