text: Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.
source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, Book II, Part III, Section III
context: Hume's most provocative line. Reason can tell us how to get what we want, but it cannot make us want anything. Our goals come from feeling.
about:
David Hume, the Scottish philosopher, wrote A Treatise of Human Nature (1739) as a young man. In this part he argues against the old picture of a battle between reason and passion.

Reason, he says, is and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never claim any office other than to serve and obey them. He knows it sounds extraordinary. His point is that reason alone never moves us to act. It can tell us how to get what we want, or what is true, but the wanting comes from feeling. We are moved by what we care about, and reason helps us pursue it well.
prompt: Which of your 'rational' decisions was really driven by a feeling?

text: Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.
source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V
context: We expect the sun to rise because it always has, not because we have proven it will. Most of what we 'know' about the future rests on habit.
about:
In An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), David Hume asks why we expect the future to resemble the past. Reason alone, he argues, cannot prove that it will.

Custom, then, is the great guide of human life. It is habit, built from experience, that makes us expect the sun to rise and bread to nourish. Without it we would know nothing beyond what is right in front of our senses. It is a humbling idea about how we know things. Much of what we take as certain rests on habit, not proof. That doesn't make it wrong, but it should keep us open.
prompt: Which of your expectations rests only on habit?

text: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.
source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X
context: From Hume's essay on miracles, but the rule works everywhere: strong evidence deserves strong belief, and weak evidence deserves doubt.
about:
David Hume's Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) has a famous section on miracles. It opens by noting that our evidence about the world comes in all degrees, from near certainty to the faintest probability.

A wise person, therefore, proportions their belief to the evidence. Where experience has never failed, they expect the result with full confidence; where it varies, they weigh the cases on each side. It is a simple rule, and the basis of careful thinking. Strong claims need strong evidence. Beliefs held more firmly than the evidence allows are a common source of error.
prompt: What do you believe more strongly than your evidence allows?

text: Be a philosopher; but, amidst all your philosophy, be still a man.
source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I
context: Hume imagines Nature giving this advice. Think deeply, she says, but don't let thinking cut you off from action, company, and ordinary life.
about:
In the first section of his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (first published in 1748), David Hume imagines Nature herself giving advice to anyone tempted by deep philosophy.

Indulge your passion for science, she says, but let it be human; she warns that abstract research will be punished with melancholy, endless uncertainty and a cold reception. Be a philosopher, she says; but, amid all your philosophy, still be a human being. It is good advice from a philosopher. Thinking deeply is worthwhile, but it should not cut us off from ordinary life, friendship, action and society.
prompt: Where has thinking replaced living for you lately?

text: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
source: David Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste'
context: Hume states this common view, then asks whether some judgements of taste are still better than others. He concludes they are: experience and practice train the eye.
about:
David Hume's essay Of the Standard of Taste (1757) asks whether there is any right answer in matters of beauty. He first sets out the view that judgments of taste are simply feelings.

Beauty, on this view, is no quality in things themselves; it exists only in the mind that sees them, and each mind perceives a different beauty. One person may find ugliness where another finds beauty. Hume takes this seriously, but goes on to argue that some judges of taste are better than others, through practice and good sense. Beauty may live in the eye, but eyes can be trained.
prompt: What did you once dislike that you have learned to see as beautiful?

text: The mind must be strong that resolutely forms its own principles; for a kind of intellectual cowardice prevails which makes many men shrink from the task, or only do it by halves.
source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, ch. 1
context: It takes a strong mind to form your own principles, and most people are too cowardly to try, or only half try. Wollstonecraft (1759–1797) wanted women to have the education to do it.
about:
Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argues that women deserve the same education and the same use of reason as men. Early on, she notes that most people use reason to justify prejudices they picked up without knowing how.

The mind must be strong, she says, that firmly forms its own principles, for a kind of intellectual cowardice makes many shrink from the task, or do it by halves. It takes courage to think things through for ourselves. It is easier to borrow our views, and then defend them. Wollstonecraft asks for the harder work, and believed women as well as men were capable of it.
prompt: Which of your principles did you form yourself, and which did you inherit?

text: Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience; but, as blind obedience is ever sought for by power, tyrants and sensualists are in the right when they endeavour to keep women in the dark, because the former only want slaves, and the latter a play-thing.
source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, ch. 2
context: Educate women's minds and they will stop obeying blindly; that is exactly why tyrants keep them ignorant. Written in 1792, it is one of the founding texts of feminism.
about:
Mary Wollstonecraft argues in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) that society has kept women ignorant on purpose, flattering them while denying them education.

Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, she says, and there will be an end to blind obedience. But since power always seeks blind obedience, tyrants and sensualists are right, from their point of view, to keep women in the dark. It is a sharp argument. Ignorance is not an accident; it serves those in power. Education, by contrast, is the first step to freedom, for anyone denied it.
prompt: Where might someone benefit from you not asking questions?

text: Good sense is, of all things among men, the most equally distributed; for every one thinks himself so abundantly provided with it, that those even who are the most difficult to satisfy in everything else, do not usually desire a larger measure of this quality than they already possess.
source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part I
context: The witty first line of Descartes' Discourse (1637). Everyone believes they have plenty of good sense, which is exactly why so few question their own judgment.
about:
The French philosopher René Descartes opens his Discourse on Method, translated by John Veitch, with this gently ironic line.

Good sense is the most evenly shared thing in the world, he says, for everyone thinks they have so much of it that even those hardest to please in everything else rarely want more. The joke has a serious point. If we all have reason, the difference between us lies not in how clever we are, but in how well we use it. That is why Descartes thought method mattered so much: good sense needs good direction.
prompt: Where might your good sense be less reliable than you think?

text: I think, therefore I am.
source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part IV
context: After doubting everything he could, Descartes found one thing he couldn't doubt: that he was thinking. Modern philosophy of mind starts here.
about:
In his Discourse on Method, René Descartes decided to doubt everything he could, even whether his waking life was any more real than a dream, to find something certain.

But while he was thinking that everything was false, he noticed that he, the one thinking, had to be something. I think, therefore I am: this truth was so certain that no doubt could shake it. He made it the first principle of his philosophy. It is one of the most famous sentences ever written. Whatever else we doubt, the fact that we are doubting shows that we exist.
prompt: What is the one thing about yourself you cannot doubt?

text: …to endeavor always to conquer myself rather than fortune, and change my desires rather than the order of the world …
source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part III
context: One of Descartes' personal rules for living, close to Stoic advice: work on what you can change, which is yourself.
about:
While rebuilding his beliefs from scratch, René Descartes gave himself a few rules to live by, set out in his Discourse on Method. This is the third.

Try always to conquer yourself rather than fortune, he writes, and to change your desires rather than the order of the world. Nothing, he adds, is fully in our power except our own thoughts. It is close to the Stoics, and very practical. We often exhaust ourselves trying to change what we can't. Adjusting what we want, where we can't change what is, brings a calmer and more effective life.
prompt: Which desire could you change instead of trying to change the world?

text: …the perusal of all excellent books is, as it were, to interview with the noblest men of past ages …
source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part I
context: Reading great books is a conversation with the best minds of the past, a little like what this app tries to offer.
about:
Looking back on his schooling in his Discourse on Method, René Descartes lists what each subject offered him: languages, fables, history and books.

Reading all the excellent books, he says, is like a conversation with the noblest people of past ages who wrote them, and a prepared conversation, in which they show us only their best thoughts. It is a lovely picture of reading. Through books we can meet minds long gone, at their best. Descartes went on to say he had to think for himself as well. But the conversation is a good place to start.
prompt: Which writer from the past would you most like to talk with?

text: How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it, except the pleasure of seeing it.
source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I
context: Better known for economics, Adam Smith (1723–1790) began his career with this book on sympathy. Even selfish people, he says, are moved by others' joy and pain.
about:
Adam Smith opens The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), his book on how we judge feelings and actions, with this observation on sympathy.

However selfish people may be, he says, there are clearly some principles in our nature that make us care about the fortunes of others, and make their happiness necessary to us, though we gain nothing from it but the pleasure of seeing it. We wince at another's pain and smile at their joy. For Smith, this fellow-feeling is the root of our moral life. We are not only selfish creatures, but connected ones.
prompt: Whose happiness matters to you, though you gain nothing from it?

text: Hatred and anger are the greatest poison to the happiness of a good mind.
source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I
context: Smith notes that hostile feelings hurt the one who carries them first.
about:
The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) is Adam Smith's book about how we judge feelings, our own and other people's. This line comes from a chapter on what he calls “the unsocial passions”: hatred and resentment.

His point is that these feelings harm the person who carries them, not only their target. Anger is harsh and restless inside us. It destroys the calm that happiness needs, a calm Smith thinks is best kept by gratitude and love. He does not say we should never feel anger, only that it must be brought far lower than our untrained nature would raise it. Holding on to resentment, then, mostly hurts the one who holds it.
prompt: Which resentment are you carrying that hurts you more than anyone else?

text: The sentiment of love is, in itself, agreeable to the person who feels it.
source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I
context: The opposite of the previous thought: kindness and affection make the giver happier, whatever they get back.
about:
Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) contrasts the harsh feelings of hatred and resentment with the gentler ones of love and kindness, which he calls the social passions.

The feeling of love, he says, is pleasant in itself to the person who feels it. It soothes and calms the heart, seems to help the body's vital motions, and supports good health. Smith's point is that kindness rewards the kind. It is not only good for those who receive it. Feeling warmth towards others makes our own lives easier and calmer, while hatred tears at us.
prompt: When did loving someone make you feel good, regardless of the result?

text: …every wise man will endeavour to place his happiness on such objects chiefly as depend upon himself …
source: David Hume, 'Of the Delicacy of Taste and Passion'
context: Hume agrees with the Stoics here: the more our happiness depends on things outside our control, the more fragile it is.
about:
David Hume's essay Of the Delicacy of Taste and Passion (1741) compares two kinds of sensitivity: being easily shaken by life's events, and being keenly alive to beauty in books and art.

The good and bad accidents of life, he says, are little in our control, but we choose what books we read, what pleasures we enjoy and what company we keep. Philosophers have tried to make happiness wholly independent of outside things, which is impossible. But a wise person will try to place their happiness mainly on things that depend on themselves. Cultivating taste is one of the best ways to do it.
prompt: How much of your happiness depends on things you can't control?

text: …nothing is so improving to the temper as the study of the beauties, either of poetry, eloquence, music, or painting.
source: David Hume, 'Of the Delicacy of Taste and Passion'
context: Hume believed that time spent with art calms and refines us, making us less ruled by passing passions.
about:
In his essay Of the Delicacy of Taste and Passion (1741), David Hume argues that a refined taste in art makes us less prone to violent emotions, and more open to tender ones.

Nothing improves the temper so much, he says, as studying the beauties of poetry, eloquence, music or painting. They give an elegance of feeling, soft and tender, that draws the mind away from the rush of business, encourages reflection and inclines us to calm. It is a gentle case for the arts. Time spent with a good poem or piece of music is not wasted; it shapes who we are.
prompt: Which art calms you down when you need it?

text: …a delicacy of taste is favourable to love and friendship, by confining our choice to few people …
source: David Hume, 'Of the Delicacy of Taste and Passion'
context: People with refined taste have fewer friends, Hume says, but deeper ones.
about:
David Hume's essay Of the Delicacy of Taste and Passion (1741) gives two reasons why a fine taste in the arts is good for us. The first is that it softens the temper. This is the second.

A delicate taste, he says, is favourable to love and friendship, because it narrows our choice to a few people, and makes us indifferent to the company of most. Someone with refined taste looks for deeper qualities in others, and finds them in fewer people. The result is fewer friendships, but closer ones. It is a reminder that depth of friendship matters more than number.
prompt: Do you have many friends or a few close ones, and which do you want?

text: Under the guidance of reason we should pursue the greater of two goods and the lesser of two evils.
source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Proposition LXV
context: A simple rule, hard to follow when emotions pull us toward the smaller, nearer good.
about:
Spinoza's Ethics argues that something good which stops us from enjoying a greater good is, in fact, an evil, and the reverse for lesser evils.

Under the guidance of reason, he concludes, we should pursue the greater of two goods and the lesser of two evils. It sounds obvious. Yet emotions often push us the other way: towards the smaller good that is nearer, or away from a small pain that would spare us a larger one later. Reason's job, for Spinoza, is to weigh things by their real size, not by how close or vivid they feel.
prompt: Where are you choosing a smaller good because it is closer?

text: The man, who is guided by reason, does not obey through fear.
source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Proposition LXXIII
context: For Spinoza, free people do the right thing because they understand why, not because they are afraid of punishment.
about:
Near the end of the fourth part of his Ethics, Baruch Spinoza argues that a person guided by reason is freer living under shared laws in a state than alone and independent.

The person guided by reason, he says in the proof, does not obey through fear. They keep the laws because they understand why common rules help everyone, including themselves, to live well. It is a subtle idea of freedom. Obeying from fear is a kind of slavery. Following good rules because we see their point is a choice we make for ourselves.
prompt: Which rules do you follow from understanding, and which from fear?

text: …dependence of body naturally produces dependence of mind …
source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
context: Wollstonecraft argued that women kept physically and financially dependent would also be kept from thinking for themselves.
about:
Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) criticises the way girls of her time were raised to be delicate and weak, and their health neglected.

The bad effects of ignoring health in childhood and youth, she says, go further than people think: dependence of body naturally produces dependence of mind. Someone always ill, or kept weak, can hardly think or act freely. It is an argument that body and mind are linked, and that strength in one supports strength in the other. Freedom, for Wollstonecraft, needs health as well as education.
prompt: Where does depending on someone limit how freely you think?

text: …as sound politics diffuse liberty, mankind, including woman, will become more wise and virtuous.
source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
context: Her hopeful belief: freedom makes people better, and that must include women.
about:
Women, Mary Wollstonecraft argues in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), have only seemed inferior because they have always been held down. Brute force has governed the world so far, and the science of politics is still in its infancy.

Her hopeful conclusion: as sound politics spread liberty, humanity, including women, will become wiser and more virtuous. Freedom, for her, is not a reward for being good; it is what lets people become good. It was a radical claim in 1792. Her belief that liberty and education improve everyone, women included, has shaped much of what came after.
prompt: What freedom made you a better person?

text: We are happy only through tastes or passions that are satisfied.
source: Émilie du Châtelet, Discourse on Happiness
context: Émilie du Châtelet (1706–1749), physicist and mathematician, translated Newton into French. In this essay she defends passions as necessary to happiness, against the Stoic ideal of having none.
about:
Émilie du Châtelet (1706–1749) was a French mathematician and thinker. Her Discourse on Happiness was published only after her death, in 1779. Here she argues against moralists who tell us to suppress our passions in order to be happy.

We are happy only through tastes or passions that are satisfied, she says (our translation). Since we don't always have passions, we must be content with tastes. It is a frank and warm view. Happiness doesn't come from wanting nothing, but from having things we love: interests, pleasures, people. Du Châtelet's advice is not to kill our desires, but to choose good ones, and feed them.
prompt: Which passion makes your life feel alive?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: …the love of study is, of all the passions, the one that contributes most to our happiness.
source: Émilie du Châtelet, Discourse on Happiness
context: Du Châtelet found her deepest joy in learning. Unlike love or fame, she says, study depends on no one but ourselves.
about:
Émilie du Châtelet (1706–1749), a French mathematician, wrote her Discourse on Happiness near the end of her life; it was published in 1779. The less our happiness depends on others, she argues, the easier it is to be happy.

For that reason, the love of study is, of all passions, the one that does most for our happiness (our translation). It depends only on us. She adds that it holds a love of glory too, which for half the world, women, is the only kind open to them, though education denies them the means. It is a personal statement from a woman who did serious science in her time. Learning gave her a joy no one could take.
prompt: What are you learning right now just for the joy of it?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Another source of happiness is to be free from prejudice.
source: Émilie du Châtelet, Discourse on Happiness
context: For du Châtelet, prejudices are borrowed opinions that weigh us down. Thinking for ourselves is part of being happy.
about:
In her Discourse on Happiness, published in 1779, thirty years after her death, the French mathematician Émilie du Châtelet lists the conditions for being happy.

Another source of happiness, she says, is to be free from prejudice (our translation), and it is up to us to get rid of it. We all have enough sense to examine what we are told to believe, and in her century, she adds, there is no lack of help for learning. It is a confident, Enlightenment idea. Thinking for ourselves isn't only a duty; it makes life lighter, freer and happier.
prompt: Which prejudice have you dropped, and how did it feel?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it.
context: Mill's definition of liberty: living your own way, as long as you don't stop others from living theirs.
about:
In the first chapter of On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill lists the freedoms a free society must protect: of thought and speech, of choosing our own way of life, and of joining with others for any purpose that harms no one.

The only freedom worth the name, he says, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, as long as we don't deprive others of theirs or block their efforts to get it. Each person is the proper guardian of their own health, body and mind. It is a simple, powerful principle. We may disagree with how others live, but that alone is not a reason to stop them.
prompt: Where are you pursuing someone else's idea of your good, instead of your own?

text: Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.
context: Mill draws a line around the individual: where our choices affect only ourselves, they are ours alone to make. This idea shaped modern thinking about personal freedom.
about:
John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859) sets out one principle for when society may interfere with a person: only to prevent harm to others.

The only part of our conduct for which we answer to society, he says, is the part that concerns others. In what concerns only ourselves, our independence is, by right, absolute. Over themselves, over their own body and mind, the individual is sovereign. Mill adds that this applies to adults, not children. It is the heart of his case for liberty: our own life is ours to run.
prompt: Which decision about yourself are you letting others make?

text: All the grand sources, in short, of human suffering are in a great degree, many of them almost entirely, conquerable by human care and effort.
context: Mill's hope: poverty, disease and much misfortune are not fate. Most suffering can be reduced by human effort, slowly but surely.
about:
Mill, defending the idea that we should aim at the greatest happiness in Utilitarianism (1863), considers the great causes of human misery: poverty, disease, the loss of those we love, bad luck.

All the great sources of human suffering, he says, are to a large degree, many almost entirely, conquerable by human care and effort. Their removal is grievously slow, and will take many generations. But every mind wise and generous enough to help will find noble enjoyment in the struggle. It is a hopeful, active view. Much suffering is not fate. It is a problem we can work on, together.
prompt: What suffering near you could your care and effort reduce?

text: The dictum that truth always triumphs over persecution, is one of those pleasant falsehoods which men repeat after one another till they pass into commonplaces, but which all experience refutes.
context: It is comforting to believe that truth always wins in the end. Mill points out that history disagrees: truths have been crushed many times, so they need defending.
about:
In On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill takes on a comforting argument for silencing unpopular views: that the truth will win out anyway.

The saying that truth always triumphs over persecution, he says, is one of those pleasant falsehoods people repeat until it becomes a commonplace, but all experience refutes it. History is full of truths put down by persecution, sometimes for centuries. It is a sobering reminder. Truth doesn't protect itself. It needs people willing to speak it, and societies willing to let them.
prompt: Which truth could use your defending?

text: All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility.
context: Mill's point is sharp: to shut down a discussion is to claim we cannot be wrong. Since no one is infallible, silencing others always risks silencing the truth.
about:
Those who want to suppress an opinion, John Stuart Mill writes in On Liberty (1859), of course deny that it is true. But they are not infallible.

To refuse to hear an opinion because we are sure it is false, he says, is to treat our certainty as absolute certainty. All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility. It is a sharp argument, because it turns the censor's confidence against them. No one is beyond error. Letting others speak is not only fair to them; it protects us from our own mistakes.
prompt: Which conversation have you shut down because you were sure?

text: Eccentricity has always abounded when and where strength of character has abounded; and the amount of eccentricity in a society has generally been proportional to the amount of genius, mental vigour, and moral courage which it contained.
context: Mill sees a society's tolerance of odd and unusual people as a sign of its strength. Where nobody dares to be different, new ideas and courage grow rare.
about:
In On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill worries about what he calls the tyranny of opinion: the pressure to fit in. In such a time, he says, simply refusing to bow to custom is itself a service.

Eccentricity has always abounded where strength of character has abounded, and the amount of eccentricity in a society has generally matched its genius, mental vigour and moral courage. That so few now dare to be eccentric, he adds, is the chief danger of the time. It is a defence of the odd and the different. Societies need people willing to stand apart.
prompt: Where could you allow yourself to be a little more eccentric?

text: Even in what people do for pleasure, conformity is the first thing thought of; they live in crowds; they exercise choice only among things commonly done: peculiarity of taste, eccentricity of conduct, are shunned equally with crimes: until by dint of not following their own nature, they have no nature to follow.
context: Mill warns that people who always do what others do, even in their free time, slowly lose their own tastes. In the end they have no nature of their own left to follow.
about:
John Stuart Mill describes, in On Liberty (1859), how people of his day asked themselves what suits their position, or what people above them usually do, not what they themselves would like.

Even in what people do for pleasure, he says, conformity is the first thing thought of: they live in crowds and choose only among things commonly done. Their minds are bowed to the yoke. It still sounds familiar. Much of what we enjoy is what everyone else enjoys. Mill asks whether we have ever asked ourselves what we would choose, if no one were watching.
prompt: What would you enjoy if nobody else's taste mattered?

text: The habit of analysis has a tendency to wear away the feelings: as indeed it has, when no other mental habit is cultivated, and the analysing spirit remains without its natural complements and correctives.
context: Mill was trained from childhood to analyse everything. At twenty he found that constant analysis had dried up his feelings, and he learned to balance it with poetry and emotion.
about:
John Stuart Mill was raised by his father on a strict diet of logic and analysis. In his Autobiography (1873), looking back on a depression in his twenties, he asks what that training had cost him.

The habit of analysis, he concluded, tends to wear away the feelings, when no other habit of mind is cultivated alongside it. Picking everything apart can leave us able to explain life but unable to enjoy it. Mill's cure came partly through poetry, which taught him to feel again. Clear thinking matters, but it works best alongside a cultivated heart.
prompt: What are you over-analysing that might simply need feeling?

text: The internal sanction of duty, whatever our standard of duty may be, is one and the same—a feeling in our own mind; a pain, more or less intense, attendant on violation of duty.
context: Mill says that beyond laws and reputation, our strongest guard is conscience: the inner discomfort we feel when we fall short of what we believe is right.
about:
In Utilitarianism (1863), John Stuart Mill asks what makes people keep moral rules. Outward pressures, such as praise, blame and the law, are part of it, but not the deepest part.

The inner force of duty, he says, whatever our standard of duty may be, is always the same: a feeling in our own mind, a pain, more or less intense, that comes with breaking it. We call it conscience. However morality is defined, it lives in us as this feeling. That is why a well-raised conscience matters so much. Rules work best when we feel them from the inside.
prompt: Which duty, when you neglect it, gives you that small inner pain?

text: Has not every even moderately honourable man sometimes found that, where by an otherwise inoffensive lie he might either have withdrawn himself from an unpleasant business, or even have procured some advantages for a loved and well-deserving friend, he has avoided it solely lest he should despise himself secretly in his own eyes?
context: Kant observes that sometimes the only thing stopping a convenient lie is knowing we could not respect ourselves afterwards. Self-respect, for him, is a real moral force.
about:
In the Critique of Practical Reason, Immanuel Kant argues that the idea of our own dignity as moral beings inspires respect, and humbles our self-conceit. Ordinary people feel it too, he says, and gives an example.

Hasn't every moderately honourable person sometimes found that a harmless lie could have got them out of an unpleasant situation, or helped a friend, and yet they refused, simply so as not to despise themselves in secret? Kant's point is that this inner respect for ourselves can be stronger than any gain. Keeping faith with who we want to be is a powerful motive, even when no one would ever know.
prompt: When did self-respect stop you from taking an easy way out?

text: To secure one's own happiness is a duty, at least indirectly; for discontent with one's condition, under a pressure of many anxieties and amidst unsatisfied wants, might easily become a great temptation to transgression of duty.
context: Kant is often seen as stern, but here he defends looking after our own happiness. Constant worry and unmet needs, he says, make it harder to act well.
about:
Kant's Groundwork is famous for its strictness: actions have moral worth, he argues, only when done from duty, not just from inclination. Here he adds something surprising.

Securing our own happiness is a duty, at least indirectly, he says, because discontent, amid many worries and unmet needs, can easily become a great temptation to do wrong. It is a human touch in a demanding book. Looking after ourselves is not selfish. A person crushed by misery finds it harder to act well. Caring for our own wellbeing is part of being able to do right.
prompt: How is looking after yourself part of doing right?

text: Intelligence, wit, judgement, and the other talents of the mind, however they may be named, or courage, resolution, perseverance, as qualities of temperament, are undoubtedly good and desirable in many respects; but these gifts of nature may also become extremely bad and mischievous if the will which is to make use of them, and which, therefore, constitutes what is called character, is not good.
context: Kant says talents like intelligence and courage are good, but they can serve bad ends. What makes them good or dangerous is the will behind them: our character.
about:
Right after the opening line of his Groundwork, that nothing is good without qualification except a good will, Immanuel Kant explains what he means.

Intelligence, wit, judgment and other talents, or courage, resolution and perseverance, are good and desirable in many ways, he says. But they can also become extremely bad and harmful if the will that uses them is not good. A brave villain is more dangerous than a timid one. Talents are tools. What makes them good or bad is the will that directs them, which is why Kant puts the good will first.
prompt: Which of your gifts depends on good will to stay good?

text: Ready must you be to burn yourself in your own flame; how could you become new if you have not first become ashes!
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Way of the Creating One'
context: Zarathustra speaks to someone setting out on their own path. Real renewal asks us to let an old self burn away.
about:
Friedrich Nietzsche, the German philosopher, wrote Thus Spake Zarathustra as a kind of prose poem, in which the prophet Zarathustra speaks to his followers. In the chapter on the way of the creating one, he warns that the hardest enemy we meet on our own path is ourselves.

Be ready, he says, to burn yourself in your own flame: how could you become new if you have not first become ashes? It is a dramatic image of change. Real growth can feel like a kind of destruction: old habits, beliefs and versions of ourselves have to burn away. Nietzsche doesn't make this sound easy. He makes it sound necessary, if we want to create something new in ourselves.
prompt: What old version of yourself might need to become ashes?

text: One must still have chaos in one, to give birth to a dancing star.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue 5
context: Zarathustra warns against a life made so comfortable and orderly that nothing new can arise from it. Inner turmoil can be the raw material of creation.
about:
In the prologue of Friedrich Nietzsche's Thus Spake Zarathustra, the prophet Zarathustra comes down from his mountain to speak to the people in a market square. He warns of a time when humans will stop longing for anything beyond themselves.

One must still have chaos in oneself, he says, to give birth to a dancing star. And you still have chaos in you. It is one of Nietzsche's most loved lines. Inner turmoil, restlessness and contradiction are not only problems to fix. They can be the raw material of creativity. A mind with no chaos left may be calm, but it may also have stopped growing.
prompt: What unsettled part of you might be the beginning of something?

text: In one’s friend one shall have one’s best enemy. You shall be closest to him with your heart when you withstand him.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Friend'
context: For Nietzsche, a true friend challenges us rather than flatters us, and we are closest to them when we push back.
about:
In the chapter of Thus Spake Zarathustra on friendship, Nietzsche's Zarathustra says that true respect sometimes asks a friend to be our enemy: to challenge us, not just to agree.

In your friend, he says, you should have your best enemy, and you should be closest to them in heart when you stand against them. It is an unusual view of friendship. We often think good friends always support us. Nietzsche suggests the deepest friends also resist us: they tell us the truth, push back, and refuse to flatter. Such friction, offered with love, makes both people stronger.
prompt: Which friend challenges you, and do you challenge them?

text: He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster. And if you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into you.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 146
context: Nietzsche warns anyone fighting something they despise: the struggle can slowly reshape us into what we oppose. The longer we stare at darkness, the more it gets into us.
about:
Beyond Good and Evil, by the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, is made largely of short, sharp aphorisms, here in Helen Zimmern's translation. Number 146 is among the most quoted.

Whoever fights monsters should take care not to become one in the process. And if you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes back into you. The warning fits many struggles. Fighting cruelty can make us cruel; studying darkness can darken us. Nietzsche isn't telling us not to fight. He is telling us to watch what the fight is doing to us.
prompt: What are you fighting against, and are you starting to resemble it?

text: Amor fati: let that henceforth be my love! I do not want to wage war with the ugly. I do not want to accuse, I do not want even to accuse the accusers. Looking aside, let that be my sole negation! And all in all, to sum up: I wish to be at any time hereafter only a yea-sayer!
context: Nietzsche resolves to love his fate, everything that happens, including the ugly parts, and to stop complaining and blaming. 'Amor fati' is Latin for 'love of fate'.
about:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote The Joyful Wisdom (also known as The Gay Science) in short numbered sections. Section 276 is a New Year's wish: a thought he hopes will sweeten all his future life.

Amor fati, love of fate: let that be my love from now on, he writes. I don't want to wage war on what is ugly; I don't want to accuse, not even the accusers. Looking away will be my only no. It is a striking resolution. Instead of resisting what life brings, Nietzsche wants to see what is necessary in things as beautiful. Loving our fate means saying yes to life, including its hard parts.
prompt: What in your life could you say 'yes' to, rather than resist?

text: You shall become what you are.
context: Nietzsche borrowed this line from the Greek poet Pindar and made it his motto. Growing up, for him, means discovering and becoming who we already are, not copying others.
about:
Friedrich Nietzsche's Joyful Wisdom contains a run of short questions and answers, a kind of personal creed. Section 270 asks: what does your conscience say?

Its answer: you shall become what you are. It is a paradox: how can we become what we already are? Nietzsche means that each of us has a self waiting to be realised, which we can neglect or grow into. Conscience, here, is not a voice of rules from outside. It is the call to become fully ourselves. The work of a life is to find out who that is, and to live it.
prompt: Who are you becoming, and is it who you are?

text: Flee, my friend, into your solitude! I see you deafened with the noise of the great men, and stung all over with the stings of the little ones.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Flies in the Market-place'
context: Nietzsche's prophet Zarathustra describes the market-place as full of noise, fame, and petty attacks. He urges his friend to step away and recover himself in solitude.
about:
Zarathustra opens this chapter of Friedrich Nietzsche's Thus Spake Zarathustra by urging his friend to flee the market place: the world of noise, fame and petty quarrels.

Flee into your solitude, he says. I see you deafened by the noise of the great and stung all over by the little ones. Forest and rock know how to be silent with you. It is a call that sounds even more urgent today. Constant noise, opinions and small attacks can wear us down without our noticing. Solitude, for Nietzsche, is not running away. It is where we recover our own voice.
prompt: Which noise could you step away from today?

text: “I did that,” says my memory. “I could not have done that,” says my pride, and remains inexorable. Eventually—the memory yields.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 68
context: In two lines, Nietzsche shows how self-deception works. When memory and pride disagree about something we did, pride usually wins, and we come to believe our own story.
about:
Friedrich Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil is a book of short, sharp aphorisms. This one, number 68, is a tiny drama in three lines.

I did that, says my memory. I could not have done that, says my pride, and remains unshakeable. In the end, memory gives way. It is a precise and uncomfortable observation. When we've done something we're ashamed of, our pride often rewrites the story until we half believe it. Nietzsche shows how easily we deceive ourselves. Knowing this habit is the first step to resisting it.
prompt: What has your pride persuaded your memory to forget?

text: Above all, don’t lie to yourself. The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 2
context: Advice from the elder Zosima to Fyodor Karamazov, a man who constantly plays the fool. Self-deception starts small, but over time it blinds us to the truth in ourselves and around us, and with it goes our respect for both.
about:
Early in Fyodor Dostoevsky's novel The Brothers Karamazov, the family visits the wise old monk Zossima. The father, a shameless buffoon, asks what he must do, and Zossima tells him: above all, don't lie.

Above all, don't lie to yourself. Whoever lies to themselves and listens to their own lie, he says, comes to a point where they can't tell the truth within them or around them, and so lose all respect for themselves and others. It is a deep diagnosis. Small lies to ourselves grow into a fog. Honesty with ourselves is the ground of every other honesty.
prompt: What small lie have you been telling yourself?

text: “What is hell?” I maintain that it is the suffering of being unable to love.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 3
context: From the teachings of the elder Zosima, gathered after his death. Hell is not a place but a condition: the loss of the capacity to love.
about:
Book VI of Fyodor Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov gathers the teachings of the elder Zossima, written down after his death by the young Alyosha. One of them asks what hell is.

I maintain, Zossima says, that it is the suffering of being unable to love. It is a startling answer. Not flames or punishment, but a closed heart. The worst state a person can reach, in this view, is to have lost the ability to love. Whatever we believe about the next world, the idea speaks to this one. Being unable to love is a suffering many people know, and a reason to keep our hearts open.
prompt: Where has your capacity to love grown thin?

text: Love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4
context: Zosima to a woman who dreams of serving humanity but cannot bear ingratitude. Real love is slow, unglamorous and costly.
about:
In Fyodor Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, a wealthy lady confesses to the elder Zossima that she dreams of serving the poor, but fears she would give up the moment anyone was ungrateful.

Zossima answers gently: love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Love in dreams wants quick results, seen by everyone. Love in action is work and endurance, and for some people, a whole science. It is one of the wisest lines in the novel. Loving humanity in our imagination is easy. Loving a real, difficult person, day after day, is the harder and truer thing.
prompt: Where is your love still in dreams, and where is it in action?

text: Every one is really responsible to all men for all men and for everything.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 2
context: Spoken by Zosima's dying brother Markel, who in his last days discovers a joyful sense of connection to everyone.
about:
In Book VI of Fyodor Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, the elder Zossima recalls his older brother Markel, who died young of an illness. In his last weeks, Markel changed completely, and spoke words his mother found strange.

Everyone, he told her, is really responsible to all people, for all people and for everything. It is a radical idea, and Markel admits he can't explain it. We usually see ourselves responsible only for our own actions. Dostoevsky's characters see a web of connection, in which every life touches every other. It doesn't make us guilty of everything. It makes us part of everything.
prompt: What would change if you felt responsible for those around you?

text: The more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4
context: Zosima recalls a doctor's confession: loving humanity in the abstract is easy; loving the person in front of us is hard.
about:
A wealthy lady in Fyodor Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov confesses that she can love humanity only in theory. The elder Zossima answers with a story about a doctor he once knew.

The doctor said: I love humanity, but I wonder at myself. The more I love humanity in general, the less I love people in particular. In dreams he would die for mankind, but couldn't bear to share a room with anyone for two days. It is uncomfortably familiar. Big ideals can be easier than small kindnesses. Loving the people in front of us is the real test.
prompt: Who is the particular person you find hardest to love?

text: Let us be, first and above all, kind, then honest and then let us never forget each other!
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Epilogue, ch. 3
context: The closing scene of the novel. After all its darkness, Dostoevsky ends with a simple order of priorities.
about:
The Brothers Karamazov, Fyodor Dostoevsky's novel, ends with the young Alyosha speaking to a group of boys after the funeral of their friend Ilusha, a poor schoolboy.

Let us be, first and above all, kind, then honest, and then let us never forget each other, he says. He promises to remember every face. It is a gentle ending to a long, dark novel. After all its arguments about faith, freedom and suffering, Dostoevsky closes with something simple: kindness, honesty and loyal memory. Those may be enough to build a good life on.
prompt: Who should you make sure never to forget?

text: Man is fond of reckoning up his troubles, but does not count his joys. If he counted them up as he ought, he would see that every lot has enough happiness provided for it.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground II, ch. 6
context: Dostoevsky gives this line to a bitter, unhappy narrator, yet it rings true: we keep a careful count of our troubles and forget to count our joys.
about:
Fyodor Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground is told by a bitter, isolated man in St Petersburg. In its second part, he talks late at night with Liza, a young woman with a hard life, and says this to her.

People are fond of counting their troubles, he says, but don't count their joys. If they counted them as they should, they would see that every life has enough happiness in it. It is a surprisingly wise line from an unhappy narrator. Our minds dwell on what hurts and pass quickly over what is good. Counting our joys as carefully as our troubles changes the balance.
prompt: What joys could you count today?

text: What man wants is simply independent choice, whatever that independence may cost and wherever it may lead.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground I, ch. 7
context: The Underground Man rebels against the idea that people are calculating machines who always choose what is best for them. Above all, he says, we want to choose for ourselves, even against our own interest.
about:
The narrator of Fyodor Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground mocks the thinkers of his day who believe people always act in their own rational interest, and that a perfect society could be calculated.

What people want, he says, is simply independent choice, whatever that independence costs and wherever it leads. We will even act against our own advantage, just to prove we are free. It is a sharp warning about plans to perfect human life from above. People are not machines that run on self-interest. The need to choose for ourselves runs very deep, even when we choose badly.
prompt: Where are you choosing freely, and where just following?

text: …all the misfortunes of men arise from one thing only, that they are unable to stay quietly in their own chamber.
context: Pascal saw that we fill our days with work, games, and noise to avoid sitting alone with our thoughts. The trouble isn't the quiet room; it's what we're running from when we leave it.
about:
Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician and thinker. His Pensées are notes for an unfinished book, published in 1670, after his death. In one note, he looks at all the ways people keep themselves busy.

All the misfortunes of men, he concludes, come from one thing: they cannot stay quietly in a room. A person with enough to live on would not chase dangers at court or in war, if only they could enjoy staying at home. The line feels written for our age of constant distraction. Many of our troubles begin when we can't bear to sit still with ourselves.
prompt: What would happen if you sat quietly, alone, for ten minutes today?

text: Man is but a reed, weakest in nature, but a reed which thinks.
context: Perhaps Pascal's most famous line. A drop of water can kill us, he says, but we know that we die, and the universe knows nothing. Our fragility is real; so is the dignity that thinking gives us.
about:
Blaise Pascal's Pensées, unfinished notes published in 1670 after his death, often weigh the greatness and the weakness of human beings. Human greatness, one note says, lies in thought.

A human being is only a reed, the weakest thing in nature, but a reed that thinks. A breath of vapour or a drop of water can kill us. Yet even if the universe crushed us, we would be nobler than what kills us, because we know we are dying, and the universe knows nothing. Space can swallow us like a speck; by thought, we take in the whole of space.
prompt: What can your thinking do that keeps you strong even when you feel weak?

text: Thus we never live, but hope to live, and while we always lay ourselves out to be happy, it is inevitable that we can never be so.
context: Pascal, the French mathematician and thinker, saw that we live mostly in memories and plans. Always preparing to be happy later, we miss the only time we can be happy.
about:
In one of the notes of his Pensées, Blaise Pascal, the French mathematician, observes that our thoughts are nearly always taken up with the past or the future.

We hardly think of the present, he says, and when we do, it is only to plan the future. So we never live, but only hope to live, and always getting ready to be happy, we never are. It is a sharp picture of a common habit. We wait for the weekend, the holiday, the next stage of life. Pascal asks whether happiness, always postponed, ever actually arrives.
prompt: Which 'I'll be happy when…' sentence do you keep repeating?

text: The heart has its reasons, which reason knows not.
context: Pascal, a brilliant mathematician, insisted that not all knowing is logical. Some truths are felt before they are proven.
about:
Blaise Pascal, the French mathematician and thinker, kept notes for a book he never finished, published after his death as the Pensées. This note asks how we come to believe things.

The will, he says, turns the mind towards what it likes, so we judge by what we prefer to see. Then this line: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know. We all feel it in a thousand cases. It is often quoted about love. But Pascal means something wider. Much of what we believe and value comes from a kind of knowing that logic alone cannot reach or explain.
prompt: What does your heart know that your reason can't explain?

text: The one thing which consoles us for our miseries is diversion, yet this itself is the greatest of our miseries. For this it is which mainly hinders us from thinking of ourselves, and which insensibly destroys us.
context: Distraction comforts us, but it is also our biggest problem, because it stops us from thinking about our lives, and slowly wrecks us without our noticing.
about:
Blaise Pascal's Pensées, notes published in 1670 after his death, return again and again to diversion: the games, hunts, chatter and busyness we fill our lives with.

The one thing that consoles us for our miseries is diversion, he says, and yet it is itself the greatest of our miseries, because it keeps us from thinking about ourselves, and slowly leads us to ruin. Without it we would be bored, and boredom might push us to look for a deeper answer. It is a challenging thought for any age of endless entertainment. Distraction soothes, but it also keeps us from what matters.
prompt: What distraction keeps you from reflecting on your life?

text: A man can be himself only so long as he is alone; and if he does not love solitude, he will not love freedom; for it is only when he is alone that he is really free.
context: Schopenhauer never married and lived alone for most of his later life. In company we keep adjusting to others; alone, we can follow our own mind.
about:
Arthur Schopenhauer, the German philosopher, gave practical advice for living in his Counsels and Maxims, translated by T. Bailey Saunders. Every society, he says, demands that its members adjust to one another and restrain themselves.

So a person can be fully themselves only when alone, and if they do not love solitude, they will not love freedom, for only alone are they really free. Schopenhauer is famously gloomy, and he doesn't much like company. But his point has truth in it. Time alone, without pressure to please, lets us think and feel as we really are. Learning to enjoy it is a kind of freedom.
prompt: Who are you when nobody needs anything from you?

text: …we should never forget that the present is the only reality, the only certainty.
context: The future rarely turns out as we expect, and the past was not quite as we remember it. The present is the only part of life we actually hold.
about:
Many people, Arthur Schopenhauer writes in his Counsels and Maxims, live in a constant illusion: always chasing a future goal, living only for the time being, until at last they die.

Instead of anxious planning or regret for the past, he says, we should never forget that the present is the only reality, the only certainty. The future almost always turns out differently from what we expect, and the past was different from what we remember. It is a surprisingly hopeful note from a famous pessimist. The present is where life is actually lived.
prompt: What are you postponing until a future that may never look the way you imagine?

text: …if, over and above freedom from pain, there is also an absence of boredom, the essential conditions of earthly happiness are attained.
context: Schopenhauer saw two enemies of happiness: pain when we lack things, and boredom when we have them. Keep both away, and you have about as much happiness as life allows.
about:
Arthur Schopenhauer opens his Counsels and Maxims with a sober view of happiness. Measuring a life by its pleasures, he says, is a mistake, because pain is what we really feel; pleasure is mostly its absence.

And if, as well as freedom from pain, there is also an absence of boredom, the essential conditions of happiness on earth are met. Everything else is fantasy. It is a modest definition, and a useful one. Instead of chasing intense pleasures, which come and go, Schopenhauer suggests aiming at a life free from pain and boredom. Ordinary calm, filled with interest, may be as good as it gets.
prompt: Which pulls at your life more right now: strain or boredom?

text: Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.
source: Arthur Schopenhauer, Studies in Pessimism, 'Further Psychological Observations'
context: Schopenhauer compares it to the horizon, where earth and sky seem to meet. We each mistake the edge of what we can see for the edge of what exists.
about:
Arthur Schopenhauer, the German philosopher, gathered short reflections in his Studies in Pessimism, translated by T. Bailey Saunders. This one stands alone, between notes on tragedy and other subjects.

Everyone, he says, takes the limits of their own field of vision for the limits of the world. It is an error of the mind as unavoidable as the trick of the eye that makes sky and earth seem to meet at the horizon. We can't fully escape our point of view. But knowing that it is a point of view, and not the edge of reality, helps us listen to others.
prompt: What might lie just past the edge of your view?

text: Reading is thinking with some one else's head instead of one's own.
source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The Art of Literature, 'On Thinking for Oneself'
context: A heavy reader himself, Schopenhauer warned that reading can replace thinking rather than feed it. Ideas we work out ourselves stay with us; borrowed ones often don't.
about:
Arthur Schopenhauer's essay On Thinking for Oneself compares a person who thinks for themselves to a fine painting, and a mere collector of learning to a palette of colours with no harmony.

Reading, he says, is thinking with someone else's head instead of our own. It is a provocative claim from a great reader. Schopenhauer doesn't say reading is bad. He warns that if we only read, we can fill our heads with other people's thoughts and never form our own. Books are best as a starting point. Afterwards, we have to put them down and think.
prompt: Which idea that you hold did you truly think through yourself?

text: The capacity to give one's attention to someone who is suffering is a very rare and very difficult thing; it is almost a miracle; it is a miracle.
source: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies' (1942)
context: Simone Weil (1909–1943), French philosopher and activist, was a contemporary of the existentialists rather than one of them. For her, truly attending to another person's pain is the highest thing we can do.
about:
Simone Weil (1909–1943), a French philosopher, wrote an essay in 1942 on what schoolwork is really for: training attention. Here she turns from study to people who are suffering.

The capacity to give one's attention to someone who suffers, she says (our translation), is very rare and very difficult; it is almost a miracle. Most who think they have it don't. Warmth, enthusiasm and pity are not enough. What is needed is to look at the person as they really are, and to ask, as in an old legend of the Grail, what are you going through? Attention, for Weil, is the heart of kindness.
prompt: Who in your life needs your full attention, not your advice?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Those who suffer need nothing else in this world but people capable of giving them their attention.
source: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies' (1942)
context: Weil believed that most of us rush to fix, explain, or reassure. What people in pain need first is simply to be seen.
about:
In her 1942 essay on schoolwork and attention, the French philosopher Simone Weil (1909–1943) argues that the attention we train in study is the same we need for loving our neighbour.

Those who suffer, she says (our translation), need nothing else in this world but people able to give them their attention. Not advice, not solutions, not even sympathy first, but real attention. It is a simple and demanding idea. When someone is struggling, we often rush to fix things or reassure. Weil suggests something harder and more valuable: being fully present to them, as they are.
prompt: When did someone's attention help you more than their words?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Never, in any case, is a true effort of attention lost.
source: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies' (1942)
context: Weil wrote this to students: even a school problem you fail to solve trains your attention, and that capacity carries into everything else.
about:
Simone Weil (1909–1943), the French philosopher, wrote in 1942 that the real purpose of school exercises is to train attention, whatever the subject. Even a geometry problem we fail to solve, she says, is not wasted.

Never, in any case, is a true effort of attention lost (our translation). It bears fruit, even if we never see how. It is a consoling thought for any student, and anyone who has worked hard on something that didn't succeed. The answer may not come, but the attention we gave grows in us, and will be there when we need it.
prompt: What effort felt wasted at the time but trained you for something later?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Attention consists in suspending our thought, leaving it available, empty, and open to its object.
source: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies' (1942)
context: Paying attention means holding back our own thoughts and opinions so that we can really take in what is in front of us. For Weil it is a kind of patient waiting, not effort.
about:
In her 1942 essay on schoolwork, the French philosopher Simone Weil (1909–1943) warns that most of what we call attention is muscular effort: frowning, holding our breath, straining. That only tires us.

Attention, she says (our translation), consists in suspending our thought, leaving it available, empty and open to its object. Real attention is less like gripping and more like waiting: holding what we know lightly in the background while we stay open to what is in front of us. It applies to a problem, a text, or a person. The best attention is quiet and receptive.
prompt: What would you notice today if you held back your opinion for a moment?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Need and struggle are what excite and inspire us; our hour of triumph is what brings the void.
context: William James (1842–1910), the American philosopher and psychologist, noticed that we feel most alive while striving, and oddly empty once we arrive.
about:
William James, the American psychologist and philosopher, asked in his lecture Is Life Worth Living? (published in 1897) what keeps people going. Hardship, he notices, rarely lessens our love of life; it often sharpens it.

The chief source of melancholy, he says, is having too much. Need and struggle excite and inspire us; our hour of triumph is what brings the void. It is a familiar experience. We work hard for a goal, reach it, and feel strangely empty. James suggests we are made for striving, not for resting on success. A worthwhile struggle may be part of a good life, not just a step towards it.
prompt: When did reaching a goal leave you feeling empty?

text: It is only by risking our persons from one hour to another that we live at all.
context: For James, a life without risk is barely a life. Every choice that matters involves stepping into the unknown.
about:
William James, the American philosopher, argues in Is Life Worth Living? (1897) that life is full of maybes. Every victory, every act of courage and kindness, every scientific experiment rests on something uncertain.

It is only by risking ourselves from one hour to the next that we live at all, he says. And often our faith in an uncertain result is what makes it come true. James doesn't mean recklessness. He means that waiting for certainty before we act would leave us doing nothing. A full life asks us to commit, try and trust, without a guarantee.
prompt: What risk would make you feel more alive?

text: Not a victory is gained, not a deed of faithfulness or courage is done, except upon a maybe.
context: We never act with certainty. Courage means acting on a 'maybe', without knowing how it will turn out.
about:
Critics of belief, William James notes in Is Life Worth Living? (1897), sneer at maybes: what use, they ask, has a scientific life for them? James replies that science itself is full of them.

Not a victory is won, he says, not a deed of faithfulness or courage is done, except upon a maybe. Every generous act, every experiment, every book might turn out to be a mistake. It is a defence of acting under uncertainty. Life does not wait for proof. The people we admire most were often those who acted bravely without knowing how it would turn out.
prompt: What are you waiting to be certain about before acting?

text: The most interesting and valuable things about a man are his ideals and over-beliefs.
source: William James, The Will to Believe, Preface
context: James' 'over-beliefs' are the convictions we hold beyond what can be proven. They shape a life more than any fact.
about:
William James wrote the preface to The Will to Believe (1897), a collection of his essays, to explain what he was arguing for. Faiths and beliefs, he says, do harm only when they forget they are hypotheses and claim authority.

The most interesting and valuable things about a person, he says, are their ideals and over-beliefs: the hopes and convictions that go beyond what can be proved. The same is true of nations and eras. It is a generous view. What we believe in, and strive for, beyond the evidence says more about us than any list of facts. Our ideals are who we are trying to become.
prompt: What do you believe that you can't prove but live by?

text: My life came to a standstill.
context: At around fifty, rich, famous, and with a loving family, the author of War and Peace fell into a crisis: he could no longer see what his life was for.
about:
Leo Tolstoy, the Russian novelist, describes in A Confession a crisis that struck him when he was not yet fifty: a loving wife, good children, a large estate, fame and respect, and yet one question he could not answer.

What will come of what I am doing today or tomorrow? Unable to answer, he writes, my life came to a standstill. He could still breathe, eat, drink and sleep, but there was no life, because no wish seemed reasonable to fulfil. It is a stark, honest account. Success had not answered the question of meaning. Many people meet that question at some point, and Tolstoy's book is about the search that followed.
prompt: Has your life ever come to a standstill, and what restarted it?

text: I saw the dragon clearly and the honey no longer tasted sweet.
context: Tolstoy retells an Eastern fable: a man hangs over a well with a dragon below, licking drops of honey from a branch while mice gnaw at it. Once he saw death clearly, the pleasures lost their taste.
about:
In A Confession, Leo Tolstoy tells an old Eastern fable. A traveller fleeing a wild beast hides in a dry well, and sees a dragon waiting at the bottom. He clings to a branch, while two mice, one white and one black, gnaw at it.

He finds drops of honey on the leaves and licks them. Tolstoy says he is that traveller: the dragon is death, the mice are day and night, and the honey is the pleasure that once comforted him. I saw the dragon clearly, and the honey no longer tasted sweet. It is a powerful image of what happens when we can no longer ignore our mortality, and why we need a deeper meaning than pleasure.
prompt: What would still taste sweet to you if you looked at death clearly?

text: If any one long and obstinately desires to appear something, he finds it difficult at last to be anything else.
context: Playing a role for long enough turns it into who we are. Nietzsche's warning to anyone building an image.
about:
Friedrich Nietzsche's Human, All-Too-Human is a book of short reflections, translated by Helen Zimmern. Number 51 is about how pretending can turn into being.

Someone who long and stubbornly wants to appear something, he says, finds it hard in the end to be anything else. A role played for years becomes a person. It can work both ways. Pretending to be confident or kind can, over time, make us so. But pretending to be important or hard can also trap us in a mask. It's worth asking which roles we are playing, and who they are making us.
prompt: Which image of yourself have you kept up so long that it became you?

text: I swear, gentlemen, that to be too conscious is an illness—a real thorough-going illness.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground I, ch. 2
context: The Underground Man thinks so much about everything that he can't act at all. Overthinking, Dostoevsky shows, can trap us.
about:
The narrator of Fyodor Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground is a retired official who has withdrawn from the world. He opens by explaining why he could never become anything, not even an insect.

To be too conscious, he swears, is an illness, a real, thorough illness. Ordinary awareness would be quite enough for everyday life. He thinks so much about everything that he can't act. It is a dark, comic portrait, and an influential one. Thinking is good, but too much self-awareness can freeze us. Sometimes we need to stop analysing and simply live.
prompt: Where is overthinking keeping you from acting?

text: Man likes to make roads and to create, that is a fact beyond dispute. But why has he such a passionate love for destruction and chaos also?
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground I, ch. 9
context: We are builders, yet we are drawn to breaking things too. The Underground Man refuses any picture of humans as simply rational.
about:
Dostoevsky's narrator in Notes from Underground mocks the idea that people only want what is reasonable and good for them. Humans love building roads and creating, he admits.

But why, he asks, do we also have such a passionate love of destruction and chaos? Perhaps, he suggests, we love the road-making more than the destination, and fear arriving. It is an unsettling question, and an honest one. People are not purely rational builders. Part of us enjoys breaking things, including our own plans. Understanding that is part of understanding ourselves.
prompt: What do you build, and what do you secretly want to break?

text: Why, suffering is the sole origin of consciousness.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground I, ch. 9
context: A dark claim: we become truly aware of ourselves through pain. Comfort keeps us asleep.
about:
In Notes from Underground, Fyodor Dostoevsky's narrator attacks the dream of a perfect, rational society, the crystal palace, in which there would be no doubt and no suffering.

But humans will never give up real suffering, he says, for suffering is the only source of consciousness. Although he called consciousness humanity's greatest misfortune, he knows we prize it and would not give it up for any satisfaction. It is a dark claim, and not the whole truth. But it points to something real: our deepest awareness often comes through difficulty, not comfort.
prompt: What did suffering wake you up to?

text: Either to be a hero or to grovel in the mud—there was nothing between.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground II
context: The narrator describes his youth: he could only imagine glory or humiliation, never an ordinary decent life. Many perfectionists will recognise it.
about:
In the second part of Notes from Underground, Fyodor Dostoevsky's narrator recalls his twenties: long periods of shameful behaviour, followed by dreams of glory in which he would ride out crowned with laurel.

Either be a hero or grovel in the mud, he writes; there was nothing in between. That was my ruin. When he was in the mud, he comforted himself that at other times he was a hero. It is a sharp picture of all-or-nothing thinking. Refusing anything but greatness can keep us from the ordinary, decent middle, which is where most good lives are lived.
prompt: Where do you think in all-or-nothing terms?

text: What a man has in himself is, then, the chief element in his happiness.
source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The Wisdom of Life, ch. I
context: Schopenhauer divides happiness into what we are, what we have, and how others see us. The first counts by far the most.
about:
Arthur Schopenhauer's The Wisdom of Life, translated by T. Bailey Saunders, sorts the things that make up happiness into three: what a person is, what they have, and how others see them. He mocks a life spent piling up gold for an heir.

What a person has in themselves, he concludes, is the chief element in their happiness. Because most people have little inside, even those free from poverty feel as unhappy as the poor. It is a stern view, but a useful one. Health of mind, interests and character shape our happiness more than possessions. They are worth cultivating first.
prompt: What do you have in yourself that no one can give or take?

text: Health outweighs all other blessings so much that one may really say that a healthy beggar is happier than an ailing king.
source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The Wisdom of Life, ch. I
context: We rarely notice health until it is gone. Schopenhauer puts it above wealth and status.
about:
Arthur Schopenhauer argues in The Wisdom of Life that what goes on inside us matters far more for our happiness than outside circumstances. Hunger is the best sauce, as the saying goes.

Health outweighs all other blessings so much, he says, that a healthy beggar is happier than a sick king. A calm and cheerful temperament, a sound body and a clear mind make up most of our happiness. It is a plain truth we often forget until illness comes. Looking after our health, of body and mind, is one of the wisest investments we can make.
prompt: What are you trading your health for these days, and is it worth it?

text: Riches, one may say, are like sea-water; the more you drink the thirstier you become; and the same is true of fame.
source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The Wisdom of Life, ch. III
context: Money and fame never quench the thirst they create. The more we have, the more we want.
about:
In The Wisdom of Life, Arthur Schopenhauer notices that we are only unhappy about the things we expected to get. What lies beyond our horizon doesn't trouble us; the poor are not upset by the wealth of the rich.

Wealth, he says, is like sea-water: the more you drink, the thirstier you become; and the same is true of fame. It is a vivid image. Gaining more doesn't satisfy the desire; it feeds it. Schopenhauer's point is not that money is bad, but that it cannot fill the gap it seems to promise. Contentment has to come from elsewhere.
prompt: What are you drinking that only makes you thirstier?

text: Cheerfulness is a direct and immediate gain,—the very coin, as it were, of happiness …
source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The Wisdom of Life, ch. II
context: Surprising from the great pessimist: he says a cheerful mood is worth more than almost anything, because it is happiness itself, paid in cash.
about:
Arthur Schopenhauer was famously pessimistic, but in The Wisdom of Life he has warm words for cheerfulness. When it knocks at our door, he says, we should throw the door open, instead of first wondering whether we have reason to be happy.

Cheerfulness is a direct and immediate gain: the very coin of happiness, not a cheque on the bank. It makes us happy right now, in the present, which is all we really have. It is lovely advice from an unexpected source. We often wait for a reason to be cheerful. Schopenhauer suggests welcoming good spirits whenever they come.
prompt: What lifts your mood without costing anything?

text: Intelligence can only be led by desire.
source: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies' (1942)
context: Weil believed we learn best what we want to learn. Forcing the mind works less well than awakening its interest.
about:
Simone Weil (1909–1943), a French philosopher, wrote in 1942 about what schoolwork is really for. Willpower, the gritting of teeth that helps in manual work, she says, has almost no place in study.

Intelligence can only be led by desire (our translation). For there to be desire, there must be pleasure and joy. It reverses a common idea of learning as discipline and strain. Weil thought we learn best when we want to: when curiosity and enjoyment pull us forward. Forcing the mind to learn rarely works for long. Wanting to understand does.
prompt: What do you learn easily because you want to?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Intelligence grows and bears fruit only in joy.
source: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies' (1942)
context: Joy is not a reward after learning but the soil it grows in.
about:
Simone Weil (1909–1943) was a French philosopher. In a 1942 essay on what schoolwork is really for, she argued that one of its main aims is to train attention, whatever the subject.

Here she makes a surprising claim about how that works. We usually think learning takes willpower: gritting our teeth and pushing through. Weil thought willpower has almost no place in study. The mind follows desire, and desire needs pleasure and joy; the joy of learning, she says, is as necessary to study as breathing is to a runner.
