It warns against planning as if we had forever. Remembering that life is short is not meant to make us gloomy. It is meant to help us choose, and to put first what truly matters while there is still time.
prompt: Which of your plans assumes you have unlimited time?

text: Good people shine from afar, like the snowy mountains; bad people are not seen, like arrows shot by night.
context: Goodness is visible from a distance, like snow on a peak. Harm works in the dark.
about:
This verse sits in “Miscellaneous”, one of the 26 chapters of the Dhammapada. Its first image is of snow-covered mountains, which can be seen from very far away.

Good people shine from afar, like snowy peaks; bad people are not seen, like arrows shot by night. The image has two sides. Goodness tends to become visible over time: people notice who is kind and reliable, even from a distance. Harm, by contrast, works in the dark and often goes unseen. The verse doesn't promise that goodness is always quickly recognised. It says that, like a mountain, it is hard to hide for long.
prompt: Who shines from afar in your life?

text: Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.
context: 'Earnestness' translates appamada: being alert and wholehearted. It is what moves us forward while others drift.
about:
This verse comes from the Dhammapada's chapter called “On Earnestness”, whose Pali title names heedfulness: staying awake to what we are doing. A hack was a tired old horse, the opposite of a racer.

Among the thoughtless, the wise person is earnest; among the sleepers, awake. And so they move ahead like a racehorse leaving an old nag behind. The point is not to beat others, but how attention changes a life. Two people can live through the same days: one drifts, the other notices. Over the years the difference becomes enormous. Being awake to our own life is, in this view, the first step on any path.
prompt: Where are you sleepwalking instead of being awake?

text: 'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity.
context: Seeing that everything changes and ends is, for the Buddha, the beginning of peace. 'Passive' here means no longer thrown around by pain.
about:
Three verses in a row share the same shape in the Dhammapada's chapter called “The Way”, and this is the first of them: the next two say that all created things are grief and pain, and that all forms are unreal.

Everything made will pass away. Whoever truly sees this, the verse says, becomes “passive in pain”: no longer thrown about by it. That doesn't mean feeling nothing. It means that loss, change and endings stop coming as a shock, because we have understood that they are part of how things are. Seeing impermanence clearly is, for the Dhammapada, not a reason for despair but the beginning of peace.
prompt: What would hurt less if you remembered that it will pass?

text: Fools follow after vanity, men of evil wisdom. The wise man keeps earnestness as his best jewel.
context: Vanity chases appearances; wisdom treasures steady, wholehearted effort.
about:
In “On Earnestness”, a chapter of the Dhammapada, the verse after this one continues: do not follow vanity, nor the pleasures of love and lust; whoever is earnest and meditative finds ample joy.

Fools chase vanity: looking good, being admired, the next shiny thing. The wise keep earnestness as their best jewel. It's an unexpected choice of treasure: not wealth or talent, but steady, wholehearted attention to how we live. Unlike a real jewel, it can't be stolen or lose its value. It grows with use, and it makes every other good thing in life easier to keep.
prompt: What vanity is drawing your attention away from what matters?

text: As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.
context: A beautiful picture of living lightly: take what you need from the world and leave it unharmed.
about:
In the Dhammapada's chapter called “Flowers”, many verses use flowers to talk about how to live.

A bee takes nectar and flies off without harming the flower, its colour or its scent. So, the verse says, should a sage live in a village. It's a beautiful picture of living lightly: taking what we need from the world and from others, and leaving them unharmed. It applies far beyond villages. In families, workplaces and friendships we can ask the same question: do we leave people and places as whole as we found them?
prompt: Where could you take what you need without harming anything?

text: If you see an intelligent man who tells you where true treasures are to be found, who shows what is to be avoided, and administers reproofs, follow that wise man; it will be better, not worse, for those who follow him.
context: Someone who honestly points out our faults is giving us treasure. The Buddha advises seeking such people out.
about:
From the Dhammapada's chapter “The Wise Man” comes this verse. The next one adds that someone who warns and teaches others will be loved by the good, and hated by the bad.

If you meet someone intelligent who shows you where the real treasures are, warns you what to avoid and corrects you when you go wrong, follow them; it will be better for you, not worse. The striking part is that being corrected is listed as a gift, alongside being shown treasure. Most of us dislike criticism. The verse suggests that an honest friend who points out our faults is worth more than many who only praise us.
prompt: Who tells you the truth about yourself, and do you listen?

text: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler.
context: We sift other people's faults carefully and hide our own. An old observation that psychology has since confirmed.
about:
This verse sits in “Impurity”, one of the 26 chapters of the Dhammapada. Winnowing was the way grain was cleaned: tossing it in the air so that the wind carried off the light, useless chaff.

We winnow our neighbour's faults with great care, sorting out every bit of chaff. Our own we hide, like a cheat hiding a bad die. The verse catches something all of us do. Others' mistakes look vivid to us; ours look small, explainable or invisible. The next verse warns that someone who is always looking for others' faults only feeds their own. The more useful habit is to turn the winnowing on ourselves.
prompt: Which of your own faults are you hiding from yourself?

text: Let no one forget his own duty for the sake of another's, however great; let a man, after he has discerned his own duty, be always attentive to his duty.
context: Helping others matters, but not at the cost of neglecting our own path. Find your task and give it attention.
about:
This verse closes the Dhammapada's chapter called “Self”. Just before it, the chapter says that we make ourselves better or worse, and that no one can purify another.

Then comes a practical rule: don't neglect your own duty for someone else's, however important theirs seems. First work out what your own task is, then give it steady attention. It's easy to get absorbed in other people's business, advising, worrying, comparing, while our own work waits. The verse isn't against helping others. It reminds us that our own path is the one only we can walk.
prompt: Where have you neglected your own path while helping others with theirs?

text: And he who lives a hundred years, idle and weak, a life of one day is better if a man has attained firm strength.
context: A short life lived with energy is worth more than a long one lived half-asleep.
about:
Several verses in the Dhammapada's chapter called “The Thousands” begin the same way, this one included: “And he who lives a hundred years”.

Each one weighs a long, empty life against a single good day. Here it is a hundred years lived idle and weak, against one day lived with firm strength. The idea is not that long lives are bad. It is that the worth of a life lies in how it is lived, not in how long it lasts. A day of real effort and presence counts for more than years spent half-asleep.
prompt: What would one fully lived day look like for you?

text: A man who has learnt little, grows old like an ox; his flesh grows, but his knowledge does not grow.
context: Getting older doesn't make us wiser on its own. Without learning, we only grow in body.
about:
This verse sits in “Old Age”, a chapter of the Dhammapada. The verse just before it notes that even the brilliant chariots of kings fall apart, and the body too, but the virtue of good people does not decay.

A person who has learnt little grows old like an ox: their flesh grows, but their knowledge does not. The picture is blunt, and meant to wake us up. Getting older doesn't make us wiser on its own. The years bring experience, but only learning turns it into understanding. The verse invites us to keep growing in the one way that age cannot stop.
prompt: What have you learned recently that made you grow?

text: There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed.
context: Four vivid images for the forces that harm us from inside.
about:
The Dhammapada's chapter called “Impurity” includes this verse. A similar list appears in the chapter on happiness: there is no fire like passion, and no losing throw like hatred.

Here are four images for the forces that harm us from inside. Passion burns like fire. Hatred grabs like a shark. Folly catches us like a snare. Greed sweeps us away like a torrent. Each image shows a different danger: burning, biting, trapping, drowning. Naming them clearly is a first step. Once we see the fire for what it is, we can stop feeding it.
prompt: Which of the four, passion, hatred, folly, or greed, catches you most often?

text: If a traveller does not meet with one who is his better, or his equal, let him firmly keep to his solitary journey; there is no companionship with a fool.
context: Better to walk alone than in company that pulls you down.
about:
The Dhammapada is an early Buddhist collection of short verses, in the Pali language, about how to live. This one comes from its chapter called “The Fool.” There, a fool is not someone without schooling but someone who will not learn; the chapter even says that a fool who knows his foolishness “is wise at least so far.”

The verse is about how strongly our company shapes us. Slowly, we take on the habits, worries and values of the people we spend our days with. So it advises us to look for companions who are better than us, or at least our equal. If there are none, walking alone for a while is no failure. It can be the wiser path.
prompt: Which company lifts you up, and which pulls you down?

text: Then thus, ask as I may, I can discover no chariot. Chariot is a mere empty sound.
source: The Questions of King Milinda, Book II
context: The monk Nagasena asks a Greek king in India whether the chariot is its pole, wheels, or axle. It is none of them alone: 'chariot' is just a name for parts working together. So too, he says, is the self.
about:
The Questions of King Milinda is a dialogue in Pali between the Buddhist monk Nāgasena and King Milinda, usually identified with Menander, an Indo-Greek king of the 2nd century BCE. When the king asks his name, Nāgasena says it is only a convenient term: there is no lasting self behind it.

The king objects, and Nāgasena answers with the chariot the king came in. Is the chariot the pole, the axle, the wheels? None of them alone, and nothing apart from them. So, he teases, “chariot” is a mere empty sound. The king replies that the word names all the parts together, and Nāgasena agrees: so does his own name. The self, in this view, is less a hidden thing inside us than a name for many parts working together.
prompt: If you are not any one of your parts, what are you?

text: Let the wise man guard his thoughts, for they are difficult to perceive, very artful, and they rush wherever they list: thoughts well guarded bring happiness.
context: Thoughts arrive quickly and quietly, and they pull us wherever they like. The Buddha's advice is not to stop them, but to watch over them, the way you would guard a door.
about:
The verse before this one, in the Dhammapada's chapter “Thought”, calls the mind flighty and hard to hold, rushing wherever it likes.

Here the advice is to guard our thoughts. They are hard to notice, very artful, and they go wherever they please. Anyone who has caught themselves halfway through a worry they didn't choose knows the feeling. The verse doesn't say we must stop thoughts from coming. It says to watch over them, as a guard watches a gate: noticing what comes in, and not letting every passing thought take charge.
prompt: Which thought has been rushing wherever it likes today?

text: Let no man think lightly of good, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little.
context: Goodness is built drop by drop. No single kind act seems to matter much, but small acts repeated fill a life, just as small faults do.
about:
This verse sits in “Evil”, one of the 26 chapters of the Dhammapada. It is the twin of the verse before it, which uses the same image of water-drops to warn about small wrongs.

Here the drops are good ones. We may think a small kindness hardly matters: one patient answer, one thank-you, one moment of honesty. But a water-pot fills drop by drop, and so does a good character. No single act seems to count, and yet together they fill a life. The verse encourages us not to wait for big chances to be good, because most of the good we do is made of small acts.
prompt: What small good thing could you add to the pot today?

text: Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage! No sufferings befall the man who is not attached to name and form, and who calls nothing his own.
context: Anger and pride both hold on to something: a grievance, an image of ourselves. The Buddha's advice is to loosen the grip; what we don't cling to can't hurt us in the same way.
about:
The Dhammapada's chapter called “Anger” opens with this verse, and goes on to picture anger as a runaway chariot that only a real driver can stop.

It asks us to leave anger, give up pride and overcome every kind of bondage. Anger and pride both cling to something: a grievance, or an image of ourselves we feel we must defend. The verse ends with a promise: no suffering comes to someone who is not attached and calls nothing their own. That doesn't mean owning nothing. It means holding things, and even ourselves, loosely enough that losing them doesn't break us.
prompt: What are you holding on to that keeps your anger going?

text: This mind of mine went formerly wandering about as it liked, as it listed, as it pleased; but I shall now hold it in thoroughly, as the rider who holds the hook holds in the furious elephant.
context: Early Buddhist texts often picture the untrained mind as a wild elephant. The rider doesn't fight it; with steady attention, he learns to guide it.
about:
This verse comes from “The Elephant”, a chapter of the Dhammapada. Elephants were tamed and ridden, and the rider guided the animal with a hook.

The speaker looks back: my mind used to wander wherever it liked; now I will hold it in, as a rider holds in a furious elephant. The image is honest about the mind's strength. An elephant cannot be overpowered by force alone. It is guided by skill and steady attention, over a long time. The next verse puts it simply: watch your thoughts, and pull yourself out of the wrong way, like an elephant out of mud.
prompt: Where did your mind wander today, and how did you bring it back?

text:
Finally, this is better, that one do
His own task as he may, even though he fail,
Than take tasks not his own, though they seem good.
context: Better to walk your own path imperfectly than someone else's perfectly. In the Gita this is dharma: the duty that fits who you are.
about:
The Bhagavad Gita, a section of the great Indian epic the Mahabharata, is a conversation on the battlefield of Kurukshetra between the prince Arjuna and Krishna, his charioteer and guide. In chapter III, in Edwin Arnold's verse translation, Krishna explains that every being follows its own nature.

Better, he says, to do your own task as you can, even if you fail, than take on tasks not yours, however good they look. It is a striking idea for an age of comparison. We often envy other people's paths and neglect our own. The Gita suggests that our own work, done honestly, even imperfectly, is worth more than someone else's done well. Finding and doing our part is the point.
prompt: Whose path are you trying to walk instead of your own?

context: Krishna admits that the human heart is hard to control and restless, but says it can be trained by habit. Arjuna had complained it was as hard to hold as the wind.
about:
The Bhagavad Gita, a section of the great Indian epic the Mahabharata, is a conversation on the battlefield of Kurukshetra between the prince Arjuna and Krishna, his charioteer and guide. In chapter VI, Arjuna protests that the peaceful mind Krishna describes is impossible: the human heart is restless, wilful and strong, as hard to hold as the wind.

Krishna agrees. Beyond doubt, he says, the heart is hard to restrain and wavering. Yet it can be restrained by habit, by steady self-command. It is an encouraging exchange. The teacher doesn't pretend the mind is easy to master. He admits it is difficult, and then offers a way: practice, repeated over time. Calm is not a gift, but a habit we can build.
prompt: What small daily practice could steady your mind?

text:
And like the ocean, day by day receiving
Floods from all lands, which never overflows
Its boundary-line not leaping, and not leaving,
Fed by the rivers, but unswelled by those;—
So is the perfect one!
context: The ocean receives rivers from every land and never overflows. A wise person is like that: pleasures and temptations flow in without disturbing their calm.
about:
The Bhagavad Gita, a section of the great Indian epic the Mahabharata, is a conversation on the battlefield of Kurukshetra between the prince Arjuna and Krishna, his charioteer and guide. In chapter II, Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom is like, and Krishna answers with a series of pictures.

Like the ocean, he says in Edwin Arnold's verse, which receives floods from every land day after day, yet never overflows its shore, fed by rivers but not swollen by them: so is the perfect one. Desires and impressions keep pouring in, but they don't overwhelm such a person. It is a calming image. We can't stop the rivers coming. We can become deep enough to receive them without flooding.
prompt: What keeps pouring into your days, and how do you stay steady?

text: The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man. It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end.
context: In the Katha Upanishad, Death himself teaches a young seeker called Nachiketas. His first lesson: what feels good now and what is good are often different roads.
about:
The Katha Upanishad, one of the ancient Indian texts called the Upanishads, tells of a boy, Nachiketas, who meets Death and asks him what happens after we die. Death tests him first, offering wealth, long life and every pleasure instead.

The good is one thing, Death says, and the pleasant another. Both bind us. It is well with the one who clings to the good; whoever chooses the pleasant misses the goal. The boy has refused the pleasant, and so he is ready to learn. It is a choice we face constantly, in small ways. What feels nice now and what is truly good often point in different directions.
prompt: Where are you choosing the pleasant over the good?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins.
context: An image close to Plato's charioteer, from a different culture. The body is the vehicle, the mind holds the reins, and the self sits inside. So who is steering?
about:
In the Katha Upanishad, Death teaches the boy Nachiketas with a picture: the self as a person riding in a chariot.

The self sits in the chariot, the body is the chariot, the intellect is the driver and the mind is the reins. The senses, the text goes on, are the horses, and the objects of the senses are the roads they run on. With an unwise driver and loose reins, the horses run wild; with a wise driver, they go where they should. It is close to Plato's charioteer. The question is who holds the reins in our lives.
prompt: Who is really holding the reins in your life right now?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard.
context: A call to wake up and understand the gifts we have been given. The path to knowing yourself is as narrow as a razor's edge. Somerset Maugham took the title of his novel The Razor's Edge from this verse.
about:
The Katha Upanishad is a conversation between the boy Nachiketas and Death, who teaches him about the self and how to know it.

Rise, awake! Death urges. Having gained your gifts, understand them. The wise say the path is hard, like walking the sharp edge of a razor. It is a call to wake up, and an honest warning. Deep understanding isn't comfortable or quick; it asks for balance and care. The famous words were later used by Swami Vivekananda as a motto. They still speak to anyone setting out on something hard.
prompt: What gift or chance have you received but not yet used?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: And he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it. When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?
context: Someone who sees all beings as part of themselves, and themselves in all beings, can't turn away from anyone, and has nothing left to fear or grieve. The Upanishads teach that the deepest self is one with everything.
about:
The Isha Upanishad is one of the ancient Indian texts called the Upanishads, translated by Max Müller in the Sacred Books of the East. It describes a reality that is both far and near, inside all things and outside them.

Whoever sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, the text says, never turns away from it. For one who understands, when the self has become all things, what sorrow or trouble can there be? It is an ancient picture of deep connection. If we see ourselves in others and others in ourselves, cruelty and loneliness become much harder.
prompt: How would you treat the people around you if you saw them as part of yourself?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 1 (1879)

text: And here they say that a person consists of desires. And as is his desire, so is his will; and as is his will, so is his deed; and whatever deed he does, that he will reap.
context: A chain from the inside out: desire shapes will, will shapes action, and action shapes what comes back to us. It is one of the earliest statements of the idea of karma.
about:
The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the ancient Indian Upanishads translated by Max Müller, says that a person becomes what they do: good by good deeds, bad by bad ones.

And here they say that a person consists of desires. As is their desire, so is their will; as is their will, so is their deed; and whatever deed they do, that they will reap. It is a short chain with a big lesson. What we want shapes what we choose, what we choose shapes what we do, and what we do shapes who we become. Change begins with our desires.
prompt: Which of your desires is quietly shaping your actions?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Your business is with action alone; not by any means with fruit. Let not the fruit of action be your motive to action. Let not your attachment be fixed on inaction.
context: The Gita is a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and the god Krishna before a great battle. Its central teaching: do your work well and let go of the outcome, without using that as an excuse to do nothing.
about:
In chapter II of the Bhagavad Gita, part of the great Indian epic the Mahabharata, Krishna gives the prince Arjuna one of its most famous teachings, here in K. T. Telang's translation for the Sacred Books of the East.

Your business is with action alone, not with its fruit. Don't let the fruit be your motive, and don't be attached to doing nothing either. It is a demanding balance. We are to act fully and well, but let go of controlling results, which are never fully ours. It frees us from paralysis and from anxiety at once. Do the work; release the outcome.
prompt: What would you do differently if you stopped worrying about the result?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: He whose heart is not agitated in the midst of calamities, who has no longing for pleasures, and from whom the feelings of affection, fear, and wrath have departed, is called a sage of steady mind.
context: Krishna's portrait of a steady mind: not cold, but no longer thrown around by every gain and loss.
about:
In chapter II of the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna how to recognise a person of steady mind: how they speak, sit and move.

Such a person, Krishna answers, is not shaken by calamities and does not long for pleasures; affection, fear and anger have left them. They have become a sage of steady mind. It is a portrait of inner calm. Life will still bring trouble and temptation. What changes is that they no longer throw us about. Steadiness is less about what happens to us than about how far it reaches inside.
prompt: What knocks you off balance most easily?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: The man who ponders over objects of sense forms an attachment to them; from that attachment is produced desire; and from desire anger is produced; from anger results want of discrimination; from want of discrimination, confusion of the memory; from confusion of the memory, loss of reason; and in consequence of loss of reason, he is utterly ruined.
context: Dwelling on something leads to wanting it; wanting leads to anger when we don't get it; anger clouds judgment; and lost judgment ruins us. The easiest place to break the chain is the first link.
about:
In chapter II of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna warns that the senses can carry away even a wise person's mind. Then he traces how it happens.

Whoever dwells on objects of the senses becomes attached to them; from attachment comes desire, from desire anger, from anger confusion, and from confusion the loss of memory and reason, until the person is ruined. It is a precise chain, still true. A passing thought becomes a fixation, then a want, then a frustration. Catching it early, at the first thought, is the easiest place to stop it.
prompt: Which thought do you keep returning to that might be the first link in a chain?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: A man should elevate his self by his self; he should not debase his self, for even a man's own self is his friend, a man's own self is also his enemy.
context: No one else can raise us up or pull us down as effectively as we can. Each of us is both our best ally and our worst opponent.
about:
In chapter VI of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes how a person rises to inner discipline, by not clinging to objects of the senses or to actions.

We should lift ourselves up by ourselves, he says, and not drag ourselves down, for our own self is our friend, and our own self is also our enemy. Whoever has mastered themselves is their own friend; whoever hasn't treats themselves like an enemy. It is a strong idea of responsibility and of hope. No one else can raise us for us, but we can be our own best ally.
prompt: Were you your own friend or your own enemy today?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: Devotion is not his, O Arjuna! who eats too much, nor his who eats not at all; not his who is addicted to too much sleep, nor his who is ever awake.
context: Like the Buddha's 'middle way' and Aristotle's 'mean', the Gita warns against extremes in both directions. Spiritual practice starts with ordinary balance.
about:
In chapter VI of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes the practice of meditation and discipline, and then corrects a common mistake about it.

Discipline is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who eats nothing; not for one who sleeps too much, nor for one always awake. It belongs to one who eats and rests in due measure, and works in due measure. It is a plea for balance, like Aristotle's mean. Extremes, even in a good cause, defeat themselves. A steady, moderate life is the ground in which calm grows.
prompt: Where in your daily life are you living at an extreme?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: Two birds, inseparable friends, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating.
context: One bird is the part of us that tastes, wants, and suffers; the other is the quiet witness within. Both live on the same tree.
about:
The Mundaka Upanishad, one of the ancient Indian Upanishads, uses an old image of two birds, close friends, sitting on the same tree.

One eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. The text goes on: on the same tree, a person sits grieving, lost and bewildered, until they see the other, calm one, and their sorrow passes. The text calls the watching bird the lord, the higher self. Many readers today also see the two birds as two sides of us: one caught up in experience, one that quietly watches. Learning to be the watcher, sometimes, can bring peace.
prompt: What do you notice when you watch your own wanting without acting on it?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Essentially man is not a slave either of himself or of the world; but he is a lover.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Relation of the Individual to the Universe'
context: Tagore (1861–1941), the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature, gave these lectures on the Upanishads at Harvard. For him, our deepest relation to the world is love, not use.
about:
Rabindranath Tagore, the Indian poet and thinker, wrote Sadhana (1913), a series of talks, most of them read at Harvard University. He warns against a life wrapped in dead habits, where a blind rush of work hides the horizon.

At heart, he says, a person is not a slave either of themselves or of the world, but a lover. Our freedom and fulfilment lie in love, which is another name for perfect understanding. It is a beautiful turn. We aren't meant to be driven by our wants or by outside demands, but to relate to the world with love. Love, here, is a way of truly comprehending.
prompt: Do you relate to your work and world more as a servant or as a lover?

text: Man's poverty is abysmal, his wants are endless till he becomes truly conscious of his soul.
context: No amount of possessions fills a gap that is really about meaning. Tagore says our wants only settle when we know what we are.
about:
In Tagore's Sadhana (1913), a series of talks, most of them read at Harvard University, he describes people as pilgrims, always broadening their awareness and seeking a wider unity.

Our poverty is bottomless, he says, and our wants endless, until we become truly aware of our soul. Until then, the world seems a constant flux, something that is and is not. It is a diagnosis of restlessness. We keep wanting more because something deeper is missing. Tagore suggests the cure is not more things, but a deeper awareness of who we are.
prompt: What are you trying to fill with things that things can't fill?

text: Man's cry is to reach his fullest expression.
context: Behind much of our restlessness, Tagore hears one longing: to become fully who we are.
about:
Tagore's Sadhana (1913), a series of talks, most of them read at Harvard University, explores what it means to live a full life. This line comes from a talk on the soul.

Our cry, he says, is to reach our fullest expression. That longing leads people to seek wealth and power. But we have to discover that accumulating is not the same as realising ourselves. It is a generous reading of ambition. Even greed, Tagore suggests, is a confused form of a real need: to become fully what we are. Seeing that, we can look for fulfilment where it can actually be found.
prompt: Which part of you is still waiting to be expressed?

text: We gain our freedom when we attain our truest nature.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Problem of Self'
context: Freedom, for Tagore, isn't doing whatever we like. It is becoming what we most deeply are.
about:
In Tagore's Sadhana (1913), he argues that the self becomes a prison when we think it is an end in itself.

We gain our freedom, he says, when we reach our truest nature. An artist finds artistic freedom when they find their ideal of art, and are freed from laborious imitation. Freedom, in this view, isn't doing whatever we like. It is becoming fully what we most deeply are. That kind of freedom takes work, but it ends the struggle of trying to be someone else.
prompt: When do you feel most like yourself?

text: …when a man loves, giving becomes a matter of joy to him, like the tree's surrender of the ripe fruit.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Problem of Self'
context: A tree does not feel it loses anything when its fruit falls. When we love, giving stops feeling like a sacrifice.
about:
Rabindranath Tagore contrasts two kinds of giving in Sadhana (1913), his talks read mostly at Harvard. The selfish person also gives, he says, but only under pressure.

That is like plucking unripe fruit: you tear it from the tree and bruise the branch. But when a person loves, giving becomes a joy, like a tree letting go of its ripe fruit. The image is gentle and exact. Giving from duty or fear hurts. Giving from love feels natural, even light. The difference isn't in what we give, but in the heart we give it from.
prompt: Where does giving feel easy for you, and where does it feel like loss?

text: …we do cross the infinite at every step, and meet the eternal in every second.
context: Tagore rejects the idea that the infinite is far away. It is present in every ordinary step and moment.
about:
In Tagore's Sadhana (1913), he takes up an old puzzle of logic: between any two points, however close, lie infinitely many points, so in theory we could never cross the distance.

But in reality, he says, we do cross the infinite at every step, and meet the eternal in every second. The puzzle exists only in logic. It is a lovely reversal. Instead of seeing the infinite as far away, Tagore finds it in each ordinary moment. Every step, every second, holds more than we can measure, if we notice.
prompt: What ordinary moment today could you treat as extraordinary?

text: Good and evil have an equal share in moulding character, and in some instances misery is a greater teacher than happiness.
context: Vivekananda (1863–1902) brought Vedanta to Western audiences in the 1890s, lecturing in English. Here he says that hard times shape us as much as good ones.
about:
Swami Vivekananda, the Indian teacher, gave the lectures collected as Karma-Yoga (1896). Karma, he explains, comes from a Sanskrit root meaning to do: all action is karma. The first chapter asks how actions shape character.

Good and evil, he says, share equally in shaping character, and sometimes misery is a greater teacher than happiness. Studying the great figures of history, he adds, we find that suffering taught them more than success. It is an old and consoling idea. Hard times are painful, but they are not wasted. They often shape us more deeply than ease.
prompt: What did a difficult time teach you that a good one couldn't?

text: Work incessantly, but be not attached to it.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 3 'The Secret of Work'
context: His summary of the Gita's teaching for modern working life: give full effort, but don't let the work own you.
about:
Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga (1896), lectures on the path of work, takes many of its ideas from the Bhagavad Gita. This chapter, The Secret of Work, names its central teaching.

Work incessantly, he says, but don't be attached to it. Work done without attachment doesn't bind us. Vivekananda compares the mind to a lake, where every action leaves ripples that shape our tendencies. It is a practical rule for anyone who works hard. Give yourself fully to the task, but don't tie your peace to it, or to its rewards.
prompt: Does your work belong to you, or do you belong to it?

text: Attachment comes only where we expect a return.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 3 'The Secret of Work'
context: We get tangled up in what we do when we keep an invisible bill for it. Giving without expecting frees us.
about:
In Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga (1896), lectures on the path of work, he asks us to treat whatever we work for, a person, a city, a cause, as a parent treats a child: expecting nothing in return.

Attachment comes only where we expect a return, he says. If we can always be the giver, offering our work freely to the world, it will not bind us. It is a simple diagnosis of much disappointment. We give, and then we wait to be paid back in thanks, praise or love. Giving without that expectation is freer, and kinder.
prompt: What are you doing mainly for what you hope to get back?

text: In helping the world we really help ourselves.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 5 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World'
context: Vivekananda suggests that the world doesn't need us as much as we need to help it. Service shapes the one who serves.
about:
Swami Vivekananda sums up a lecture in Karma-Yoga (1896), titled We Help Ourselves, Not the World, with this point. We are all in debt to the world, he says; the world owes us nothing.

In helping the world we really help ourselves. It is a great privilege to be allowed to do anything for others. The idea reverses the usual view of charity. We often think of helping as something we generously give. Vivekananda says it is something we receive: a chance to become better people. That makes service humble, not proud.
prompt: How has helping someone changed you?

text: It is not the receiver that is blessed, but it is the giver.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 5 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World'
context: Rather than feeling superior when we give, we should feel grateful for the chance to do it.
about:
In Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga (1896), he warns against giving from a high pedestal: coins in hand, saying here, my poor man.

Be grateful instead, he says, that the poor person is there, so that by giving you can help yourself. It is not the receiver who is blessed, but the giver. It is a striking reversal of pride. The person we help is not beneath us; they give us the chance to practise kindness. Gratitude, not superiority, is the right feeling when we give.
prompt: Who gave you the chance to be generous recently?

text: Life is given to us, we earn it by giving it.
context: Tagore wrote Stray Birds (1916) in English: short sayings, many inspired by Japanese haiku. Here he suggests that a life becomes truly ours through what we give.
about:
This line comes just before Tagore's saying on humility in Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings, each meant to stand alone.

Life is given to us; we earn it by giving it. We receive our lives without asking, but we make them our own by what we give: time, care, work, love. It is a short saying with a large idea. A life that only takes stays, in a way, borrowed. A life spent giving becomes truly ours.
prompt: What have you given that made you feel most alive?

text: Death's stamp gives value to the coin of life; making it possible to buy with life what is truly precious.
context: Because life ends, every hour has value, like a coin stamped by a mint. Mortality is what makes our choices matter.
about:
Rabindranath Tagore, the first person from outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, published Stray Birds in 1916: a few hundred short sayings, each standing on its own.

Death's stamp, he writes, gives value to the coin of life, making it possible to buy with life what is truly precious. A coin is worth something because it is stamped; life is precious because it ends. If we lived forever, nothing would be urgent or rare. Tagore turns death from a thief into what gives life its worth.
prompt: What would you 'buy' with your remaining time if you saw it as precious?

text: Death belongs to life as birth does. The walk is in the raising of the foot as in the laying of it down.
context: Walking needs both lifting and placing the foot. Life, Tagore says, needs both birth and death.
about:
Among the sayings of Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings, this one is about death.

Death belongs to life as birth does, he writes. Walking is as much in lifting the foot as in setting it down. We usually think of death as life's opposite. Tagore pictures it as one part of a single movement, like a step. It is a gentle and calming image. Birth and death, arrival and departure, are both part of the walk.
prompt: How would you live differently if you saw death as part of the walk?

text: He who wants to do good knocks at the gate; he who loves finds the gate open.
context: Trying hard to be good can feel like knocking on a closed door. Love opens it without effort.
about:
The saying just before this, in Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings, asks that life be beautiful like summer flowers, and death like autumn leaves.

Whoever wants to do good, Tagore writes, knocks at the gate; whoever loves finds the gate open. Trying hard to be good can feel like effort and struggle. Love makes goodness come naturally, without forcing. It is a gentle reversal. If we want to do good, perhaps the way is not more effort, but more love.
prompt: Where are you knocking when you could simply love?

text: We live in this world when we love it.
context: We can exist in the world without really living in it. Love is what makes us present.
about:
This is one of the last sayings in Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings. Just before it, Tagore asks the world to keep one phrase for him in its silence when he is dead: I have loved.

We live in this world when we love it. We can exist in the world without really living in it, passing through days without care or attention. Love, Tagore suggests, is what makes us present. It ties us to people, places and moments. The more we love, the more fully we are here.
prompt: What part of your world have you stopped loving?

text: Rest belongs to the work as the eyelids to the eyes.
context: Eyes need eyelids to keep working; work needs rest. Rest is not the enemy of effort but part of it.
about:
Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916) is a book of short sayings, many drawn from nature. The saying after this one calls man a born child, whose power is the power of growth.

Rest belongs to work, he writes, as the eyelids belong to the eyes. Eyelids aren't the enemy of seeing; they protect it, and make it possible to go on. In the same way, rest isn't the opposite of work, but part of it. It is a gentle correction for anyone who feels guilty about stopping. Good work needs good rest.
prompt: When did you last rest as part of your work, not as an escape from it?

text: If you shut your door to all errors truth will be shut out.
context: Fear of being wrong closes us to learning. Truth comes in through the same door as mistakes.
about:
In Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), he often turns ideas of truth and error upside down. The saying before this one is a little dialogue: where does the Impossible live? In the dreams of the powerless.

If you shut your door to all errors, he writes, truth will be shut out. Fear of being wrong can close us to learning. Truth often comes in through the same door as mistakes. It is a liberating thought. To find what is true, we have to risk being wrong, try ideas, and let some of them fail.
prompt: What mistake are you afraid to risk?

text: The small truth has words that are clear; the great truth has great silence.
context: Facts can be stated easily. The deepest truths, about love, death, and meaning, are harder to put into words.
about:
Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916) is a book of short sayings. In full, this one begins with an image: the water in a vessel sparkles, while the water in the sea is dark.

Then it continues: the small truth has words that are clear; the great truth has great silence. Small truths are easy to state and easy to see through, like water in a glass. Great truths are deep, like the sea, and words don't reach the bottom. It is a reminder that what matters most is often hardest to say.
prompt: What do you know deeply but can't explain?

text: We come nearest to the great when we are great in humility.
context: True greatness is not reached by pride but by humility.
about:
Rabindranath Tagore was an Indian poet and thinker, and in 1913 the first person from outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Stray Birds (1916) is a book of a few hundred very short sayings, each meant to be read on its own.

This one turns a common idea upside down. We often try to get close to greatness by making ourselves bigger: more impressive, more certain. Tagore suggests the opposite. Humility is not thinking little of ourselves, but being free of the need to show off. That freedom lets us admire, listen and learn, which is how we really come near to great people and great ideas. Pride keeps us at a distance, because it always needs to stay on top.
prompt: Where could humility bring you closer to what you admire?

text: The waterfall sings, 'I find my song, when I find my freedom.'
context: Water held back is silent; released, it sings. Our own voice appears when we are free to be ourselves.
about:
Many of the sayings in Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings, give voices to nature. The one before this pictures a bird that wishes it were a cloud, and a cloud that wishes it were a bird.

The waterfall sings: I find my song when I find my freedom. A waterfall is water released, falling freely, and its sound comes from that release. It is a gentle picture of self-expression. We often find our voice when we stop holding ourselves back. Freedom and song come together.
prompt: What would your 'song' be if you felt completely free?

text: What you are you do not see, what you see is your shadow.
context: We see only the outline we cast on the world, not our full self.
about:
Early in Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), Tagore calls his little thoughts the rustle of leaves, whispering joy in his mind. This one is among the most puzzling.

What you are you do not see; what you see is your shadow. When we look at ourselves, we see the outline we cast: our image, our reputation, how we come across. The fuller self that casts it is harder to see, because we are inside it. It is a humbling and intriguing idea. Self-knowledge may be less about staring at our shadow than about living, and letting others show us what they see.
prompt: What part of you do others see that you don't?

text: Do not insult your friend by lending him merits from your own pocket.
context: Praising a friend for qualities they don't have, or that are really ours, is a quiet insult. Real friendship sees people as they are.
about:
The sayings of Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings, are often about friendship and honesty. The one after this pictures the touch of nameless days clinging to the heart like moss on an old tree.

Do not insult your friend, Tagore writes, by lending them merits from your own pocket. Praising a friend for qualities they don't have, or that are really ours, doesn't honour them. It treats them as needing our flattery. Real friendship sees and values people as they are. That is the best compliment.
prompt: Do you see your friends as they are, or as you'd like them to be?

text: To be outspoken is easy when you do not wait to speak the complete truth.
context: Blunt speech can pass for honesty. The whole truth takes patience and care.
about:
In Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings, the saying just before this one contrasts bees, who hum thanks to the flowers, with a gaudy butterfly sure that the flowers owe thanks to him.

To be outspoken is easy, Tagore writes, when you don't wait to speak the complete truth. Blunt speech can pass for honesty, but it is often only part of the truth, delivered quickly. The whole truth takes patience, listening and care. Being frank isn't the same as being truthful. Sometimes it is just being fast.
prompt: When did your bluntness leave out part of the truth?

text: Life has become richer by the love that has been lost.
context: Lost love leaves sorrow, but also depth. Tagore sees it as a gift rather than only a wound.
about:
Among the short sayings of Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916), a book of a few hundred short sayings, this one is about loss.

Life has become richer by the love that has been lost. It is an unexpected turn. We usually see lost love only as a wound. Tagore suggests it also leaves something behind: depth, tenderness, and the memory of having loved. Grief is the shadow of love, and love, even lost, has enriched us. It doesn't remove the pain. It gives it meaning.
prompt: How has a love you lost enriched your life?

text: Kicks only raise dust and not crops from the earth.
context: Force and anger make noise but produce nothing. Growth needs patient work.
about:
Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds (1916) uses many images from farming and the earth. The saying just before this one says that the movement of life has its rest in its own music.

Kicks only raise dust, not crops, from the earth. Anger and force make noise, but produce nothing. Growing anything, a field, a skill, a relationship, takes patient work: ploughing, sowing, tending. It is a simple, earthy image with a clear point. Frustration may feel like action, but only care brings a harvest.
prompt: Where are you kicking when you should be planting?

text: His freedom and fulfilment is in love, which is another name for perfect comprehension.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Relation of the Individual to the Universe'
context: For Tagore, to love something fully is to understand it fully, and that is where we find freedom.
about:
In the first talk of Tagore's Sadhana (1913), he says that a person is great because their soul can take in everything, and that callous habits and blind busyness shut that greatness out.

Our freedom and fulfilment, he says, are in love, which is another name for perfect comprehension. To love something is to understand it from the inside, and to understand it fully is, in a sense, to love it. It is a rich idea. Love here is not only a feeling, but a way of knowing. The more we love, the more we truly see.
prompt: What do you understand best because you love it?

text: Whatever a great man does, that other men also do. And people follow whatever he receives as authority.
context: Krishna reminds Arjuna that leaders set an example whether they mean to or not. Others copy what we do more than what we say.
about:
Why should even someone who has nothing to gain keep acting? Krishna answers this in chapter III of the Bhagavad Gita, his conversation with the prince Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, in the great Indian epic the Mahabharata.

Whatever a great person does, other people also do, he says, and they follow whatever that person takes as the standard. Example spreads. Those who are admired, at home, at work or in public, set a pattern for others. It is a reminder of the responsibility that comes with influence. People don't only listen to what we say. They copy what we do.
prompt: Who is copying your example without your noticing?

text: For nobody ever remains even for an instant without performing some action …
context: Even doing nothing is a kind of action. The question is not whether to act, but how.
about:
In chapter III of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna answers Arjuna, who hopes to avoid wrongdoing by doing nothing. Not acting, Krishna says, doesn't free us from action, and giving things up doesn't make us perfect.

No one remains even for a moment without doing something; our own nature drives everyone to act. Even doing nothing is a kind of action, with its own results. It is a useful thought for anyone who avoids decisions. We can't escape acting. The real question is not whether to act, but how, and in what spirit.
prompt: What are you 'doing' by not doing anything?

text: He who is alike to friend and foe, as also in honour and dishonour, who is alike in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, who is free from attachments, to whom praise and blame are alike, who is taciturn, and contented with anything whatever …
context: Krishna's portrait of a steady person: not cold, but no longer thrown around by every change in fortune or opinion.
about:
In chapter XII of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes the people he holds most dear: those who feel no hatred, are friendly and compassionate, and are free from selfishness.

Such a person, he says, is the same to friend and foe, in honour and dishonour, in cold and heat, pleasure and pain; free from attachment; finding praise and blame alike. It is a portrait of deep evenness. Not coldness, but a steady heart that isn't thrown about by every change. Few of us reach it fully. But we can move towards it.
prompt: Which of these pairs throws you off balance most?

text: Misery comes through attachment, not through work.
context: Hard work rarely makes us miserable on its own. Clinging to its results does.
about:
Swami Vivekananda's chapter on freedom in Karma-Yoga (1896) says that pain and pleasure, poverty and wealth are passing conditions of this world, not our real nature. And yet we must keep working.

Misery comes through attachment, not through work, he says. As soon as we identify ourselves with our work, we feel miserable; if we don't, we don't feel that misery. Hard work rarely makes us unhappy on its own. Tying our whole self to its success or failure does. We can work fully, and still keep a little distance.
prompt: Is it the work, or your attachment to it, that tires you?

text: Everything that you do under compulsion goes to build up attachment.
context: What we do freely leaves us free; what we do because we feel we must binds us.
about:
In his chapter on freedom in Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga (1896), he criticises the idea of duty as a burden: something that scorches everyone who carries it.

Whatever you have to give the world, he says, give it, but not under compulsion. Everything done under compulsion builds up attachment. Acting because we feel we must ties us to the act, and to resentment. Acting freely, out of love or choice, leaves us free. It is a subtle difference, but a real one. The same action can bind us or free us, depending on why we do it.
prompt: What are you doing only because you feel you must?

text: He works best who works without any motive, neither for money, nor for fame, nor for anything else …
context: Work done for its own sake is often the best work, because nothing distracts from it.
about:
Swami Vivekananda quotes, in Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga (1896), lectures on the path of work, the Buddha's advice not to believe things just because of old books or tradition, but to reason them out, and believe what does good to all.

Whoever works best, he says, works without any motive, neither for money, nor for fame, nor for anything else. Work done for its own sake is often the best work, because nothing distracts from it: no fear of failure, no hunger for praise. It is an ideal few of us fully reach. But it points to something true: the work itself can be enough.
prompt: What would you work on if no one paid or praised you?

text: Let us do good because it is good to do good …
context: Doing good for a reward turns kindness into a trade. Vivekananda asks us to do it for its own sake.
about:
The ideal worker, Swami Vivekananda says in Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga (1896), lectures on the path of work, needs no motive beyond the inborn love of freedom. He quotes the Bhagavad Gita: to work you have the right, but not to its fruits.

Let us do good, he says, because it is good to do good. Doing good only for a reward, even a reward after death, binds us. It is a pure and demanding idea. Kindness done for praise or profit is still kindness, but it ties us to the reward. Kindness done for its own sake leaves us free, and is all the sweeter.
prompt: What good thing would you do even if no one ever knew?

text: No one was ever really taught by another; each of us has to teach himself.
context: Teachers can point the way, but understanding is something we do ourselves.
about:
Every kind of yoga, Swami Vivekananda says in Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga (1896), lectures on the path of work, follows the same order: first hear, then think, then practise. Many things will become clear only slowly.

The explanation of everything is in ourselves, he says. No one was ever really taught by another; each of us has to teach ourselves. The outer teacher gives only the suggestion that wakes up the inner teacher. Good teachers matter. But understanding is something that happens inside us. A lesson only becomes ours when we have worked it out.
prompt: What lesson have you had to teach yourself?

text: The true prevails, not the untrue …
context: In its Sanskrit form, satyameva jayate, this line is India's national motto, written beneath the national emblem.
about:
The Mundaka Upanishad, one of the ancient Indian texts translated by Max Müller, says that the self can be found through truthfulness, discipline, right knowledge and self-restraint.

The true prevails, not the untrue, it says; by the true the path is laid out, on which the old sages travelled. The opening words, in Sanskrit, became India's national motto. Here they are a statement of faith in truth itself: lies may win for a while, but truth endures and makes the way. It is an old hope, and still worth holding.
prompt: Where have you seen truth win in the end?

text: The highest excellence is like that of water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving to the contrary, the low place which all men dislike.
context: Water is Taoism's favourite teacher: it nourishes everything, never fights, and settles where nobody else wants to be.
about:
This is chapter 8 of the Tao Te Ching, the short Chinese classic of 81 chapters traditionally attributed to Laozi, in James Legge's 1891 translation. The Tao, or Way, is its name for the deep pattern of how things work.

Water, it says, comes closest to that Way. It helps everything it touches, never competes, and settles in the low places nobody wants. That is an odd model for a good life, and a deliberate one. We usually admire people who rise and push forward. Laozi admires what serves quietly and doesn't need to be on top. The chapter ends: because it does not quarrel about its low place, no one finds fault with it.
prompt: Where could you help without needing the high place or the credit?

text: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a firm will.
context: In four short contrasts, Laozi weighs outer success against inner achievement: knowing others against knowing yourself, beating others against mastering yourself.
about:
This is chapter 33 of the Tao Te Ching, the classic attributed to Laozi. It is built from short pairs, each setting an outer achievement beside an inner one.

Knowing others makes us discerning; knowing ourselves makes us intelligent. Beating others makes us strong; mastering ourselves makes us mighty. Being satisfied with what we have makes us rich. In each pair, the second is harder and less visible, and Laozi ranks it higher. Our world mostly rewards the first kind: insight into others, victories, gains. The chapter asks us to value the quieter achievements, which no one else may ever see.
prompt: Which kind of strength are you building: over others, or over yourself?

text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space for the axle, that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out from the walls to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space within, that its use depends.
context: A wheel works because of the empty hole in its centre, a bowl because of its hollow, a room because of its open space. What is empty is what makes things useful.
about:
Chapter 11 of the Tao Te Ching uses three everyday objects: a cart wheel whose thirty spokes meet at the hub, a clay pot, and a room with a door and windows cut into its walls.

In each case, what makes the thing useful is the empty part: the hole for the axle, the hollow of the pot, the space inside the room. We notice the solid parts and forget the space. Laozi turns that around. A diary with no gaps, a mind with no quiet, a conversation with no pauses can all become useless in the same way. Emptiness, here, is not a lack. It is what makes room for something to happen.
prompt: Where could some emptiness make your life more useful, not less?

text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a small heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
context: The source of the saying 'a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step'. A li is a traditional Chinese measure of distance.
about:
Chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching is where the famous saying about a journey of a thousand miles comes from. A li was a Chinese measure of distance, much shorter than a mile.

The chapter begins with advice to act early: deal with things before they appear, and keep order before disorder starts. Then come three pictures of growth. A tree too big to hug began as a tiny sprout; a nine-storey tower began as a small heap of earth; a long journey began with one step. Big things are made of small beginnings. That is a comfort when a task seems huge, and a warning when a problem seems small.
prompt: What is the single step you could take today?

text: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere.
context: The opening line of the last chapter. Polish can be a sign that something is being sold rather than said.
about:
This line opens chapter 81, the last chapter of the Tao Te Ching. Two more pairs follow in the same pattern: the skilled do not argue, and those who truly know are not widely learned.

Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Laozi is suspicious of polish. A beautiful speech can be beautiful because it is selling something, while honest words are often plain, even awkward. That doesn't mean every rough speaker is honest, or every graceful one false. It means we should not let style do the convincing. When words dazzle us, it is worth asking what they are for.
prompt: Whose plain words have you overlooked because they weren't polished?

text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness.
context: Laozi notes that overfilling and oversharpening both defeat their purpose: the full cup spills, the fine edge dulls. Knowing when to stop is a skill.
about:
Chapter 9 of the Tao Te Ching goes on to warn that when gold and jade fill the hall, no one can keep them safe, and that wealth and honours which lead to arrogance bring their own ruin.

Its two images are simple. Carry a vessel filled to the brim and it spills; keep sharpening a blade and the edge soon wears away. Both describe going too far. More is not always better: a full cup is harder to carry than a nearly full one. The chapter ends with advice about stopping in time: when the work is done, step back. Knowing when enough is enough is a skill most of us have to learn.
prompt: What are you filling to the brim that would be better left with room?

text: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. He whose desires are few gets them; he whose desires are many goes astray.
context: What bends ends up whole, what is empty gets filled, what is worn out is renewed. Those who want little get what they want; those who want much get lost.
about:
Laozi's Tao Te Ching gives this teaching in chapter 22. Like many chapters of the book, it is built on paradox.

The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. Each reversal says that what looks like a weakness can be the beginning of its opposite. Then comes advice on desire: those who want little get it, while those who want much go astray. The chapter goes on to describe the sage, who is free from self-display and therefore shines. Wanting less, and needing less attention, turns out to be a strength.
prompt: What in your life is 'crooked' now and might yet become straight?

text: Who can make the muddy water clear? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.
context: Stirring muddy water only clouds it more. Left alone, the sediment settles by itself.
about:
Chapter 15 of the Tao Te Ching describes the wise people of old: careful like someone wading a stream in winter, plain like uncarved wood, and dull like muddy water.

Then comes the question: who can make muddy water clear? Let it be still, and it will gradually clear by itself. Stirring only makes it worse. The same is true of an agitated mind, a heated argument or a confusing situation. Our instinct is to do something, to keep stirring. Laozi suggests that sometimes the wisest action is to wait, and let things settle until we can see the bottom.
prompt: What might become clear if you simply stopped stirring it?

text: To know and yet think we do not know is the highest attainment; not to know and yet think we do know is a disease.
context: Laozi places wisdom in knowing the limits of our knowledge. The sick mind is not the one that doubts, but the one that is sure it already knows.
about:
Chapter 71 of the Tao Te Ching is one of its shortest. It goes on to say that the only protection against this disease is to be pained by the thought of having it.

To know, and yet think we do not know, is the highest attainment. Not to know, and think we know, is a disease. The same idea appears in many traditions: wisdom begins with knowing the limits of our knowledge. The danger is not doubt but false certainty, which closes the mind and stops us learning. The remedy Laozi offers is simple: to feel uneasy at the thought of fooling ourselves.
prompt: What do you think you know that you might not?

text: There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
context: There is no greater wrong than encouraging greed, and no greater misfortune than never being satisfied. Knowing that you have enough is the only lasting wealth.
about:
Chapter 46 of the Tao Te Ching begins with an image of war and peace: when the Way prevails, swift horses are sent back to pull dung-carts; when it is forgotten, war-horses are bred on the borders.

Then it names the root of the trouble: ambition encouraged, discontent with one's lot, the wish always to be getting more. These, it says, are the greatest guilt, the greatest calamity and the greatest fault. The cure is contentment, the only kind of enough that lasts. It is an old answer, and still a difficult one. Whatever we gain, wanting more will always find a gap. Knowing that we have enough closes it.
prompt: What would be enough for you, really?

text: He who devotes himself to learning seeks from day to day to increase his knowledge; he who devotes himself to the Tao seeks from day to day to diminish his doing.
context: Learning adds something every day; the Tao, Laozi's 'Way' of nature, asks us to let go of something every day. Some growth comes from doing less, not more.
about:
Laozi's Tao Te Ching gives this teaching in chapter 48. The Tao, or Way, is Laozi's name for the deep pattern of how things move, which the wise follow rather than force.

Learning, it says, adds something every day; following the Way takes something away every day. What is taken away is doing: the extra effort, the forcing, the busy interfering. The chapter goes on: reduce it again and again until you reach doing nothing on purpose, and then nothing is left undone. It sounds like a paradox, and it is one. But we know the experience: some things go better the less we push them.
prompt: What could you take away from your days rather than add?

text: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have the idea of what ugliness is; they all know the skill of the skilful, and in doing this they have the idea of what the want of skill is.
context: As soon as we call something beautiful, we create the idea of ugly; as soon as we call someone skilful, we create the idea of clumsy. Every label creates its opposite.
about:
Chapter 2 of the Tao Te Ching goes on to list other pairs that create each other: existence and non-existence, difficulty and ease, length and shortness.

As soon as we call something beautiful, we also create the idea of ugly; as soon as we praise skill, we create the idea of clumsiness. Every label carries its opposite with it. Laozi isn't saying that beauty or skill are unreal. He is pointing out how much our judgements depend on comparison. That can make us gentler. The person we call clumsy is only clumsy next to someone else, on a scale we made ourselves.
prompt: When you call something beautiful or skilful, what are you quietly calling ugly or clumsy?

text: The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest; that which has no substantial existence enters where there is no crevice.
context: Water is soft, yet it wears down stone and slips through the smallest crack. Laozi sees the same quiet power in gentleness and patience.
about:
Chapter 43 of the Tao Te Ching contains this line. The chapter ends by praising the teaching without words, and the advantage of not forcing things.

The softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest; what has no substance enters where there is no crack. Laozi doesn't name it here, but water is the natural example: soft and yielding, it still wears down stone and seeps into the smallest gap. The lesson is that gentleness can be powerful. Patience, kindness and steady persistence often achieve what force cannot, because they don't meet resistance head-on.
prompt: Where could you go further by being gentler?

text: He who knows the Tao does not care to speak about it; he who is ever ready to speak about it does not know it.
context: Often quoted as 'those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know'. Deep understanding tends to be quiet.
about:
Chapter 56 of the Tao Te Ching is often quoted in a shorter form: those who know do not speak, and those who speak do not know.

The chapter goes on to describe such a person: they keep their mouth shut, blunt their sharp points and soften their brightness to blend in with others. Deep understanding, in this picture, tends to be quiet. Those who are always ready to explain the Way have probably not grasped it. It is a useful check on ourselves. When we are most eager to talk about something, it may be worth asking how well we really know it.
prompt: What do you understand best, and how little do you need to say about it?

text: But I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others.
context: Laozi's three treasures: gentleness, frugality, and not needing to be first.
about:
Laozi's Tao Te Ching gives this teaching in chapter 67. Laozi calls these his three precious things. In Legge's older English, economy means frugality, and shrinking from taking precedence means not pushing to be first.

Then he explains why they matter. Gentleness lets him be bold; frugality lets him be generous; not pushing to the front makes him fit for the highest honour. Each treasure looks weak, and turns out to make something strong possible. He also warns against the reverse: people now drop gentleness and want only boldness, drop frugality and want only to spend, and seek only to be foremost. That road, he says, ends in death.
prompt: Which of the three treasures could you practise today?

text: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. So it is with all things. Trees and plants, in their early growth, are soft and brittle; at their death, dry and withered. Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
context: Living things bend; dead things are rigid. Flexibility is a sign of life, in bodies and in minds.
about:
Chapter 76 of the Tao Te Ching goes on to say that an army which relies on its strength does not win, and that the strong tree is the one that gets cut down.

At birth we are supple; at death, stiff. Young plants are soft; dead ones are dry and withered. So firmness belongs with death, and softness with life. Laozi uses the body as a picture of the mind. Rigid views, fixed habits and an unwillingness to bend may feel strong, but they are signs of something hardening. Staying flexible, open to change and correction, is a sign of being alive.
prompt: Where have you grown rigid, and how could you soften?

text: The farther that one goes out from himself, the less he knows.
context: Laozi's paradox for a restless age: the more we chase understanding out in the world, the less we may know ourselves. Some answers are found by staying still.
about:
Chapter 47 of the Tao Te Ching begins: without going outside his door, one understands all that takes place under the sky.

The farther we go out from ourselves, the less we know. In an age of endless news and travel, it is a startling claim. Laozi isn't against seeing the world. He is saying that understanding does not come from collecting more and more impressions from outside. It comes from attention and reflection. The sages, the chapter says, gained their knowledge without travelling. Some answers are found by looking inward, not further away.
prompt: What could you understand by staying where you are?

text: The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own.
context: Laozi says generosity does not empty us. What we give to others somehow enlarges what we have, in friendship, trust, and peace of mind.
about:
This line comes from chapter 81, the last chapter of the Tao Te Ching. It follows the remark that the sage does not pile things up for himself.

The more he spends for others, the more he has of his own; the more he gives, the more he has. On paper this is impossible: giving means having less. But Laozi is talking about more than money. Kindness, time and attention given to others tend to come back as friendship, trust and a fuller life. A generous person is rarely poor in what matters most. The book ends on that note: the sage acts, but does not strive.
prompt: What could you give today that would leave you richer?

text: People in their conduct of affairs are constantly ruining them when they are on the eve of success.
context: Many projects fail at the very end, through carelessness when success is near. Laozi asks for the same care at the end as at the beginning.
about:
Chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching is the same chapter that says a journey of a thousand li begins with a single step.

People, it says, often ruin their affairs just when they are about to succeed. If they were as careful at the end as at the beginning, they would not ruin them. Most of us know the pattern: a project done carefully until the last stretch and then rushed, or a good habit dropped just before it would have stuck. Beginnings get our attention; endings need it just as much. The finish deserves the same care as the first step.
prompt: What nearly finished thing deserves your full care now?

text: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,—the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,—the creature of a season.
context: The Spirit of the Ocean speaks to a river god who thought himself great. A frog at the bottom of a well takes its circle of sky for the whole sky.
about:
Zhuangzi was a Chinese Taoist thinker of the 4th century BCE, whose book mixes stories, jokes and arguments. In this story the Spirit of a river, swollen by the autumn floods, thinks itself the greatest thing in the world, until it reaches the ocean.

Seeing the ocean, the river admits its pride. The Spirit of the Ocean answers: you cannot talk of the ocean to a frog in a well, or of ice to an insect that lives one summer. Each is limited by where and when it lives. The point is not to mock them, but to see that we, too, have our wells. Now that you know how small you are, the ocean says, I can speak to you of great things.
prompt: Which well are you looking up from, and how big is the sky beyond it?

text: Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
context: The most famous passage in Taoist literature. Zhuangzi wonders how firm the line really is between who we think we are and what we experience.
about:
Zhuangzi was a Chinese Taoist thinker of the 4th century BCE. His book's thirty-three chapters mix stories, jokes and arguments, and this short dream, from the second chapter, is one of its best-known passages.
