He dreams he is a butterfly, fluttering happily about, with no idea he is Zhuangzi. Then he wakes, and wonders: was I a man dreaming of being a butterfly, or am I now a butterfly dreaming of being a man? It is a playful question with a serious edge. How sure are we of the line between who we think we are and what we experience? Zhuangzi doesn't answer. He leaves us a little lighter about our certainties.
prompt: What are you sure about that might be less solid than it seems?

text: "See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes." "You not being a fish yourself," said Hui Tzŭ, "how can you possibly know in what consists the pleasure of fishes?" "And you not being I," retorted Chuang Tzŭ, "how can you know that I do not know?"
context: Zhuangzi and his friend, the logician Hui Shi, argue on a bridge about whether anyone can know a fish's joy. Zhuangzi turns the logic back on him: strict proof is not the only way we know things.
about:
This story comes from the book of Zhuangzi, the Chinese thinker of the 4th century BCE. Hui Tzu, his friend and frequent opponent in argument, was a chief minister in the state of Liang.

Walking on a bridge, Zhuangzi says how happy the minnows look. Hui Tzu objects: you're not a fish, so how can you know? Zhuangzi turns the logic around: you're not me, so how can you know I don't know? The story ends with Zhuangzi saying he knew it “from my own feelings on this bridge”. It's a joke with a real point: strict proof is not the only way of knowing. We also know things by being present and paying attention.
prompt: Where could you simply enjoy something instead of proving it?

text: When I first began to cut up bullocks, I saw before me simply whole bullocks. After three years' practice, I saw no more whole animals. … And now I work with my mind and not with my eye.
context: Prince Hui's cook has used the same knife for nineteen years because he follows the natural gaps instead of forcing his way. Mastery means working with the grain.
about:
This story comes from the third chapter of Zhuangzi's book. Prince Hui watches his cook cut up an ox with movements so smooth they look like a dance, and praises his skill.

The cook answers that what he cares about is the Way, which goes beyond skill. At first he saw only the whole animal. After three years he no longer saw it whole. Now he works by feel, following the natural gaps between the joints, and after nineteen years his knife is still as sharp as new, because it never forces its way. It is a picture of mastery: long practice, until we stop fighting the material and start following its grain.
prompt: Where are you hacking at something that has a natural opening?

text: "A man," replied Confucius, "does not seek to see himself in running water, but in still water. For only what is itself still can instil stillness into others."
context: Zhuangzi puts these words in the mouth of Confucius. We can only see ourselves clearly in water that is still.
about:
This passage comes from Zhuangzi's book, which often puts its own ideas into the mouth of Confucius. Here Confucius is asked why so many people follow Wang T'ai, a man whose toes have been cut off, who neither preaches nor argues.

Confucius answers with an image: no one looks for their reflection in running water, only in still water. Only what is still can bring stillness to others. People come to Wang T'ai not because he chases them, but because he is calm. It is a quiet idea about influence. We cannot settle anyone by rushing at them. Our own steadiness is what helps others steady themselves.
prompt: How could you become still enough to see yourself clearly?

text: It is wood of no quality, and of no use. That is why it has attained its present age.
context: A carpenter dismisses a huge old tree as worthless. That evening the tree appears in his dream: being 'useless' is what let it grow so old.
about:
In the fourth chapter of Zhuangzi's book, a master carpenter passes a huge old tree, so big that crowds gather to stare at it. He walks on without a glance.

His apprentice is amazed, but the carpenter explains: make a boat of it and it would sink; a coffin, and it would rot. It is useless wood, and that is why it has lived so long. That night the tree appears in his dream: useful fruit trees, it says, are stripped and broken, while being useless has let it grow great. Zhuangzi is teasing our idea of usefulness. What the world calls useless may be exactly what lets something flourish.
prompt: What 'useless' thing in your life is actually keeping you whole?

text: Great knowledge embraces the whole: small knowledge, a part only.
context: Zhuangzi contrasts two kinds of knowing: small knowledge grabs one part and takes it for everything; great knowledge keeps the whole picture in view.
about:
This line comes from the second chapter of Zhuangzi's book, a long reflection on how people take their own partial views for the whole truth.

Great knowledge embraces the whole; small knowledge, only a part. Small knowledge is not wrong about its part, but it takes the part for everything, and then quarrels with those who hold a different part. Great knowledge sees how the pieces fit together, and so has less need to fight. The chapter says the same of speech: great speech covers the whole ground, small speech is narrow. Seeing more tends to make us calmer.
prompt: What part of a situation have you been mistaking for the whole?

text: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.
context: Zhuangzi warns against trying to know everything. A limited life spent chasing limitless knowledge is exhausted before it gets anywhere.
about:
These are the opening words of the third chapter of Zhuangzi's book, the chapter that also tells the story of Prince Hui's cook.

My life has a limit, but knowledge has none. Using a limited life to chase limitless knowledge is exhausting, and leads nowhere. This is not an argument against learning. It is about choosing. We cannot read every book, follow every story or master every subject, and trying to only leaves us anxious. Zhuangzi suggests a middle course: know what you need, and care for the life you have. A full life is not a life full of information.
prompt: What are you trying to master that could never be finished?

text: When she died, I could not help being affected by her death. … passing from one phase to another like the sequence of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
context: When Zhuangzi's wife dies, his friend finds him singing and drumming on a bowl. He grieved, he explains, and then saw her death as part of nature's turning seasons.
about:
This story comes from Zhuangzi's book. When his wife dies, his friend Hui Tzu comes to offer his sympathy, and finds Zhuangzi sitting on the ground, beating time on a bowl and singing. He is shocked.

Zhuangzi explains. When she died, he was moved like anyone. Then he thought: before birth she had no form; then she was born; now, through another change, she has died, as spring turns to summer, autumn and winter. To weep and wail would be to ignore how things are. The story is not cold: he grieved first. It shows a way of meeting loss with understanding, seeing death as part of the same change that brought her life.
prompt: Which ending in your life could you see as a change of season?

text: For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep.
context: Zhuangzi uses the mirror as a picture of a free mind: it reflects whatever comes, clearly and fully, and holds on to nothing once it has gone.
about:
Zhuangzi's seventh chapter, the last of the seven known as the “inside” chapters, is the source of this passage. It describes the perfect person, who acts without forcing.

Such a person uses their mind like a mirror. It grasps nothing and refuses nothing; it receives, but does not keep. A mirror shows whatever is in front of it, fully and without judging, and when the thing goes, it lets it go. Our minds tend to do the opposite: we cling to some experiences, push others away, and replay them long after. The mirror suggests another way: meet each thing clearly, then let it pass.
prompt: What are you still holding that you could simply let pass through?

text: Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt to the sum total of existence. Life and death are as day and night.
context: Life is only borrowed, and life and death follow each other like day and night. A man says this calmly after a strange growth appears on his elbow.
about:
In the same chapter of Zhuangzi's book as the story of his wife's death, two men are looking at the tombs of old heroes in the mountains when ugly sores suddenly break out on their left elbows.

One asks the other: do you loathe this? Not I, he answers. Life is only a loan, and life and death follow each other like day and night. If the same fate as those heroes reaches me, why should I loathe it? The scene is odd, almost comic, as Zhuangzi's often are, but its point is serious. When we see our life as borrowed, we hold it less tightly, and change, even in our own body, frightens us less.
prompt: If your life is a loan, what are you doing with it?

text: The mushroom of a morning knows not the alternation of day and night. The chrysalis knows not the alternation of spring and autumn.
context: Every creature measures the world by its own lifespan. Zhuangzi invites us to imagine much longer and shorter scales than our own.
about:
In the first chapter of Zhuangzi's book, a cicada laughs at a giant bird that rises ninety thousand li before flying south: why go so high, it says, when it can barely get from tree to tree?

Zhuangzi answers that small knowledge cannot grasp great knowledge, just as a short life cannot grasp a long one. A mushroom that lives one morning never knows night and day; a chrysalis never knows spring and autumn. Every creature measures the world by its own span, and that includes us. Our sense of big and small, long and short, is shaped by our own size and lifetime. Imagining other scales loosens our certainties.
prompt: How would today's worry look on the scale of a hundred years?

text: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
context: The famous opening of the Tao Te Ching. The deepest reality, Laozi warns, can't be fully captured in words, including his own.
about:
These are the opening words of the Tao Te Ching, in James Legge's 1891 translation. Tao means way or path, which is why Legge speaks of a Tao that can be trodden.

The Tao that can be walked on is not the lasting Tao; the name that can be named is not the lasting name. So the book begins by warning us about itself. Whatever it says about the deepest reality will fall short, because words can only point. It is a humble way to open a book of wisdom. It invites us to read the rest slowly: not as definitions to memorise, but as signposts towards something we have to see for ourselves.
prompt: What matters to you that words never quite capture?

text: In the highest antiquity, the people did not know that there were their rulers. In the next age they loved them and praised them. In the next they feared them; in the next they despised them. … Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves!'
context: Laozi ranks leaders: the best are barely noticed, and when the work is done, people feel they did it themselves.
about:
Chapter 17 of the Tao Te Ching ranks rulers from best to worst.

In the earliest times, people hardly knew they had rulers. Next came rulers they loved and praised, then ones they feared, then ones they despised. When the best rulers' work was done, the people all said: we did it ourselves. Laozi's ideal leader is nearly invisible, and their success shows in how capable everyone else feels. It is a demanding standard for any leader, parent or teacher: to help so well that others hardly notice the help.
prompt: When did you help others in a way that let them say they did it themselves?

text: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk easily. So, he who displays himself does not shine; he who asserts his own views is not distinguished …
context: Straining to look bigger makes us unsteady. Showing off rarely earns the respect it seeks.
about:
Chapter 24 of the Tao Te Ching ends by comparing self-display to leftover food, or a tumour on the body: things everyone dislikes.

Standing on tiptoe, we cannot stand firm; taking huge strides, we cannot walk far. Laozi turns these into lessons about showing off. Those who display themselves do not shine; those who push their views are not respected; those who boast do not get credit. Straining to look bigger makes us unsteady, and other people can tell. Standing flat on our feet, as we are, is both easier and more convincing.
prompt: Where are you standing on tiptoe?

text: Or fame or life, / Which do you hold more dear? / Or life or wealth, / To which would you adhere? … Who is content / Needs fear no shame. / Who knows to stop / Incurs no blame.
context: A simple test of priorities: if you had to choose between fame or wealth and your own life, which would you keep? Knowing when to stop keeps us safe.
about:
This is chapter 44 of the Tao Te Ching, which James Legge translated as a short rhyming poem.

It asks a simple question: which is dearer, fame or your life? Which matters more, your life or your wealth? Put that way, the answer is obvious, yet many people trade health, time and peace for reputation and money. The poem goes on: whoever clings to fame gives up something greater. Its ending is the key. Whoever is content need fear no shame, and whoever knows when to stop stays out of danger, and lives long.
prompt: What are you trading your life for?

text: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.
context: Deal with problems while they are small, and build great things step by step.
about:
Chapter 63 of the Tao Te Ching advises tackling difficult things while they are still easy, and doing great things while they are still small. It also says to repay injury with kindness.

Every difficult thing, it says, began as something easy, and every great thing as something small. That cuts two ways. Problems are easiest to fix early, before they grow: a misunderstanding, a leak, a bad habit. And great achievements are built from small steps, taken one at a time. The chapter adds a warning: whoever thinks everything easy will find it hard. Taking small things seriously is how big things go well.
prompt: Which small problem today could become a big one if you ignore it?

text: That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they; … So it is that the sage ruler, wishing to be above men, puts himself by his words below them, and, wishing to be before them, places his person behind them.
context: The sea gathers all rivers because it lies lowest. Laozi's model of leadership is humble service, long before the modern phrase 'servant leadership'.
about:
Chapter 66 of the Tao Te Ching contains this line. Rivers and seas are called the kings of all the valley streams, because every stream flows down into them.

They can receive all that water because they lie lower than the streams. In the same way, Laozi says, a wise ruler who wants to be above people puts himself below them in his words, and one who wants to lead them walks behind them. Then, the chapter adds, people do not feel his weight. It is an early picture of leadership as service: authority is earned by lowering ourselves, not by pressing down on others.
prompt: How could you lead by putting yourself lower?

text: Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place …
context: Those who don't push themselves forward often end up trusted and in front.
about:
Chapter 7 of the Tao Te Ching begins with heaven and earth: they last so long, it says, because they do not live for themselves.

Then comes the lesson for people. The sage puts himself last, and finds himself first; he treats his own person as if it were not his concern, and it is preserved. The chapter asks: is it not because he has no selfish aims that his aims are achieved? It is an observation as much as a moral. People who don't push themselves forward are often the ones others trust, and so they end up leading.
prompt: When did putting others first bring you forward?

text: He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it.
context: Laozi is speaking about power over a kingdom, but the lesson fits much else: grip something too hard and it slips away.
about:
Chapter 29 of Laozi's Tao Te Ching speaks of someone who wants to seize a kingdom by force: the kingdom, he says, is a spirit-like thing that cannot be got by active doing.

Whoever tries to win it that way destroys it; whoever tries to grip it loses it. The lesson reaches far beyond kingdoms. Grip sand and it runs through your fingers. Try to control a friendship, a child or a team too tightly, and you damage the very thing you wanted to hold. The chapter ends with the sage putting away excess, extravagance and indulgence. Some things can only be kept with an open hand.
prompt: What are you gripping so hard that it's slipping away?

text: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
context: Small fish fall apart if you keep stirring them. Good leaders don't keep interfering.
about:
This is the opening of chapter 60 of the Tao Te Ching. Small fish are delicate: turn them too often in the pan and they fall apart.

Governing a great state, Laozi says, is like cooking them. The point is restraint. A good ruler doesn't keep stirring with new rules, reforms and interference, because every turn breaks something. It is advice for more than governments. Managers, parents and anyone in charge can do harm by doing too much. Sometimes the most skilful thing is to set things up well, keep the heat steady, and leave them alone.
prompt: Where would less interference from you help things work?

text: Who thinks his great achievements poor / Shall find his vigour long endure.
context: Those who don't rest on their successes keep their energy longer.
about:
The Tao Te Ching is a short Chinese classic of 81 chapters, traditionally attributed to Laozi, and a founding text of Taoism. Much of it teaches through paradox, and chapter 45 is full of them: the greatest skill looks clumsy, the greatest fullness seems empty.

This opening line is about energy. When we think our achievements are great, we start defending them: our reputation, our image, our place. That takes effort and makes us stiff. Someone who sees their successes as modest stays open, keeps learning, and has nothing to guard. In Laozi's picture, real strength often looks quiet from the outside.
prompt: Which success are you resting on too comfortably?

text: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared …
context: Praise and blame both make us dependent on others' opinion. Laozi advises being free from both.
about:
In the Tao Te Ching, this is part of chapter 13. Laozi then explains what he means: winning favour makes us afraid of losing it, and losing it makes us fear something worse.

Favour and disgrace, then, are equally to be feared. That sounds strange: surely favour is good? But favour ties us to whoever gives it. Once we enjoy praise, a promotion or someone's approval, we start worrying about keeping it, and so we are no longer free. Disgrace hurts precisely because the favour mattered so much. Laozi's advice is to depend less on both, and so to stand on our own feet.
prompt: Which unsettles you more, praise or criticism, and why?

text: He who in Tao's wars has skill / Assumes no martial port; / He who fights with most good will / To rage makes no resort.
context: Laozi describes the skilled fighter in a short verse: the strongest don't look aggressive, and the best don't need anger. Real strength is calm.
about:
This is chapter 68 of the Tao Te Ching, which James Legge translated as a short rhyming poem. Its subject is the skilled warrior.

The one most skilled does not put on a warlike look; the one who fights best does not give way to rage. The poem goes on: the true master humbly plies his art, and his might lies in never contending. It describes strength as calm. Those who need to look fierce, or who lose their temper, are often less sure of themselves than those who stay quiet. Real confidence doesn't need to be shown off.
prompt: Where could you be firm without being angry?

text: May not the Way of Heaven be compared to the method of bending a bow? The part of the bow which was high is brought low, and what was low is raised up.
context: Nature balances itself, lowering what is too high and lifting what is too low. Laozi wishes human society did the same.
about:
Chapter 77 of the Tao Te Ching contains this line. To string a bow, its top is bent down and its bottom drawn up.

Laozi uses the bow as a picture of how nature works: it lowers what is too high and raises what is too low, taking from excess and adding where there is lack. Then comes his complaint: the way of men is different. People take from those who do not have enough, to add to their own excess. It is one of the book's sharpest lines on fairness. Nature tends towards balance; human greed pulls the other way.
prompt: Where is your life out of balance, and what needs lowering or raising?

text: A duck's legs, for instance, are short, but if we try to lengthen them, it occasions pain; and a crane's legs are long, but if we try to cut off a portion of them, it produces grief.
context: Each creature is right as it is. Forcing anyone to fit a single standard causes suffering.
about:
The eighth chapter of Zhuangzi's book, in James Legge's 1891 translation, argues that the right path is not to lose the real character of the nature we are born with.

A duck's legs are short, but stretching them would hurt; a crane's are long, but cutting them would cause grief. What is long by nature is not too long, and what is short is not too short. Zhuangzi uses this against those who want everyone to follow one standard. Each creature, and each person, has their own shape. Forcing them to fit our idea of normal does harm, however well meant.
prompt: Where are you trying to 'lengthen' or 'shorten' yourself or someone else?

text: Was it better for the tortoise to die, and leave its shell to be thus honoured? Or would it have been better for it to live, and keep on dragging its tail through the mud? … Go your ways. I will keep on drawing my tail after me through the mud.
context: Offered a high office, Zhuangzi points to a sacred tortoise shell kept in a temple. He'd rather be alive and free in the mud than honoured and dead.
about:
This story comes from Zhuangzi's book, in Legge's 1891 translation. Zhuangzi is fishing by a river when two high officers arrive from the king of Khû (Chu), asking him to take charge of the whole kingdom. Legge notes that Zhuangzi did refuse high office from King Wei of Khû.

Without looking up from his rod, Zhuangzi mentions a spirit-like tortoise that died 3000 years ago, whose shell the king keeps wrapped in his ancestral temple. Would the tortoise rather be dead and honoured, or alive and dragging its tail through the mud? Alive, the officers admit. Then go your ways, says Zhuangzi: I'll keep dragging my tail in the mud. Honour and power can cost us our freedom, and he chose freedom.
prompt: What honour would cost you your freedom?

text: A keeper of monkeys, in giving them out their acorns, once said, 'In the morning I will give you three measures and in the evening four.' This made them all angry, and he said, 'Very well. In the morning I will give you four and in the evening three.'
context: The monkeys got the same amount either way, but one version made them happy. We too react to how things are framed.
about:
This story comes from Zhuangzi's book, in Legge's 1891 translation. Zhuangzi tells it about people who wear themselves out insisting on their own view, without seeing what it shares with others'. He calls this “In the morning three”.

A keeper offers his monkeys three measures of acorns in the morning and four in the evening. They are furious. Very well, he says: four in the morning and three in the evening. They are delighted. The total is the same; only the framing has changed. It's a funny story, and an uncomfortable one. We often fight over the form of a thing when the substance is the same. The wise, Zhuangzi says, see this and don't get stuck.
prompt: Which of your reactions depends on framing more than substance?

text: If a man is crossing a river in a boat, and another empty vessel comes into collision with it, even though he be a man of a choleric temper, he will not be angry with it. … If a man can empty himself of himself, during his time in the world, who can harm him?
context: We don't get angry at an empty boat that bumps us, only at one with someone in it. Zhuangzi suggests being like the empty boat: without an ego to bruise.
about:
Advice to a ruler weighed down by his troubles: that is the setting of this passage, from the twentieth chapter of Zhuangzi's book in Legge's 1891 translation.

If an empty boat drifts into yours as you cross a river, you won't get angry, even if you have a quick temper. But if someone is in it, you shout, then shout again, then swear. The bump is the same; what changed is that there was someone to blame. Zhuangzi turns this into advice: if we can empty ourselves of ourselves, who can harm us? With less ego to bruise, other people's bumps hurt less, and we cause fewer ourselves.
prompt: What would bump into you without hurting if you took it less personally?

text: Fishing-stakes are employed to catch fish; but when the fish are got, the men forget the stakes. … Words are employed to convey ideas; but when the ideas are apprehended, men forget the words.
context: Words are tools for catching ideas. Once we understand, we no longer need to hold onto the exact words.
about:
This passage closes the twenty-sixth chapter of Zhuangzi's book, in Legge's 1891 translation. It uses three simple tools: fishing-stakes, snares for hares, and words.

Stakes are used to catch fish; once we have the fish, we forget the stakes. Snares catch hares; once we have the hare, we forget the snare. Words carry ideas; once we have the idea, we can forget the words. Then Zhuangzi adds: how I would love to talk with someone who has forgotten words! Understanding is the point, not the exact phrasing. We can get so attached to words that we miss what they were for.
prompt: What idea do you understand well enough to forget the words you learned it in?

text: He who is contending for a piece of earthenware puts forth all his skill.
context: Zhuangzi goes on: shooting for a brass buckle, the archer grows nervous; shooting for gold, he is as if blind. The more the prize matters, the more it spoils our skill.
about:
In the nineteenth chapter of Zhuangzi's book, in Legge's 1891 translation, these words are given to Confucius. They describe an archer competing for prizes.

Shooting for a piece of pottery, he uses all his skill. Shooting for a brass buckle, he grows nervous; shooting for gold, he is as if blind. His skill hasn't changed. What has changed is how much the prize matters to him. Anyone who has frozen in an exam or an important conversation knows this. Fixing on outside rewards makes us worse at the thing itself. Calm comes from caring about the doing, not the prize.
prompt: Where does caring too much about the prize make you clumsy?

text: To look at him, you would say he was a cock of wood.
context: A trainer prepares a fighting cock for forty days, until it no longer reacts to other birds. Its calm makes rivals flee. Mastery looks like stillness.
about:
A man named Kî Hsing-dze is training a fighting cock for the king, and the king keeps asking whether it is ready. The story comes from Zhuangzi's book, in Legge's 1891 translation.

After ten days it is still vain and quarrelsome. After twenty, it still reacts to other birds. After thirty, it still glares, full of spirit. After forty, it no longer changes when another cock crows; it looks like a cock made of wood, and other birds run from it. The story is a little strange, which is part of its charm. True strength, it suggests, looks like stillness. Someone who doesn't need to react has nothing to prove.
prompt: Where could calm do more for you than a show of strength?

text: Perfect enjoyment is to be without enjoyment; the highest praise is to be without praise.
context: Zhuangzi turns our ideas upside down: the deepest happiness doesn't chase pleasures, and the greatest worth doesn't need praise. Wanting them is what keeps us restless.
about:
This line comes from the eighteenth chapter of Zhuangzi's book, in Legge's 1891 translation, a chapter on what real happiness is. Zhuangzi watches people chase their pleasures as if they could not stop.

What they call enjoyment, he says, would not be enjoyment to him. He thinks the great enjoyment lies in not straining after it, and quotes a saying: perfect enjoyment is to be without enjoyment; the highest praise is to be without praise. It sounds like a riddle, but it describes something familiar. The harder we chase happiness or praise, the more they slip away. Contentment tends to arrive when we stop grasping.
prompt: What do you enjoy without needing anything from it?

text: The marquis was trying to nourish the bird with what he used for himself …
context: A ruler welcomes a sea-bird with feasts and royal music, and it dies of fear in three days. Caring for others means giving them what they need, not what we like.
about:
In a story from Zhuangzi's book, in Legge's 1891 translation, a sea-bird lands in the countryside of Lû, and the marquis treats it as an honoured guest: he brings it to his ancestral temple, has royal music played for it, and orders a feast.

The bird looks dazed and sad. It eats nothing and drinks nothing, and in three days it dies. The marquis fed it with what pleased himself, not with what a bird needs: forests, rivers, small fish, freedom. It is a sharp story about kindness. We often care for others by giving them what we would want. Real care starts by asking what they need, which may be very different.
prompt: Who are you caring for in your way rather than theirs?

text: In making a wheel, if I proceed gently, that is pleasant enough, but the workmanship is not strong; if I proceed violently, that is toilsome and the joinings do not fit. If the movements of my hand are neither too gentle nor too violent, the idea in my mind is realised. But I cannot tell how to do this by word of mouth; there is a knack in it.
context: Wheelwright Phien tells a duke that the books he reads are only the leftovers of dead sages. Real skill lives in the hands and can't be put into words.
about:
A wheelwright named Phien asks his duke what he is reading, in a story from Zhuangzi's book (Legge's 1891 translation). The words of the sages, says the duke. Are they alive? No, dead. Then, says Phien, you are reading only their dregs.

Threatened with death unless he explains, Phien talks about his own craft. Work too gently and the wheel is weak; too roughly and the joints don't fit. The right touch lives in his hands. He cannot put it into words, or teach it to his son, so he is still making wheels at seventy. Books can point the way, the story suggests, but the deepest skills, and perhaps the deepest wisdom, have to be learned by doing.
prompt: What do you know how to do that you could never fully explain?

text: Horses can with their hoofs tread on the hoarfrost and snow, and with their hair withstand the wind and cold; they feed on the grass and drink water; they prance with their legs and leap:—this is the true nature of horses.
context: Zhuangzi goes on to describe how a famous trainer broke horses with brands and bridles, and many died. Forcing living things against their nature harms them.
about:
This is the opening of the ninth chapter of Zhuangzi's book, called Horses' Hoofs in Legge's 1891 translation.

Left to themselves, horses walk on frost and snow, keep out the cold with their coats, eat grass, drink water and leap about: that is their true nature. Then a famous trainer, Po-lâo, says he knows how to manage them. He brands them, clips them, bridles and stables them, and many of them die. Zhuangzi uses the horses to criticise every attempt to force living things, people included, into shapes that suit someone else.
prompt: What part of your true nature has been trained out of you?

text: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and then we see them return to their original state. When things in the vegetable world have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness.
context: Laozi watches plants grow, flourish, and return to their roots. Rest and return are part of life's cycle, not its failure; stillness is where growth begins again.
about:
Chapter 16 of the Tao Te Ching begins by asking us to empty the mind completely and to guard its stillness.

Then it watches nature. Everything goes through its time of activity and returns to where it began. Plants grow lush, and each returns to its root. That return, Laozi says, is stillness: the sign that a thing has fulfilled its purpose. It is a gentle way to see rest, ageing and endings. They are not failures but part of a cycle. In winter the roots are not dead. They are where the next spring begins.
prompt: What root do you need to return to?

text: The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps; the skilful speaker says nothing that can be found fault with or blamed.
context: Laozi says real skill leaves no visible trace of effort. The best traveller, speaker, or leader works so naturally that no one notices how hard it was.
about:
Chapter 27 of the Tao Te Ching continues the list: the skilful counter needs no tallies, the skilful closer needs no bolts, and the skilful binder needs no knots.

The skilful traveller leaves no tracks; the skilful speaker says nothing that can be faulted. In each case, mastery means leaving no marks of effort. Think of a host who makes a party feel effortless, or a writer whose sentences seem obvious once read. The work is there, but hidden. Laozi sees the same in the wise, who help people so naturally that nothing seems to have been done.
prompt: What do you do so naturally that nobody sees the effort?

text: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?
context: The opening lines of the Analects, the sayings of Confucius collected by his students. Learning, friendship and not needing recognition: the whole book in three questions.
about:
The Analects, the collection of sayings of the Chinese teacher Confucius put together by his disciples and their followers, open with these words. James Legge translated it in 1861.

Isn't it pleasant to learn with constant perseverance and practice? Isn't it delightful to have friends come from far away? The book begins not with rules but with two joys: learning, and friendship. The next line adds a third: not being upset when others don't recognise us. It is a gentle opening to a whole philosophy of life. Learning and good company are pleasures, not chores.
prompt: Which of the three would make today a good day: learning something, seeing a friend, or not needing to be noticed?

text: I will not be afflicted at men's not knowing me; I will be afflicted that I do not know men.
context: Confucius turns a common worry around. Instead of fretting that others don't understand us, he asks whether we understand them.
about:
This saying closes the first book of the Analects. Just before it, Confucius praises a disciple who understood his point at once, and took it further.

I won't be troubled that others don't know me, he says; I will be troubled that I don't know others. It turns a common worry around. We often fret about being noticed, understood or appreciated. Confucius suggests the more useful worry is whether we understand the people around us. Recognition is not in our power. Understanding others is.
prompt: Who in your life might you not yet really know?

text: If a man keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, he may be a teacher of others.
context: Good teachers keep returning to what they know until it yields something new. Old knowledge is not a shelf but a garden.
about:
Confucius said this in the second book of the Analects, the sayings of Confucius collected by his followers, just after a saying on how to judge a person: see what they do, note their motives, and observe what they rest in.

If someone keeps cherishing what they already know, and so keeps learning new things, he says, they can be a teacher of others. Good teachers don't drop old knowledge or stop at it. They keep revisiting what they know, and it leads them to new understanding. It is a picture of learning as a living thing. The best teachers are still learners.
prompt: What do you already know that might teach you something new if you went back to it?

text: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
context: Reading without reflecting changes nothing; reflecting without learning goes round in circles. Confucius wants both, together.
about:
Confucius, whose sayings make up the Analects, put this teaching in two short halves. The saying just before it says that the superior person is broad-minded, not partisan.

Learning without thinking is labour lost; thinking without learning is dangerous. Reading and memorising, without reflecting, leaves knowledge dead. Thinking alone, without learning from others, can lead us far astray. We need both: input and reflection. It is one of the clearest pieces of advice ever given to students, and it applies at any age.
prompt: Are you lately more at risk of learning without thinking, or thinking without learning?

text: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;— this is knowledge.
context: Spoken to Zilu, a bold student who was quick to speak. Like Socrates, Confucius places wisdom in being honest about where our knowledge ends.
about:
In this saying from the Analects, the sayings of Confucius collected by his followers, Confucius speaks to his disciple Yu (Tsze-lu), who was known for being bold and quick to act. Shall I teach you what knowledge is? he asks.

When you know something, to hold that you know it; when you don't, to admit that you don't: that is knowledge. It sounds simple, but it is hard. Pride makes us pretend to know; fear makes us hide what we don't. Being honest about the edges of our knowledge is the beginning of real knowledge. It is the same humility Socrates taught in Athens.
prompt: Where do you pretend to know more than you do?

text: He acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.
context: Asked what makes a person of true quality, Confucius points to the order of things: first do it, then talk about it.
about:
In the Analects, the sayings of Confucius collected by his followers, the disciple Tsze-kung asks what makes a superior person, the ideal of character Confucius taught. This is his answer.

Such a person acts before speaking, and then speaks according to their actions. It is a simple order: deeds first, words after. Many people promise, explain and boast before doing anything. Confucius admired those whose words follow their actions, and so can be trusted. Talk is easy. Letting what we do speak first is a mark of character.
prompt: What are you talking about doing that you could simply start?

text: I am not concerned that I have no place, I am concerned how I may fit myself for one. I am not concerned that I am not known, I seek to be worthy to be known.
context: Confucius spent years without the position he hoped for. He suggests turning the worry about recognition into work on oneself.
about:
Confucius, whose sayings were gathered in the Analects, often spoke about wanting position and recognition. This saying addresses both.

I am not concerned that I have no position, he says; I am concerned with how to fit myself for one. I am not concerned that I am not known; I seek to be worth knowing. It moves attention from what others give us to what we make of ourselves. We can't control whether we get the job or the fame. We can control whether we deserve it.
prompt: What would make you worthy of the place you want, whether or not you get it?

text: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
context: Everyone we meet is a lesson: the admirable show us what to aim for, the others what to look for in ourselves.
about:
This saying from the Analects follows one contrasting two kinds of mind: one at home with what is right, the other with what is profitable.

When we see people of worth, Confucius says, we should think of matching them; when we see the opposite, we should turn inward and examine ourselves. Both kinds of people can teach us. The admirable inspire us to grow. The others hold up a mirror: do I do that too? It is a practical way to learn from everyone we meet, and to judge less and reflect more.
prompt: Whose behaviour annoyed you recently, and is any of it in you too?

text: Virtue is not left to stand alone. He who practises it will have neighbors.
context: Confucius reassures those who try to live well: goodness may feel lonely at first, but it draws like-minded people to it in time.
about:
Confucius said this in the fourth book of the Analects, just after a saying that the superior person is slow to speak and earnest in action.

Virtue is not left to stand alone, he says. Whoever practises it will have neighbours. Goodness can feel lonely, as if we were the only one trying. Confucius promises the opposite: virtue draws others to it. Kind, honest people tend to find each other, and inspire others to join them. Being good is not a solitary road for long.
prompt: Who has your kindness quietly drawn closer to you?

text: Admirable indeed was the virtue of Hui! With a single bamboo dish of rice, a single gourd dish of drink, and living in his mean narrow lane, while others could not have endured the distress, he did not allow his joy to be affected by it.
context: Yan Hui was Confucius' favourite student, poor all his life and dead young. His joy did not depend on what he owned.
about:
Hui (Yan Hui) was Confucius' favourite disciple, who died young, and the Analects record the Master's grief at his death. In this saying Confucius praises him.

With a single bamboo dish of rice, a single gourd of drink, living in a mean narrow lane, others could not have endured the distress, he says, but Hui did not let it affect his joy. Admirable indeed was the virtue of Hui! It is a portrait of someone whose happiness didn't depend on comfort. Poverty couldn't touch his joy, because it came from within.
prompt: What joy of yours would survive losing your comforts?

text: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
context: Confucius describes three stages in our relationship with anything worth learning: knowing it, loving it, and finally finding real delight in it.
about:
In this saying from the Analects, Confucius describes three ways of relating to the truth, or to the right way of living.

Those who know it are not equal to those who love it, and those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it. Knowing is good; loving is better; delighting is best. It is a lovely ladder. We can know what is good and not care. We can care and still find it hard. The deepest stage is when doing right has become a joy.
prompt: What do you know well but no longer delight in?

text: The wise find pleasure in water; the virtuous find pleasure in hills. The wise are active; the virtuous are tranquil. The wise are joyful; the virtuous are long-lived.
context: Water moves and adapts; hills stay put. Confucius sees two temperaments, the quick mind and the steady heart, and honours both.
about:
Confucius said this in the sixth book of the Analects. Just before, he defines perfect virtue as making the difficulty to be overcome the first business, and success only a later thought.

The wise find pleasure in water, he says; the virtuous find pleasure in hills. The wise are active; the virtuous are calm. The wise are joyful; the virtuous live long. Water moves and adapts, like a quick mind; hills stand still and endure, like a steady heart. Both are needed. It is a poetic way to describe two sides of a good life.
prompt: Are you more water or hill these days, and what could the other teach you?

text: With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow;— I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud.
context: Confucius on simple living. Wealth gained wrongly means as little to him as a cloud drifting past.
about:
Confucius often spoke about simple living. In this saying from the Analects, he describes his own.

With coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and my bent arm for a pillow, I still have joy in the midst of these things, he says. Riches and honours gained by unrighteousness are to me like a floating cloud. It is a calm and free picture. Happiness doesn't need luxury, and wealth gained wrongly isn't worth having. What he values can't be bought, or blown away.
prompt: What simple thing gives you joy that money couldn't improve?

text: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them.
context: Confucius says any two companions can teach us: the good qualities of one show us what to follow, the faults of the other what to avoid in ourselves.
about:
In one passage of the Analects, the saying just before this tells us what Confucius did not talk about: marvels, feats of strength, disorder and spirits. He preferred ordinary life.

When I walk with two others, he says, they may serve as my teachers. I will pick out their good qualities and follow them, their bad ones and avoid them. Every companion can teach us something, either by example or by warning. It is a humble and practical way to learn. We don't need to find a great master. The people beside us are enough.
prompt: What did the last two people you spent time with teach you?

text: Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
context: Confucius insists goodness is not far away, waiting for the perfect moment. It begins the moment we sincerely want it.
about:
This short saying comes from the seventh book of the Analects. Confucius taught that goodness is not a distant goal reserved for sages.

Is virtue a thing far away? he asks. I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand. The moment we truly want to be good, we can begin. It is an encouraging idea. We often think of goodness as something we will reach one day, after a lot of effort. Confucius says it is as close as the next kind choice.
prompt: What good thing are you postponing that you could begin right now?

text: Learn as if you could not reach your object, and were always fearing also lest you should lose it.
context: Confucius describes the eager student: always reaching ahead, and holding on to what was learned as if it might slip away.
about:
In this saying from the Analects, Confucius describes the attitude of a real learner.

Learn as if you could never reach your goal, he says, and were always afraid of losing what you have. It sounds anxious, but it is about eagerness. A good learner never thinks they have arrived, and keeps reviewing what they know so it doesn't slip away. It is the opposite of complacency. Learning, for Confucius, is a lifelong practice, always in motion.
prompt: What are you learning that deserves this kind of eagerness?

text: There were four things from which the Master was entirely free. He had no foregone conclusions, no arbitrary predeterminations, no obstinacy, and no egoism.
context: Confucius had four qualities his students admired: he didn't jump to conclusions, wasn't rigid, wasn't stubborn, and wasn't self-centred.
about:
Confucius' disciples recorded not only his sayings but his character. In this passage from the Analects, they describe four things he was entirely free from.

He had no fixed conclusions in advance, no arbitrary predeterminations, no stubbornness, and no egoism. It is a portrait of an open mind. He didn't decide before he looked, didn't cling to his views for their own sake, and didn't put himself at the centre. These four freedoms are rare, and worth practising. They make listening, learning and fair judgment possible.
prompt: Which of the four do you hold on to most tightly?

text: It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!
context: Confucius, standing by a river, watches it flow without pause. He sees life passing the same way, which makes every moment worth using well.
about:
In this passage from the Analects, Confucius stands by a stream, watching it flow. The very next saying is a sigh of a different kind: “I have not seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty.”

It passes on like this, he says, never stopping, day or night! The words are simple, and have been read in many ways. Some hear a sigh at how fast time goes. Others hear encouragement: like the stream, we should keep going and keep learning. Either way, the image holds. Life flows on without pause, and we are part of its current, whether we notice it or not.
prompt: What is flowing past you right now that you would like to notice?

text: The commander of the forces of a large state may be carried off, but the will of even a common man cannot be taken from him.
context: Confucius says an army can lose its general, but no one can take away a person's will. Even the most ordinary life holds this inner freedom.
about:
Confucius compares an army with an ordinary person in this saying from the Analects.

The commander of a large state's army may be carried off, he says, but the will of even a common man cannot be taken from him. An army is powerful, but its leader can be captured. A single person's resolve, if they hold it, can't be seized by force. It is a strong statement of inner freedom. Whatever else can be taken from us, our will is our own.
prompt: What choice is entirely yours today, whatever happens around you?

text: When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
context: Pines and cypresses stay green through winter. Character, like an evergreen, shows itself in the hard seasons.
about:
This saying from the Analects uses an image from the Chinese winter.

When the year grows cold, Confucius says, we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves. In warm weather all trees look alike. Only in winter do we see which stay green. In the same way, hard times show who is steadfast. It is a quiet tribute to loyalty and endurance. Character is tested by the cold.
prompt: Who stayed green for you during a hard winter?

text: To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short.
context: Asked which of two students was better, one who overdid things and one who fell short, Confucius refused to choose. The ideal is the balanced middle, the due mean, much like Aristotle's.
about:
In the Analects, the disciple Tsze-kung asks which of two fellow students is better: Shih, who goes beyond the mean, or Shang, who falls short of it.

Then Shih is better, I suppose? Tsze-kung says. Confucius answers: to go beyond is as wrong as to fall short. Overdoing isn't better than underdoing; both miss the mark. It is the same idea as Aristotle's golden mean, reached on the other side of the world. Enthusiasm doesn't make excess right. The goal is the right measure.
prompt: Where are you overdoing something, and where falling short?

text: When internal examination discovers nothing wrong, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear?
context: Asked about the person of true quality, Confucius says they live without anxiety or fear, not because life is safe but because their conscience is clear.
about:
In one passage of the Analects, the disciple Sze-ma Niu, a worried man, asks about the superior person. Such a person, Confucius says, has neither anxiety nor fear. Niu is surprised: is that all?

When looking inside finds nothing wrong, Confucius replies, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear? Peace comes from a clear conscience. If we have done our best and acted rightly, outside troubles lose much of their grip. It is a simple and deep answer. Much anxiety comes from knowing, somewhere, that we haven't lived as we should.
prompt: What would clear your conscience enough to let a worry go?

text: To be poor without murmuring is difficult. To be rich without being proud is easy.
context: Confucius is honest about which test is harder. Grace in hardship asks far more of us than modesty in comfort.
about:
Just before this saying, in the fourteenth book of the Analects, Confucius praises a minister who had a city taken from a rival family, which then lived on coarse rice without a single complaint.

To be poor without grumbling is hard, he says. To be rich without being proud is easy. It is an honest comparison. Poverty tests us more than wealth. Bearing hardship without bitterness takes real strength. Confucius doesn't excuse arrogance in the rich. He simply notes which trial is heavier, and honours those who pass it.
prompt: Which is harder for you: going without and not complaining, or having plenty and not boasting?

text: In ancient times, men learned with a view to their own improvement. Now-a-days, men learn with a view to the approbation of others.
context: A complaint from 2,500 years ago that sounds very modern: learning to grow, versus learning to impress.
about:
Elsewhere in the Analects, Confucius compares the students of his own day with those of old.

In ancient times, he says, people learned for their own improvement. Nowadays, they learn to win the approval of others. It is a complaint that sounds very modern: learning to impress, to get grades, to look clever. Confucius values learning that changes us from the inside. Studying to be admired fades when the applause stops. Studying to grow lasts.
prompt: What do you study mainly so that others will notice?

text: With what then will you recompense kindness? Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness.
context: Someone asks whether we should repay injury with kindness. Confucius replies with a question: then what is left for those who are kind to us? Fairness for harm, kindness for kindness.
about:
In this passage from the Analects, someone asks Confucius about an old principle: that injury should be repaid with kindness.

With what, then, will you repay kindness? he replies. Repay injury with justice, and kindness with kindness. It is a balanced answer. Confucius isn't calling for revenge, but he doesn't ask us to treat wrong and right the same way either. Justice means fair, measured response. Kindness deserves to be answered with kindness. Each gets what is fitting.
prompt: Where would fairness serve better than forced kindness, or the other way round?

text: He who requires much from himself and little from others, will keep himself from being the object of resentment.
context: Confucius offers a simple recipe for fewer grudges: high standards for ourselves, generous ones for others. It protects our relationships in both directions.
about:
In the fifteenth book of the Analects, Confucius gives this simple rule for getting along with others. The next saying shows his patience with the opposite habit: he can do nothing with someone who never asks, “What shall I think of this?”

Whoever demands much of themselves and little of others will keep themselves from being resented. It is practical and wise. We often reverse it: harsh with others, easy on ourselves. That breeds resentment on both sides. Holding ourselves to high standards, while being generous with others, makes for calmer relationships and better character. It also keeps our attention on the one person we can actually change.
prompt: Whom are you holding to a higher standard than you hold yourself?

text: What the superior man seeks, is in himself. What the mean man seeks, is in others.
context: 'Superior man' is the old translation of junzi, a person of noble character. Such a person looks inward for causes and remedies; the petty person looks for someone to blame.
about:
In the Analects, Confucius often contrasts the superior person with the petty one. The sayings around this one say the superior person is troubled by their own lack of ability, not by others failing to know them.

What the superior person seeks is in themselves, he says; what the petty person seeks is in others. One looks inward for improvement, approval and strength; the other depends on praise, blame and favours from outside. It is a good test for our own motives. Where do we look for our sense of worth?
prompt: What are you seeking from others that you could find in yourself?

text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
context: Asked for one word to live by, Confucius chose shu, reciprocity, and summed it up in this line: a version of the golden rule found in many cultures.
about:
Elsewhere in the Analects, the disciple Tsze-kung asks Confucius whether there is one word that can guide a whole life. Confucius answers: reciprocity.

What you don't want done to yourself, don't do to others. It is one of the oldest forms of what is now called the golden rule, found in many traditions. Its power lies in its simplicity. We don't need complex theories to know how to treat people. We only need to imagine being in their place, and act accordingly.
prompt: Where today could you treat someone the way you would want to be treated?

text: By nature, men are nearly alike; by practice, they get to be wide apart.
context: We start out much the same; what we do again and again makes us different. Aristotle would have agreed.
about:
In the Analects, Confucius makes a short, hopeful observation about human nature. The saying that follows adds a limit: only “the wise of the highest class, and the stupid of the lowest class” cannot be changed.

By nature, people are nearly alike; by practice, they become far apart. We start with much the same possibilities. What makes us differ so greatly is what we do, again and again: our habits, studies and choices. It is a democratic idea. No one is born far above others, and almost everyone can change. Character is built, day by day, and anyone can build it.
prompt: Which daily habit is quietly shaping who you are becoming?

text: The faults of the superior man are like the eclipses of the sun and moon. He has his faults, and all men see them; he changes again, and all men look up to him.
context: Zigong, a student of Confucius, on how a good person handles mistakes: openly, in full view, and then changed.
about:
This saying in the Analects is from Tsze-kung, one of Confucius' leading disciples, about the faults of the superior person.

Their faults, he says, are like eclipses of the sun and moon. They have their faults, and everyone sees them; they change, and everyone looks up to them. The image is striking. Eclipses are visible to all, and they pass. Good people make mistakes too, in plain sight. What sets them apart is that they correct them openly, and are respected for it.
prompt: Which mistake of yours could you own more openly?

text: To have faults and not to reform them,— this, indeed, should be pronounced having faults.
context: Confucius accepts mistakes as human. The real fault, he says, is refusing to correct them once we know.
about:
Confucius often said that faults are less important than what we do about them. This saying in the Analects puts it most sharply.

To have faults and not to reform them: that, indeed, is to have faults. Everyone errs. The real failing is refusing to change. It is a forgiving and demanding idea at once. Mistakes are human, and not the end of the story. But knowing a fault and keeping it, out of pride or laziness, is a choice, and that choice is the real fault.
prompt: Which of your faults have you made peace with that you could still change?

text: The man of perfect virtue is cautious and slow in his speech.
context: Confucius distrusted quick talkers. Speaking slowly leaves time to check that our words match what we will actually do.
about:
Elsewhere in the Analects, the anxious disciple Sze-ma Niu asks about perfect virtue. Confucius gives him an answer suited to him: the person of perfect virtue is cautious and slow in speech.

Is that what perfect virtue means? Niu asks, surprised. Confucius replies that when doing is hard, how can speaking be anything but slow? Words should not run ahead of what we can do. It is good advice for anyone who talks quickly. Careful speech is a sign of respect: for the truth, for others, and for the effort that real action takes.
prompt: When did speaking too quickly cost you?

text: The superior man seeks to perfect the admirable qualities of men, and does not seek to perfect their bad qualities.
context: 'Superior man' is Legge's word for junzi, a person of noble character. Such a person helps others grow in what is good in them, not in their worst habits.
about:
Confucius contrasts, in this saying from the Analects, the superior person with the petty one.

The superior person, he says, tries to bring out the good qualities of others, and does not encourage their bad ones. The petty person does the opposite. It is a description of how we affect those around us. Some people help us become our best; others feed our worst habits, or enjoy our failures. Confucius asks us to be the first kind.
prompt: Whose good qualities could you help grow?

text: To govern means to rectify. If you lead on the people with correctness, who will dare not to be correct?
context: A ruler asks Confucius about government. His answer: lead by your own example, and others will follow.
about:
In one passage of the Analects, Chi K'ang, a powerful official, asks Confucius about government.

To govern means to rectify, Confucius replies. If you lead the people with correctness, who will dare not to be correct? Good government begins with the ruler's own conduct. Laws and orders mean little if those in charge don't live by them. It is a lesson for any leader. The surest way to set things right is to start with ourselves.
prompt: What would change around you if you set a better example?

text: Let your evinced desires be for what is good, and the people will be good.
context: When a ruler suggests killing wrongdoers, Confucius replies that people follow what their leader visibly wants. He goes on: the leader is like the wind, the people like grass that bends with it.
about:
In a short exchange in the Analects, the official Chi K'ang asks Confucius whether he should kill the unprincipled for the good of the principled.

Why use killing at all? Confucius replies. Let your desires be for what is good, and the people will be good. The relation between leaders and people, he adds, is like that between the wind and the grass: when the wind blows, the grass bends. Example works more deeply than fear. Leaders shape those below them, for good or ill.
prompt: What do the people around you see you wanting?

text: Faithfully admonish your friend, and skillfully lead him on. If you find him impracticable, stop.
context: Good friends tell each other hard truths, gently. But Confucius adds a limit: if they won't listen, stop, before you lose the friendship.
about:
Elsewhere in the Analects, the disciple Tsze-kung asks Confucius about friendship. Just before, another disciple has been puzzling over the Master's advice to employ the upright and put aside the crooked.

Faithfully advise your friend, Confucius says, and skilfully lead them on. If they won't listen, stop. Don't disgrace yourself. It is a wise balance. Real friends tell each other the truth, gently and with tact. But nagging a friend who won't change only harms both people, and the friendship too. Knowing when to speak, and when to step back and let them find their own way, is part of caring well.
prompt: Is there a friend you need to speak to honestly, or stop pushing?

text: The superior man on grounds of culture meets with his friends, and by their friendship helps his virtue.
context: Shared learning and interests bring friends together, and good friends help each other become better.
about:
This saying closes the twelfth book of the Analects. It is spoken not by Confucius but by his disciple, the philosopher Tsang.

The superior person meets friends through shared learning and culture, he says, and through their friendship strengthens their virtue. Friendship, in this view, isn't only for pleasure or support. It is a way of helping each other grow. Good friends sharpen our minds and steady our character. We become better together than alone.
prompt: Which friend makes you a better person?

text: When a prince's personal conduct is correct, his government is effective without the issuing of orders.
context: A leader whose own behaviour is right hardly needs to give orders. People follow example more than instructions.
about:
In the Analects, Confucius often spoke to rulers about how to govern. This saying sums up his view.

When a ruler's own conduct is right, he says, government works without orders being given. When it is not, orders are given but not obeyed. People follow what leaders do, not just what they say. It is a lesson for anyone in charge, at home, at work or in public. Example carries authority that commands alone cannot.
prompt: Where are you giving orders instead of setting an example?

text: The superior man is easy to serve and difficult to please.
context: A person of quality is easy to work for, because they don't ask for flattery, but hard to please, because they expect what is right.
about:
Confucius describes, in the Analects, what it is like to work for a superior person and for a petty one.

The superior person is easy to serve and hard to please, he says. You can't please them by doing what is wrong; but they use people according to their abilities. The petty person is hard to serve and easy to please: flattery works, but they expect everything of everyone. It is a sharp portrait of good and bad bosses. The best are fair, not flattered.
prompt: When did someone try to win you over by the wrong means, and how did you respond?

text: The superior man has a dignified ease without pride. The mean man has pride without a dignified ease.
context: Real confidence is relaxed; pride is tense. Confucius contrasts the person of quality with the 'mean' or petty person.
about:
This short saying in the Analects follows Confucius' portrait of good and bad people to work for. The one after it names the qualities that come close to virtue: “The firm, the enduring, the simple, and the modest”.

The superior person has dignified ease without pride, he says. The petty person has pride without dignified ease. Real dignity is relaxed: it doesn't need to show off. Pride, by contrast, is tense and defensive, always proving itself. It is an observation worth remembering. Those most sure of themselves are often the least boastful, and the easiest to be around.
prompt: Where are you proud without being at ease?

text: When the love of superiority, boasting, resentments, and covetousness are repressed, this may be deemed perfect virtue.
context: A student lists four faults he has overcome and asks if that is perfect virtue. Confucius replies that it is difficult, but he is not sure it is enough: goodness is more than avoiding faults.
about:
The fourteenth book of the Analects opens with a disciple, Hsien, asking what is shameful. Then he asks about this.

If the love of being superior, boasting, resentment and greed are held in check, may that be called perfect virtue? Confucius answers that it is hard, but whether it is perfect virtue, he doesn't know. It is an honest reply. Holding back our worst impulses is difficult and worthwhile. But goodness, for Confucius, is more than restraint: it is also warmth and active care.
prompt: Which of the four, superiority, boasting, resentment, or envy, do you still struggle with?

text: There is no greater delight than to be conscious of sincerity on self-examination.
context: Mencius (c. 372–289 BCE) was Confucius' greatest follower. For him, the deepest joy comes from looking inside and finding nothing false.
about:
Mencius was a later teacher in the school of Confucius, and his book, translated by James Legge, records his conversations. This saying is about looking inward.

There is no greater delight, he says, than to find sincerity when we examine ourselves. The next line adds: if we work hard at treating others as we would wish to be treated, we will find goodness close by. It is a quiet, deep joy. Not praise or success, but finding, on honest reflection, that we have been true. Few pleasures are more solid.
prompt: When did honesty with yourself last bring you a quiet kind of joy?

text: The sense of shame is to a man of great importance.
context: Mencius saw shame not as a burden but as a moral compass. Someone who feels no shame has lost something essential.
about:
Mencius, a later teacher of the Confucian school, often spoke about feelings that guide us to goodness. This passage is about shame.

The sense of shame is of great importance to a person, he says. Those who form clever, crafty schemes have no use for shame. It is an unusual praise of an uncomfortable feeling. Shame, rightly felt, tells us when we have fallen below ourselves. People who lose it lose an inner check. Mencius suggests we keep it, and listen to it.
prompt: What does your sense of shame protect you from?

text: Let a man not do what his own sense of righteousness tells him not to do …
context: Mencius believed we already know right from wrong. The work is to listen to that inner sense.
about:
Mencius, who taught in the school of Confucius, believed that every person has an inner sense of right and wrong. This passage tells us how to use it.

Let a person not do what their own sense of righteousness tells them not to do, he says, and not desire what it tells them not to desire: that is all. It is simple, and hard. We usually know, deep down, what we shouldn't do. The work is to listen to that voice, and not argue it away. Morality, for Mencius, begins with that inner sense.
prompt: What is your conscience telling you not to do?

text: …if men suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they will without exception experience a feeling of alarm and distress.
context: Mencius' famous argument that humans are naturally good: anyone seeing a child about to fall feels an immediate urge to help, before any thought of reward.
about:
Mencius, a later teacher of the Confucian school, argued that all people have a heart that cannot bear to see others suffer. Here he gives his most famous example.

If people suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, he says, they will all feel alarm and distress, not to win the parents' favour or their neighbours' praise, nor from dislike of the child's cries. The feeling is simply there. It is a strong argument that goodness is natural. Compassion arises before any calculation. Our task is to grow it.
prompt: When did you feel an instant urge to help someone?

text: The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence.
context: Mencius, Confucius' great follower, saw compassion as a seed of goodness in every person. Looked after, it grows into kindness toward everyone.
about:
Mencius, having argued that everyone feels distress at a child about to fall into a well, explains what such feelings mean. They are, he says, essential to being human.

The feeling of compassion is the beginning of benevolence; shame and dislike, of righteousness; modesty, of propriety; approving and disapproving, of wisdom. We have these four beginnings as we have four limbs. It is a hopeful picture. Goodness is not imposed from outside. Its seeds are already in us, waiting to be grown.
prompt: How do you tend the seed of compassion in yourself?

text: I daily examine myself on three points:— whether, in transacting business for others, I may have been not faithful;— whether, in intercourse with friends, I may have been not sincere;— whether I may have not mastered and practised the instructions of my teacher.
context: Zengzi, one of Confucius' students, describes his daily review: Was I reliable for others? Was I sincere with friends? Did I practise what I was taught?
about:
This saying in the Analects comes not from Confucius but from his disciple Tsang, who, Legge's notes say, followed the Master from the age of sixteen.

I examine myself daily on three points, he says: whether, working for others, I have been unfaithful; whether, with friends, I have been insincere; whether I have failed to practise what I was taught. It is a simple daily review. Three questions, honestly asked each evening, can do more for our character than many good intentions.
prompt: Run through Zengzi's three questions for today. Which one makes you pause?

text: The prosecution of learning may be compared to what may happen in raising a mound. If there want but one basket of earth to complete the work, and I stop, the stopping is my own work. It may be compared to throwing down the earth on the level ground. Though but one basketful is thrown at a time, the advancing with it is my own going forward.
context: Confucius compares learning to building a mound one basket of earth at a time. Whether we stop one basket short or keep going, the choice is always ours.
about:
In a short exchange in the Analects, Confucius compares learning to building a mound of earth, basket by basket.

If only one basket is missing to complete it, and I stop, the stopping is my own work, he says. If I am levelling ground and have thrown down just one basket, and go on, the going on is my own work. Progress depends on us, one basket at a time. Giving up at the end is our choice; so is starting. Each small step counts.
prompt: What are you one basket away from finishing, or from starting?

text: The perfect circle of the full moon lasts only for a very short time; soon it begins to wane, though one who pays no attention to it may think that in a single night there is little or no change perceptible.
context: Kenkō was a 14th-century poet and monk whose short essays on beauty and impermanence remain beloved in Japan. Change, he notes, is often too slow to see.
about:
Yoshida Kenkō, a Japanese courtier who became a Buddhist monk and died around 1350, filled his Essays in Idleness with short notes on every subject. William N. Porter's translation gives this one the title On Procrastination.

The full moon, he says, stays perfectly round only a very short time before it starts to wane, though someone not paying attention may think little changes in one night. Our lives slip away the same way, unnoticed, until it is late. It is a gentle warning against putting things off. The moon doesn't wait, and neither does our time.
prompt: What is quietly changing in your life, too slowly to notice?

text: A certain man who was learning archery faced the target with two arrows in his hand. But his instructor said, ‘A beginner ought never to have a second arrow; for as long as he relies upon the other, he will be careless with his first one. At each shot he ought to think that he is bound to settle it with this particular shaft at any cost.’
context: A teacher tells his student to carry only one arrow, because a second one makes the first careless. Kenkō applies it to every moment of life.
about:
Kenkō, the 14th-century Japanese monk, tells a short story in his Essays in Idleness about a man learning archery, who faced the target holding two arrows.

His teacher said a beginner should never have a second arrow: while you rely on the second, you are careless with the first. Shoot each time as if this arrow were the only one. Kenkō draws the lesson: we waste time because we think there will be another chance. Giving full attention to what we are doing now, as if it were our only chance, changes how well we do it.
prompt: What 'second arrow' is making you careless with the first?

text: Is it only when the flowers are in full bloom and when the moon is shining in spotless perfection that we ought to gaze at them? … The twigs which bear no blossoms as yet and a garden strewn with withered petals are equally to be admired.
context: Kenkō's most famous essay. Beauty isn't only in the peak moment, but in anticipation, in absence, and in what has already passed.
about:
This passage from Kenkō's Essays in Idleness, translated by William N. Porter in 1914, opens a section on different points of view. Many readers count it among the most loved passages in Japanese writing about beauty.

Should we look at flowers only in full bloom, he asks, and at the moon only when it is cloudless? To long for the moon while watching the rain, or to stay at home wondering where the spring has gone, deepens our feelings. Beauty is not only in perfection. Anticipation, memory and incompleteness have their own depth. Missing something can make us feel it more.
prompt: What 'not yet' or 'no longer' could you admire today?

text: The dew upon Adashi Moor never fades away, nor is Toribe Moor ever free from smoke; what a state of things we should have, were our existence never to be cut short! There would be no feelings of pity left in the world. Far better is it to have no certainty as to the length of life.
context: If we lived forever, we would lose all tenderness; it is better not to know how long we have. Adashi Moor and Toribe Moor were burial grounds near Kyoto, so their dew and smoke stand for death.
about:
Kenkō's Essays in Idleness mention two places near Kyoto, Adashi Moor and Toribe Moor, where the dead were buried and cremated. This section argues against wishing for an endless life.

If the dew on Adashi Moor never faded, he says, and the smoke over Toribe Moor never cleared, if we never died, how dull it would be! Life is precious because it is uncertain. Even the longest life would seem short if we clung to it. It is a calm view of mortality. What passes is what moves us; a life that never ended would lose its poignancy.
prompt: How does knowing life is uncertain make it more precious to you?
