text: Nothing is more refreshing than to make friends with those who are no longer to be seen in this life by means of an open book, a lamp, and solitude.
context: Kenkō, a 14th-century Japanese monk, describes the pleasure of reading alone at night by lamplight. A book lets us befriend people who died long ago.
about:
In a section called On Reading, Kenkō, the 14th-century Japanese monk, describes one of his favourite pleasures.

Nothing is more refreshing, he says, than to make friends, by lamplight and alone, with people long gone, through an open book. He goes on to name the books he loves. It is a warm picture of reading as company. Books let us meet minds from other centuries, at their best and most honest. Solitude with a good book isn't loneliness. It is a kind of friendship across time.
prompt: Which book has felt like a friend, and when did you last spend an evening with it?

text: The order of the four seasons is fixed, while none know the time of death; it comes not from in front, but ever presses on from behind.
context: Seasons arrive in order; death doesn't announce itself. Kenkō's image: the tide comes in while the beach still looks dry.
about:
Kenkō's Essays in Idleness describe the seasons overlapping: leaves fall because new buds push from beneath. Birth, age, sickness and death turn the same way.

But the order of the seasons is fixed, he says, while no one knows the time of death. It doesn't come from in front, where we can see it, but presses on from behind. We know we will die, but we don't expect it, and so it takes us by surprise. It is a sobering image, meant not to frighten but to wake us. If death comes from behind, the time to live well is now.
prompt: What would you stop postponing if you felt time pressing from behind?

text: He who afflicts his whole life by spending it in the pursuit of riches and fame, leaving himself no leisure for quiet, is but a fool.
context: Kenkō judges a life spent chasing wealth and reputation, with no time left for quiet, as foolish. Riches, he adds, cannot even protect their owner.
about:
This section of Kenkō's Essays in Idleness, translated by William N. Porter in 1914, is titled On the Vanity of Human Desires.

Whoever spends their whole life chasing riches and fame, leaving no time for quiet, is a fool, he says. However great their wealth, it can't protect them; it only brings worries. It is a theme that runs through the book. Kenkō isn't against comfort. He is against wasting the only life we have on things that don't last and don't satisfy. Leisure and calm are worth more.
prompt: What would you have to give up to make room for quiet each day?

text: How can a man ever find it wearisome to live at leisure? Free from surrounding cares, it is good merely to be alone.
context: Kenkō defends solitude: away from the noise of the world, we stop being blown about by everyone else's moods.
about:
Just before this section of Kenkō's Essays in Idleness, he writes that fools long for things to stay the same forever, not knowing that change is the law of nature.

How can anyone find it wearisome to live at leisure? he asks. Free from cares, it is good simply to be alone. Living in the world, our hearts are captured by its dust and noise. It is a praise of quiet, from a man who chose it. Kenkō suggests that being alone isn't boredom, but freedom: room to think, and to be ourselves.
prompt: When did you last enjoy being alone?

text: He who mixes with the experts while he is himself still stiff and imperfect, and is not ashamed when others laugh and mock at him, will enjoy overcoming such discouragement; and, though he have not the natural talent for it, he will not lag far behind the others.
context: Someone who practises among experts while still clumsy, and doesn't mind being laughed at, will in time catch up even without natural talent. Kenkō's case for being an open beginner.
about:
Kenkō describes, in his Essays in Idleness, a common habit: people who want to learn a skill often hide until they are good at it, hoping to impress later. Such people, he says, never master anything.

But whoever mixes with experts while still clumsy and unskilled, and isn't ashamed when others laugh, will overcome the discouragement; even without natural talent they will not lag far behind, and in time may surpass the expert who grows careless. It is encouraging advice for any beginner. Being seen to be bad at something is the price of getting good. The ones who keep going, in public, are the ones who improve.
prompt: What are you avoiding because you're not good at it yet?

text: You may propose to do a certain thing to-day, but some unforeseen matter of importance crops up and you spend the time wrongly on it; or perhaps somebody you had expected cannot come, and some unexpected visitor arrives instead. At all events you fail to do what you had planned, and it is only the unlooked for that actually happens.
context: Kenkō on plans: the day rarely goes as expected, and neither do years. Better to hold plans lightly.
about:
In a section titled On the Uncertainty of the Future, Kenkō, the 14th-century Japanese monk, notes how rarely our plans go as expected.

You plan to do something today, he says, but something else comes up; the person you were waiting for doesn't come, while someone unexpected does; what we dreaded turns out fine, and what looked easy proves heart-breaking. It is a calm acceptance of life's surprises. Kenkō doesn't say we shouldn't plan. He reminds us to hold plans loosely, because the future is never in our hands.
prompt: What unexpected thing happened today, and what did it bring?

text: Generally speaking, uniformity in anything at all is bad; it is better to leave a little imperfection.
context: Kenkō praises frayed silk covers and mismatched books. Perfection, he suggests, leaves nothing to grow into.
about:
In his Essays in Idleness, Kenkō quotes a monk named Koyu: things made exactly alike are the work of people with little taste; it is better to have some difference.

In general, Kenkō says, uniformity in anything is bad; it is better to leave a little imperfection. Some say, he adds, that a palace should always be built with one small part left unfinished. It is a key idea of Japanese aesthetics. Perfection can be lifeless. A little irregularity makes things feel natural, alive and open to growth.
prompt: Where could a little imperfection make something better?

text: The moon when full begins to wane; where there has been increase there is bound to be decrease; and in every case he who has reached the very front soon gets a set-back.
context: Kenkō observes that every full moon starts to wane, and every peak begins a descent. He uses it to warn against chasing the very top.
about:
In his Essays in Idleness, Kenkō tells of a high minister who refused promotion to the highest rank, saying he would stop where he was. A dragon that reaches the heavens, they say, fears a fall.

The full moon starts to wane, he goes on; where there has been increase, there must be decrease; whoever reaches the very top soon meets a setback. It is a quiet warning about ambition. Rising always means a later fall. Knowing when to stop, short of the peak, can be wiser than climbing all the way.
prompt: Where could you be content with less than the very top?

text: Nothing is harder to forsake than the customs and conventionalities of life, whatever they may be.
context: Kenkō notices how hard it is to step away from social customs and obligations, even when we know they keep us from what matters most.
about:
Kenkō says, in his Essays in Idleness, that people in mourning are excused from all social duties, and so should be the old, the sick and those who have left the world behind.

Nothing is harder to give up, he says, than the customs and conventions of life, whatever they may be. If we can't stop meddling in worldly matters, we will be tied to them forever. It is a sharp observation. We often keep up habits and obligations simply because others do. Letting some go can free our time and minds for what matters.
prompt: Which convention are you keeping only out of habit?

text: Those who cannot feel the littleness of great things in themselves are apt to overlook the greatness of little things in others.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: People who can't see their own smallness miss the greatness of small things in others. Okakura aimed this at Westerners who mocked the tea ceremony as quaint.
about:
Kakuzo Okakura was a Japanese art expert who wrote The Book of Tea in English, published in New York in 1906, to explain the tea ceremony, and Asian ideas of beauty, to Western readers.

Those who cannot feel the littleness of great things in themselves, he says, tend to overlook the greatness of little things in others. It is a subtle line. If we think too much of our own importance, we miss the quiet value of small things, like a cup of tea, a simple room, or another person's modest gift. Humility opens our eyes to them.
prompt: What small thing in someone else have you overlooked?

text: Let us dream of evanescence, and linger in the beautiful foolishness of things.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura invites us to accept that everything passes, and to enjoy the lovely, silly little things while they last. 'Evanescence' means passing quickly.
about:
The first chapter of Kakuzo Okakura's The Book of Tea, written in English and published in New York in 1906, ends with a picture of an afternoon: light on the bamboos, fountains bubbling, the sound of pines in the kettle. Meanwhile, he says, let us have a sip of tea.

Let us dream of evanescence, and linger in the beautiful foolishness of things. Evanescence means passing away, like steam or blossom. Okakura invites us to stop worrying about large problems for a moment, and enjoy what is fleeting and small. It is not a call to ignore the world. It is a reminder that beauty lives in passing moments, if we pause for them.
prompt: What passing thing could you linger over today?

text: The art of life lies in a constant readjustment to our surroundings.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: Kakuzo Okakura wrote The Book of Tea in English in 1906 to explain Japanese culture to the West. Drawing on Taoism, he says living well means constantly adjusting, not following a fixed recipe.
about:
In the third chapter of Kakuzo Okakura's The Book of Tea, written in English and published in New York in 1906, he explains how Taoism shaped Japanese ideas of beauty. Taoism, he says, deals with the present: with ourselves.

The art of life, he writes, lies in constant readjustment to our surroundings. Nothing stays still, so we must keep adapting, like water finding its way. Taoism, he adds, accepts the everyday world as it is, and tries to find beauty in it. It is a gentle philosophy of flexibility. Living well isn't following one fixed plan, but adjusting gracefully as things change.
prompt: What change around you are you resisting instead of adjusting to?

text: Perhaps we reveal ourselves too much in small things because we have so little of the great to conceal.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. II
context: Maybe we give ourselves away in small things because we have little that is grand to hide. A wry, self-mocking line by Okakura.
about:
In the second chapter of Kakuzo Okakura's The Book of Tea, he says that the different ways people have drunk tea over the centuries reflect the spirit of each age.

Life is an expression, he says, and our unconscious actions constantly betray our innermost thoughts. Then the ironic line: perhaps we reveal ourselves too much in small things because we have so little of the great to hide. How we drink tea, set a table or greet a guest shows who we are. Small habits, Okakura suggests, say more about us than grand words.
prompt: What do your small daily habits say about you?

text: The usefulness of a water pitcher dwelt in the emptiness where water might be put, not in the form of the pitcher or the material of which it was made. … One who could make of himself a vacuum into which others might freely enter would become master of all situations.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: A pitcher is useful because of its empty space, not its shape or material. A person who leaves room for others can handle any situation. Okakura borrows the idea from Laozi.
about:
In the third chapter of Kakuzo Okakura's The Book of Tea, he explains Laozi's favourite image: the emptiness that makes things useful.

The reality of a room, he says, is the empty space inside the roof and walls, not the roof and walls themselves. The usefulness of a water pitcher is in the emptiness where water can go, not in its form or material. Okakura applies the idea to the tea room, which is kept almost empty. Space, silence and simplicity aren't absence. They make room for what matters.
prompt: How could you leave more room for others to enter?

text: True beauty could be discovered only by one who mentally completed the incomplete. The virility of life and art lay in its possibilities for growth.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: Real beauty is found by those who complete in their minds what is left unfinished. Life and art stay alive by leaving room to grow. In the tea room, things are left incomplete on purpose.
about:
Okakura contrasts, in the fourth chapter of The Book of Tea (1906), Western classical decoration, with its regular symmetry, with the Taoist and Zen idea of perfection, which cared more about the process than the finished result.

True beauty, he says, could be discovered only by one who mentally completed the incomplete. The strength of life and art lay in their possibilities for growth. That is why the tea room leaves things unfinished, for the guest to complete in imagination. It is a lovely idea. Beauty is not only what we see, but what we are invited to imagine.
prompt: What unfinished thing could you appreciate as it is?

text: In leaving something unsaid the beholder is given a chance to complete the idea and thus a great masterpiece irresistibly rivets your attention until you seem to become actually a part of it.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: Okakura says great art does not spell everything out. It leaves space for us to complete it, and in that space we become part of the work.
about:
Kakuzo Okakura explains, in the third chapter of The Book of Tea (1906), how Taoist ideas of emptiness shaped Japanese art and even the martial art of jiu-jitsu.

In art, he says, the same principle appears as the value of suggestion. By leaving something unsaid, the artist gives the viewer a chance to complete the idea, and so a great masterpiece holds our attention until we seem to become part of it. It applies to conversation and writing too. Leaving room for the listener can say more than saying everything.
prompt: What could you leave unsaid today, and let someone else complete?

text: He only who has lived with the beautiful can die beautifully.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. VII
context: Okakura writes of the great tea masters, who met even their deaths with the grace they had practised all their lives.
about:
The last chapter of Kakuzo Okakura's The Book of Tea, written in English and published in New York in 1906, tells the story of the great tea master Rikiu, who fell out with his patron, the warlord Hideyoshi, and was condemned to die. Just before, Okakura reflects on facing the storms of life calmly.

Only those who have lived with the beautiful can die beautifully, he writes. The last moments of the great tea masters, he goes on, were as refined as their lives. It is a striking thought. A life spent attending to beauty, calm and grace prepares us for its end. How we live shapes how we can meet death.
prompt: What beauty are you living with every day?

text: "Young fool," chided the tea-master, "that is not the way a garden path should be swept." Saying this, Rikiu stepped into the garden, shook a tree and scattered over the garden gold and crimson leaves, scraps of the brocade of autumn!
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: The tea master Rikyū's lesson to a son who had swept the garden perfectly clean: real beauty needs a touch of the natural.
about:
Kakuzo Okakura tells, in the fourth chapter of The Book of Tea (1906), a story about the great tea master Rikiu and his son. Rikiu watched the young man sweep and water the garden path, until not a twig or leaf was left on the ground.

Young fool, the tea master said, that is not how a garden path should be swept. He stepped into the garden, shook a tree, and scattered golden and crimson leaves over the path. Rikiu wanted cleanliness, but also beauty and nature. A perfectly bare path is tidy but lifeless. A few fallen leaves make it real, and beautiful.
prompt: Where could you allow a few leaves to fall?

text: One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time, a real comprehension of the beautiful being possible only through concentration upon some central motive.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: In the Japanese tea room, only one beautiful object is shown at a time. Okakura sees in this a lesson about attention in general: we appreciate deeply only what we focus on.
about:
The tea room, Okakura explains in the fourth chapter of The Book of Tea (1906), is kept almost empty. A single special work of art is brought in for each occasion, and everything else is chosen to set it off.

One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time, he says; real understanding of beauty is possible only by concentrating on one central theme. It is a lesson for an age of endless distraction. We see more, and feel more, when we give our attention to one thing at a time.
prompt: What one thing deserves your full attention today?

text: The current of a running stream flows on unceasingly, but the water is not the same: the foam floating on the pool where it lingers, now vanishes and now forms again, but is never lasting. Such are mankind and their habitations.
context: The famous opening of Hōjōki ('An Account of My Ten-Foot Hut', 1212), written by a poet who withdrew to a tiny mountain hut after years of fire, famine and earthquake.
about:
Kamo no Chōmei, a Japanese poet and musician, retired from the world to live as a monk in a tiny hut, and wrote his Hōjōki (1212), whose title means a record of a ten-foot-square hut. It opens with these famous lines, here in W. G. Aston's translation.

The current of a running stream flows on without ceasing, but the water is never the same; foam on a still pool vanishes and forms again, never lasting long. So it is, Chōmei goes on, with people and their houses in the world. It is a quiet meditation on impermanence. Everything we hold, even our homes, flows on like water.
prompt: What in your life is the same river, but different water?

text: It is barely ten feet square, and only seven feet high. As it was not meant for a fixed abode, the ground about it was trodden hard and left uncultivated. The walls are of mud, and it is thatched with rushes. The joints are fastened with rings and staples, for the greater convenience of removal elsewhere if any subject of dissatisfaction should arise. How little trouble it would take to rebuild it in another place!
context: Chōmei's last home was a hut small enough to take apart and move on two carts. Owning little, he could not lose much.
about:
Kamo no Chōmei describes in his Hōjōki (1212) how his homes grew smaller as he grew older. His last is like a traveller's lodging for one night, or the cocoon of an old silkworm.

It is barely ten feet square, he writes, and only seven feet high. As it was not meant to be a fixed home, the ground around it was simply trodden hard. It is a portrait of a life deliberately simplified. Chōmei had lived through fires, famines and earthquakes in the capital. In his small hut, needing little, he found a freedom the great houses never gave him.
prompt: What could you live without, and how would that lighten you?

text: When I first took up my abode in this place, I thought it was only for a little while. But five years have passed and my temporary hut has become old. Under the eaves there is a deep bed of withered leaves, and moss has gathered on the earthen floor.
context: Chōmei meant his hut to be temporary. Five years later, moss covers the floor. Life settles in while we're still telling ourselves it's for a little while.
about:
In his hut on Mount Hino, Kamo no Chōmei describes in the Hōjōki (1212) the wild animals and birds around him, and how far he feels from the world.

When I first took up my abode here, he writes, I thought it would be only for a little while. But five years have passed, and my temporary hut has grown old; moss has gathered on its earthen floor. It is a gentle observation about time. What we mean as temporary often becomes our life. Chōmei accepts it calmly, and comes to love his makeshift home.
prompt: What 'temporary' arrangement in your life has quietly become permanent?

text: When on a calm night the moon shines in at my window, I think with yearning of the men of old.
context: Alone in his hut, Chōmei finds company in the moon and in the memory of those who lived before him.
about:
Kamo no Chōmei, who lived alone in a tiny hut, describes in his Hōjōki (1212) his walks in the hills, gathering cherry branches, autumn leaves, young ferns and nuts according to the season.

When on a calm night the moon shines in at my window, he writes, I think with yearning of the men of old, and at the cry of the monkeys my sleeve is wet with tears. Solitude here is full of feeling, not empty. Nature and memory keep him company. It is a picture of a quiet life that is deeply alive to beauty and to the past.
prompt: Who from the past do you feel close to on a quiet night?

text: Things which Excite Regrets for the Past: Withered hollyhocks. On a wet day to turn over the letters of a person once loved by us. Last year's fans. Bright moonlight nights.
source: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book (Makura no Sōshi)
context: Sei Shōnagon (born around 966) served at the Japanese imperial court and kept a book of lists, moments, and opinions. Small objects, she shows, can carry great feeling.
about:
Sei Shōnagon was a lady-in-waiting to the Empress of Japan around the year 1000. Her Pillow Book, made of notes jotted down without order, includes many lists. This one, translated by W. G. Aston, is of things that make us long for the past.

Withered hollyhocks, from festivals now over. On a wet day, turning over the letters of someone we once loved. Last year's fans. Bright moonlit nights. Each item is small, but each opens a door to memory. Sei Shōnagon had a sharp eye for the feelings hidden in ordinary things. Her list still works. Most of us could add our own.
prompt: Which small object brings back a whole chapter of your life?
translation: W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: I love to watch the dawn grow gradually whiter and whiter, till a faint rosy tinge crowns the mountain's crest … In winter, how unspeakably beautiful is the snow!
source: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book (Makura no Sōshi)
context: The famous opening of the Pillow Book names the best moment of each season. It is an exercise in paying close attention to what is beautiful right now.
about:
The Pillow Book of Sei Shōnagon, a lady at the Japanese court around 1000, opens with the four seasons. Spring comes first.

In spring, she says, I love to watch the dawn grow gradually whiter, until a faint rosy tinge crowns the mountains, while thin streaks of purple cloud stretch above them. It is a moment of pure attention: one favourite time, seen exactly. She goes on to name the best moment of each season. It is an invitation to notice what we love in each part of the year, and to look for it.
prompt: What is the most beautiful moment of this season where you live?
translation: W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: Cheerful Things: A river boat going down stream. … A drink of water when awake during the night.
source: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book (Makura no Sōshi)
context: Her lists find joy in tiny, ordinary things. Making your own list is one of the oldest journaling exercises there is.
about:
Sei Shōnagon, who served at the Japanese court around 1000, filled her Pillow Book with lists of things, written down as they came to her. This one is of Cheerful Things.

A river boat going downstream. A drink of water when awake at night. A visitor, when we feel dull, neither so close as to be uninteresting, nor so distant that we can't be at ease. Her pleasures are small and exact. That is their charm. Happiness, for her, isn't one grand event, but a collection of little moments, noticed and named.
prompt: What would be on your list of 'cheerful things' right now?
translation: W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: Dreary Things: … A brazier with the fire gone out. … A letter from one's country home with no news in it.
source: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book (Makura no Sōshi)
context: She is just as precise about small disappointments. Naming them clearly takes away some of their weight.
about:
Among the many lists in Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book, written at the Japanese court around 1000, is this one of Dreary Things.

A brazier with the fire gone out. A coachman his ox hates. A letter from home with no news in it. Her eye for small disappointments is as sharp as her eye for joys. The list is funny and sad at once. Naming what makes us feel low, as she does, can make it lighter. It also reminds us how much small things shape our days.
prompt: What small, dreary thing drains you more than it should?
translation: W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: It is not only when we look at the moon or flowers with our eyes that they give us pleasure.
context: Kenkō goes on to say that imagining the moon from inside a room, or remembering the blossoms, can move us just as much. Beauty also lives in the mind.
about:
Kenkō's Essays in Idleness, quoted by W. G. Aston in his History of Japanese Literature (1899), lists just before this passage things there can be too many of: furniture, pens in a stand, words when people meet. But never too many books.

It is not only when we look at the moon or flowers with our eyes that they give us pleasure, he goes on. On a spring day, even indoors, or on a moonlit night, even in our room, just thinking of them delights us. Beauty lives in imagination and memory too. We don't always need to see something to enjoy it.
prompt: What beautiful thing can you enjoy without seeing it?
translation: C. S. Eby, quoted in W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: It is change that in all things touches us with sympathy.
context: For Kenkō, things move us because they pass. If nothing changed, nothing would touch our hearts.
about:
Yoshida Kenkō was a Japanese courtier who became a Buddhist monk in the 14th century. His Essays in Idleness is a loose collection of short notes on almost every subject, written, he tells us, simply to pass the long, empty days.

This line holds one of its central ideas: things move us because they pass. A blossom matters partly because it will fall, a season because it will end. Japanese tradition has a name for this feeling, mono no aware, roughly “the pathos of things”: a gentle sadness that is also a way of loving the world. For Kenkō, change is not only something to fear. It is what makes us notice, and care.
prompt: Which change has touched you recently?
translation: C. S. Eby, quoted in W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: Things which give one a Thrill: To see sparrows feeding their young. To pass by where infants are playing.
source: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book (Makura no Sōshi)
context: Sei Shōnagon notices the small moments that make the heart jump. Her lists invite us to keep our own.
about:
Sei Shōnagon, a lady at the Japanese court around 1000, lists in her Pillow Book things that give a thrill: small moments that quicken the heart.

To see sparrows feeding their young. To pass by where small children are playing. To notice a metal mirror starting to cloud. To be asked the way by a handsome man who stops his carriage to do it. The list mixes tenderness, worry and flirtation. It is very human. Our hearts are stirred by little things, if we pay attention.
prompt: What small sight gives you a thrill?
translation: W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: Detestable Things: Babies that cry or dogs that bark when you want to listen.
source: Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book (Makura no Sōshi)
context: A thousand years later, the irritations are familiar. Naming them with humour takes away some of their sting.
about:
Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book, written at the Japanese court around 1000, has a long list of Detestable Things.

Babies that cry, or dogs that bark, just when you want to listen. Visitors who talk on when you are in a hurry. A healer who mumbles his charms as if half asleep. Her annoyances are recognisable a thousand years later. That is part of her appeal. Some feelings don't change, and naming them honestly, with humour, makes them easier to bear.
prompt: What small annoyance could you name and laugh at?
translation: W. G. Aston, A History of Japanese Literature (1899)

text: We have developed along different lines, but there is no reason why one should not supplement the other.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura wrote to bridge East and West in 1906: different cultures, he argued, can complete rather than compete with each other.
about:
Kakuzo Okakura wrote The Book of Tea in English, published in New York in 1906, partly to answer Western mockery of Asia. You may laugh at us for having too much tea, he says, but perhaps you have no tea in your constitution.

We have developed along different lines, he goes on, but there is no reason why one should not supplement the other. It is a generous and hopeful message, written at a time of rivalry and misunderstanding. East and West, or any two cultures, need not compete. Each has gained something the other lacks. Learning from each other makes both richer.
prompt: What has someone very different from you taught you?

text: You have gained expansion at the cost of restlessness; we have created a harmony which is weak against aggression.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura is honest about both sides: the West's restless growth and Japan's fragile harmony each have a price.
about:
In the first chapter of Kakuzo Okakura's The Book of Tea, he asks East and West to stop trading insults and learn from each other.

You have gained expansion at the cost of restlessness, he says to the West; we have created a harmony that is weak against aggression. Each civilisation has paid a price for its strengths. It is an honest, balanced assessment. Neither side has everything right. Seeing our own costs, and the other's gifts, is the beginning of real exchange.
prompt: What has your way of life gained, and at what cost?

text: The masterpiece is of ourselves, as we are of the masterpiece.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. V
context: A great work of art and the person looking at it complete each other. What we see in art says something about us.
about:
Kakuzo Okakura's chapter on art appreciation in The Book of Tea (1906) describes how a great work speaks to us: memories long forgotten come back with new meaning, and hidden hopes and longings stand forth.

Our mind is the canvas on which artists lay their colour, he says; their pigments are our emotions. The masterpiece is of ourselves, as we are of the masterpiece. Art isn't only out there, to be looked at. It lives in the meeting between the work and the viewer. What we bring changes what we see, and what we see changes us.
prompt: What does the art you love say about you?

text: In joy or sadness, flowers are our constant friends.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. VI
context: Flowers mark births, weddings, illnesses, and funerals. Okakura's chapter on flowers celebrates their quiet company.
about:
In the sixth chapter of Kakuzo Okakura's The Book of Tea, he writes about flowers, and how offering the first garland made humans rise above crude necessity.

In joy or sadness, he says, flowers are our constant friends. We eat, drink, sing, dance and celebrate with them. We marry and name our children with them. We dare not die without them. It is a warm tribute to how deeply flowers are woven into human life, at every important moment. They mark our joys and comfort our griefs.
prompt: What small presence keeps you company in joy and sadness?

text: The Present is the moving Infinity, the legitimate sphere of the Relative.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: In his chapter on Taoism, Okakura says the present is not a small slice of time but the only place where eternity is actually lived. Everything real happens now.
about:
Taoism, Kakuzo Okakura writes in the third chapter of The Book of Tea (1906), has always been called by Chinese historians the art of being in the world, because it deals with the present, with ourselves.

The present is the moving infinity, he says, the true sphere of the relative. Everything changes, so everything must be understood in relation to the moment. The next line draws the lesson: the art of life lies in constant readjustment to our surroundings. It is a dense, poetic phrase. The present is where the endless and the changing meet, and where we actually live.
prompt: What in this present moment holds more than you usually notice?

text:
Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains,
Lamenting its banishment from its home:
"Ever since they tore me from my osier bed,
My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears."
context: The famous opening of the Masnavi, Rumi's long poem in Persian. The reed, cut from the riverbed, sings because it longs for home. For the Sufis, the human soul is that reed, longing to return to its source.
about:
These are the opening lines of the Masnavi, a long poem in rhyming couplets by Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207–1273), who was born in Balkh and died in Konya. Over six books it weaves together stories and reflections, and it begins here, with the sound of a reed flute.

The reed was cut from its reed bed, and its song is a lament for home. Rumi asks us to hear ourselves in it. Many of us carry a sense of being cut off from something: a place, a person, a fuller way of being. Rumi treats that longing not as a fault to fix but as the source of the music. What we miss shows us what we love, and the ache itself moves others who hear it.
prompt: What do you long for that you can't quite name?

text:
Do you know why your mirror does not reflect?
Because the rust has not been scoured from its face.
context: Mirrors in Rumi's time were polished metal, and they rusted. The heart, he says, can reflect truth only when it is cleaned of pride and selfish desire.
about:
This couplet comes at the end of the prologue of Rumi's Masnavi, which opens with a reed flute singing of its lost home. Mirrors in Rumi's day were made of polished metal, and they rusted unless someone scoured them.

The image is simple: a mirror shows what is in front of it only when it is clean. For Rumi, the heart works the same way. Pride, envy and selfish wanting build up on it like rust, until we see little but our own concerns. Clarity, then, is not something we add, like a new skill. It comes from removing what clouds us. The work is not dramatic. It is cleaning.
prompt: What 'rust' is clouding the way you see things?

text:
Look for the moon in heaven, not in the water!
If you desire to rise above mere names and letters,
Make yourself free from self at one stroke!
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, 'The Chinese and the Greek Artists'
context: In this story, one group of artists paints a wall while the other simply polishes the opposite wall until it reflects everything. The moon in the water is only a reflection, and words about truth are not the truth.
about:
In a story from Rumi's Masnavi, the Chinese and the Greeks argue over who paints better, and a sultan gives each a house to decorate. The Chinese use every colour they can find. The Greeks use none: they simply polish their walls until they shine. When the houses are shown, the Greek walls win, because they reflect all the colours of the other house.

The moon in the water is only a reflection; the real moon is in the sky. In the same way, names and words about a thing are not the thing itself. Rumi's lesson is that we reach what matters less by piling up knowledge than by clearing ourselves, like the polished wall, so that what is real can show.
prompt: Where are you settling for the reflection instead of the real thing?

text:
I regard not the outside and the words,
I regard the inside and the state of heart.
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book II, 'Moses and the Shepherd'
context: Moses scolds a simple shepherd for praying in clumsy, childlike words. God then rebukes Moses: what matters is the heart behind the words.
about:
In this story from Rumi's Masnavi, Moses hears a shepherd praying in simple, childlike words: he offers to comb the hair and sew the clothes of the one he prays to, and to fetch him milk. Moses scolds him for speaking so crudely. Then Moses himself is rebuked, and these lines are part of that rebuke.

Words are only the outside of a feeling. A clumsy sentence spoken from the heart can be worth more than a polished one spoken without it. The story also warns against the urge to correct how others express what they hold dear: what sounds wrong to us may be right for them. What counts is the state of the heart behind the words.
prompt: Whose words have you judged without seeing their heart?

text:
A true lover is proved such by his pain of heart;
No sickness is there like sickness of heart.
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, Story I
context: For Rumi, longing is not a weakness but proof of love. The ache tells us what we truly care about.
about:
These lines follow the first story of Rumi's Masnavi, in which a prince's beloved falls ill and no doctor can cure her, until a new physician sees that she is lovesick. Rumi then pauses the story to describe love itself.

His claim sounds strange at first: pain is the proof of love. But we know it from life. We do not ache for what we don't care about. Missing someone, worrying for them, feeling their absence: these are the marks of real attachment. Rumi doesn't tell us to get rid of this pain, but to read it, because it shows honestly what matters to us. He adds that however well we explain love, once we fall in love we are ashamed of our words.
prompt: What does your longing tell you about what you love?

text: The body may be compared to a steed and the soul to its rider.
source: Al-Ghazali, The Alchemy of Happiness, Chapter I
context: The body carries us, but it is not who we are. A rider who neglects the horse won't get far, and one who lets the horse choose the road won't arrive.
about:
Al-Ghazali (1058–1111) was born in Tus, in Khorasan, and became a famous professor of theology in Baghdad. The Alchemy of Happiness is his book on living well, and it begins with knowing oneself.

Here he offers a simple picture of a person. The body is like a horse and the soul like its rider. The horse matters: it carries us, and it needs food, rest and care. But it is not the one who should choose the road. Left to itself, a horse follows its hunger, not a destination. Al-Ghazali's question is who is steering our lives: our deeper aims, or our appetites. Caring for the body and being led by it are two different things.
prompt: Is your body serving your purpose, or setting the direction?

text: …the body may be figured as a kingdom, the soul as its king … Reason may be called the vizier, or prime minister, passion the revenue-collector, and anger the police-officer.
source: Al-Ghazali, The Alchemy of Happiness, Chapter I
context: Think of your body as a kingdom with the soul as its king. Reason is the prime minister, desire the tax collector, and anger the police. Things go wrong when a servant takes the throne.
about:
This image comes from the first chapter of Al-Ghazali's The Alchemy of Happiness. He describes a person as a small kingdom: the soul is the king, the senses and faculties are its army, reason is the chief minister, desire collects the taxes, and anger keeps order.

Each of these has a real job. Desire keeps us going and anger can protect us, so Al-Ghazali says they must be kept in their place, not killed or driven out. The trouble begins when they act on their own: desire, while collecting what it is owed, starts to plunder, and anger turns harsh. A healthy inner life, in this picture, is good government. Every part has its role, but reason advises and the self decides.
prompt: Where have desire or anger been acting like the king in your life lately?

text:
The eye of outward sense is as the palm of a hand,
The whole of the object is not grasped in the palm.
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book III, 'The Elephant in a Dark Room'
context: In the story, people touch an elephant in the dark: one feels a trunk, another a leg, and each is sure they know what it is. Our senses grasp only a part.
about:
In this story from Rumi's Masnavi, some people are shown an elephant in a dark room. Unable to see it, they feel it with their hands. One touches the trunk and says it is like a water-pipe, another the ear and says it is a fan, another a leg and calls it a pillar.

Each is partly right and wholly sure, and that is the trouble. Rumi compares our senses to the palm of a hand: they grasp a piece, never the whole. The story invites humility in our disagreements. When someone describes the world differently from us, they may simply be touching another part of it. Seeing more often begins with admitting how little our own hand holds.
prompt: Which part of a bigger picture are you mistaking for the whole?

text:
We, like boats, are tossed hither and thither,
We are blind though we are on the bright ocean.
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book III, 'The Elephant in a Dark Room'
context: We drift from one thing to the next, missing the vastness we are floating on. For Rumi, the ocean is the divine, all around us yet unseen.
about:
These lines follow the story of the elephant in the dark room in Rumi's Masnavi, where each person feels one part of the animal and mistakes it for the whole. Rumi widens the point with the image of the sea.

We look at the foam, the little waves rising and falling, and miss the sea that makes them. Like small boats, we are tossed from one thing to the next, busy with whatever is in front of us, and blind to what holds us all up. Rumi points to something larger than our daily concerns, always present and easy to overlook. The invitation is to lift our eyes from the foam now and then, and notice the ocean.
prompt: What big thing around you have you stopped seeing?

text:
Gaze not on your own pictures, fair or ugly,
Gaze on your love and the object of your desire.
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book III, 'The Lover who read Sonnets to his Mistress'
context: Self-absorption, whether proud or ashamed, keeps our eyes on ourselves. Rumi tells us to look toward what we love.
about:
This comes from a story in Rumi's Masnavi about a lover who is at last allowed to see the woman he loves. Instead of greeting her, he takes out a sheet of poems and reads to her about her charms and his own feelings. She stops him: what he really loves, she says, is his “own effusions and ecstatic raptures,” not her.

Rumi's lines draw the lesson. We can be so taken up with our picture of ourselves, proud of it or ashamed of it, that we stop looking at what we love. It is easy to care more about how we feel, or how we come across, than about the person in front of us. Look up, Rumi says, at the one you love.
prompt: Where are you staring at your own reflection instead of what you care about?

text:
The heart of man is like the root of a tree,
Therefrom grow the leaves on firm branches.
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book III, 'The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara'
context: What grows in a life, words, actions, and habits, starts in the heart. Tend the root and the branches follow.
about:
This comes from a story in Rumi's Masnavi about an official of the Prince of Bukhara who runs away after an offence and hides for ten years. Unable to bear being far from his lord and his home, he returns, though his friends warn him he will be punished. Moved by his love, the prince's love for him is kindled in return.

Rumi uses the story to say where things grow from. The heart is like the root of a tree, and our words, actions and habits are its branches and leaves. When the root is sound, what grows from it is sound. It reverses how we often try to change. We work on the leaves, on behaviour and appearances, when the change has to start lower down, in what we love and want.
prompt: What is growing from the root of your heart right now?

text:
Pass over names and look to qualities,
So that qualities may lead you to essence!
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book II, 'The Tree of Life'
context: In the story, a man searches for a magical tree by its name and never finds it. A wise man tells him to look for its qualities instead.
about:
In this story from Rumi's Masnavi, a king hears of a tree in India whose fruit lets you live forever, and sends a courtier to find it. He searches everywhere, is mocked and misled, and returns empty-handed. The wise man who first told of the tree laughs: it is the tree of knowledge, and the courtier has been chasing a name.

A name points to something, but it is not the thing. If we look only for the label, we may walk right past what we seek. Rumi's advice is to look for qualities instead: what something does, how it shows itself. Qualities lead to the essence. The same holds for words like success or happiness: we chase the word, when we could ask what it would actually look like.
prompt: Which title or label are you chasing, rather than the quality behind it?

text:
For it seemed that love was an easy thing,
But my feet have fallen on difficult ways.
context: Hafiz (c. 1325–1390) of Shiraz is Iran's most loved poet. Translated here by Gertrude Bell, explorer and scholar. Love looks simple from outside and turns out to be a path.
about:
Hafiz was born in Shiraz in the early 14th century and spent most of his life there. His poems are short lyrics about love, wine and longing. These are the opening lines of the first poem in Gertrude Bell's 1897 English selection of his work.

The line is honest in a way many love poems are not. From outside, love looks simple. From inside, it turns out to be a road with steep and difficult stretches. Hafiz is not saying that love was a mistake. He is admitting he underestimated it. That admission is a kind of wisdom: the things most worth having often ask more of us than we expected, and that is part of their worth.
prompt: What did you think would be easy to love, or to do, that turned out hard?

text:
Not on the lips of men Love's secret lies,
Remote and unrevealed his dwelling-place.
context: For Sufi poets, Love often means divine love. Its deepest truth can't be talked about, only lived.
about:
This poem comes from Gertrude Bell's 1897 translation of Hafiz, the 14th-century poet of Shiraz. Like Sa'di and Rumi, Hafiz was a Sufi, and in his poems love often stands for more than love between two people.

Here he says that Love's deepest secret is not found in what people say about it. That is a humbling thought for anyone who has read a book on love, or tried to explain it. Some things can be pointed at with words, but only known by living them. The poem ends with patience and wisdom drowned in a sea of tears: love is learned by going through it, not by describing it.
prompt: Which love in your life is understood better by living it than by talking about it?

text:
It flows past—so flows your life away,
So sweetly, swiftly, fleets our little day—
context: Hafiz sits by a stream and sees his life in it: sweet, quick, and passing. The feeling is close to Japanese poems on impermanence.
about:
This poem, in Gertrude Bell's 1897 translation of Hafiz, is built around a refrain: “This is enough for me!” A rosy cheek, a garden, the shadow of a cypress, a cup of wine: Hafiz lists simple pleasures and says they are enough.

Then he sits by a river and sees his life flowing past in it, sweet and swift. The thought could turn sad, but here it does the opposite. Because the day is short, what we already have is enough. Hafiz is not chasing more; he is noticing. Many traditions share this idea: contentment is less about getting what we want than about seeing what is already here.
prompt: If today is flowing past, what do you want to notice before it's gone?

text:
Except your road through affliction pass,
None may reach the halting-station of mirth;
context: Unless your road passes through hardship, you won't reach the resting place of joy. A 'halting-station' was a rest stop on a caravan route.
about:
This line comes from a poem in Gertrude Bell's 1897 translation of Hafiz, the 14th-century poet of Shiraz. A halting-station was a stopping place on a caravan route, where travellers rested after a long day's journey.

Hafiz's claim is that joy is not reached by going around hardship, but through it. That can sound bleak, but it matches common experience. The happiness that follows a hard climb, a long illness or a difficult conversation is deeper than easy pleasure, because we know what it cost. Hafiz does not praise suffering for its own sake. He says the road to the place of rest passes through it, and that the rest is real.
prompt: What hardship are you trying to go around instead of through?

text:
The span of your life is as five little days,
Brief hours and swift in this halting-place;
context: Life is a short stop on a longer journey. Hafiz's response is not sadness but an invitation to enjoy and love while we can.
about:
This comes from a poem in Gertrude Bell's 1897 translation of Hafiz in which every verse ends on the word “nought”: nothing. Here life is pictured as five little days in a halting-place, a rest stop on a caravan route.

It would be easy to read the poem as gloomy. But Hafiz's answer to the shortness of life is not despair. Rest softly, he says, while the shadow delays; while the moment is yours, fill the glass. Knowing our time is short can make us anxious, or it can make us attentive. Hafiz chooses the second: since we are only passing through, we may as well enjoy the stop, and the company.
prompt: If you had five days, what would you stop postponing?

text:
Consider the rose that breaks into flower,
Neither repines though she fade and die—
context: The rose blooms fully without complaining that it will fade. Hafiz offers it as a model for living.
about:
It belongs to the same poem as Hafiz's “five little days”, in Gertrude Bell's 1897 translation: a meditation on how short and fragile everything is, in which every verse ends on the word “nought”.

Against all that, Hafiz sets the rose. It opens fully, even though it will fade and die, and it does not complain. The rose does not hold back its flowering to protect itself from loss. Hafiz offers it as a model. We often hesitate to love, to start something or to give ourselves to it, because it might not last. The rose suggests another way. Fading is not a reason not to flower.
prompt: What would you bloom into if you stopped worrying about it ending?

text: The sons of Adam are members one of another, for in their creation they have a common origin.
source: Sa'di, Gulistan (The Rose Garden), ch. I, story 10
context: Sa'di (c. 1210–1291) of Shiraz wrote the Gulistan in prose and verse. In its verse form, this is one of the most quoted lines in Persian, a call to feel others' pain as our own.
about:
Sa'di was a Persian poet from Shiraz, and his Gulistan (“Rose Garden”, usually dated 1258) mixes short prose stories with verse. In this story, Sa'di is praying in the great mosque of Damascus when a prince known for his injustice arrives and asks Sa'di to pray with him, because he fears a powerful enemy. Sa'di tells him to have compassion on his own weak subjects instead.

Then comes this line, often quoted in its Persian verse form. Human beings are like parts of one body: when one suffers, the others feel it. Sa'di adds a sharp ending: whoever is indifferent to others' pain is unworthy of being called human. The idea is simple and demanding. Other people's suffering is not someone else's business. It is ours.
prompt: Who do you find hardest to see as part of the same human family?

text: Do not sit down soured at the revolutions of the times, for patience is bitter, yet it will yield sweet fruit.
source: Sa'di, Gulistan (The Rose Garden), ch. I, story 16
context: Times turn, and bitterness doesn't speed them up. Patience tastes bad at first and pays off later.
about:
This line comes from a story in Sa'di's Gulistan about a poor friend who wants a post at the king's court. Sa'di warns him that serving kings is risky, but helps him, and the friend rises quickly to become a royal favourite. Sa'di speaks these words as his friend's fortunes turn: hard times, he says, had not been the end.

Later the friend falls from favour and is thrown into prison, a reminder that fortune turns both ways. The line holds in both directions. When times are bad, sulking does not speed them up, and patience, though it tastes bitter, bears sweet fruit. When times are good, it is wise to remember they can change. Patience here is not passive waiting, but steadiness while the wheel turns.
prompt: What are you impatient about that may simply need time?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: If you covet riches, ask only for contentment, which is an immense treasure.
source: Sa'di, Gulistan (The Rose Garden), ch. II, story 27
context: The richest person is the one who no longer feels short. Sa'di echoes Epicurus and Laozi from a very different world.
about:
In a story from Sa'di's Gulistan, a dying king with no heir orders that the first person through the city gate the next morning shall be crowned. It turns out to be a beggar. When an old friend comes to congratulate him, the new king says: offer me condolence instead, for now I have the cares of a whole kingdom on my head.

His point is that more does not always mean better. When he was poor he worried about bread; now he worries about a country. Either way, the mind stays restless. So he says: if you want riches, ask only for contentment, which is a treasure in itself. Being content is not having everything. It is no longer feeling that we lack.
prompt: What do you already have that would be enough, if you let it?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: Be good yourself, and let people speak evil of you; it is better than to be wicked, and that they should consider you as good.
source: Sa'di, Gulistan (The Rose Garden), ch. II, story 22
context: Better to be good and misjudged than bad and admired. Reputation is what others think; character is what we are.
about:
This line comes from a story in Sa'di's Gulistan about a man who has given up his wild ways and joined a group of dervishes, but people keep gossiping that he hasn't really changed. Hurt, he complains to his teacher.

The teacher's answer is surprising: be grateful that you are better than they say. It is far better to be good and spoken ill of than to be bad and thought good. Sa'di then adds a twist about himself: everyone thinks well of him, while he knows his own faults. Reputation is what others say about us; character is what we are. We cannot fully control the first, but the second is in our hands.
prompt: Would you rather be good or be seen as good, honestly?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text:
My heart has become capable of every form: it is a pasture for gazelles and a convent for Christian monks,
And a temple for idols and the pilgrim's Ka'ba and the tables of the Tora and the book of the Koran.
I follow the religion of Love: whatever way Love's camels take, that is my religion and my faith.
source: Ibn Arabi, The Tarjuman al-Ashwaq, XI
context: Ibn Arabi says his heart can now hold every form, from a meadow for animals to a monastery or a temple, and that he follows love wherever it goes. Ibn Arabi (1165–1240) saw love as a path wide enough for all.
about:
Ibn Arabi (1165–1240) was an Arab mystic and philosopher. The Tarjuman al-Ashwaq is a collection of his love poems, on which he also wrote his own commentary; R. A. Nicholson translated both in 1911.

These lines are often read as a hymn to openness: a heart that can hold every form, from a pasture for gazelles to a monastery, a temple, and the holy books of several faiths. Ibn Arabi's own commentary reads them more narrowly, within his own faith, as a heart that receives truth in many forms. Either way, the image is striking. A heart that has grown in love becomes wide enough to recognise truth and beauty in many places, and goes wherever love leads.
prompt: How wide is the room in your heart for people who believe differently?

text: To define health and satiety, to penetrate their causes and conditions, is quite another thing from being well and satisfied. To define drunkenness … is quite a different thing to being drunk.
context: Knowing about something is not the same as knowing it. Al-Ghazali realised he could describe the spiritual life perfectly without having lived it.
about:
Al-Ghazali (1058–1111) was a celebrated professor of theology in Baghdad when doubts led him to give up his post and his fortune. Deliverance from Error is his own account of that search. Here he describes studying the books of the Sufi mystics, and realising that reading alone could not take him where he wanted to go.

His examples are vivid. Defining health is not the same as being healthy. Knowing what causes drunkenness is not the same as being drunk; the drunk man, in fact, knows least about it. There is knowing about something, and knowing it from the inside. The point holds far beyond his own search: we can read everything about kindness, courage or calm, and still have to practise them to know them.
prompt: What do you know about but have never actually experienced?

text: The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, / Moves on: nor all thy Piety nor Wit / Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line, / Nor all thy Tears wash out a Word of it.
context: Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian mathematician and astronomer. Edward FitzGerald's free English version of his quatrains (1859) became one of the most popular poems in English. What is done is done: no cleverness or regret can rewrite the past.
about:
Omar Khayyam was a Persian astronomer and poet from Nishapur, the son of a tentmaker. His Rubáiát is a collection of short four-line poems, not one continuous poem, and Edward FitzGerald's free English version of 1859 made them famous in the West.

This quatrain is about the past. Once something is written, the hand moves on, and nothing we bring, neither piety nor cleverness nor tears, can erase a line. That can sound harsh, but it also clears the mind. Regret cannot change what happened; only what we do next is still open. Khayyam invites us to stop trying to rewrite the past, and to pay attention to the page we are writing now.
prompt: What would you stop regretting if you accepted it can't be rewritten?

text: The Worldly Hope men set their Hearts upon / Turns Ashes—or it prospers; and anon, / Like Snow upon the Desert's dusty Face / Lighting a little Hour or two—is gone.
context: Whether our ambitions fail or succeed, they pass like snow on hot sand.
about:
This is one of the quatrains, or four-line poems, of the Persian astronomer-poet Omar Khayyam, in Edward FitzGerald's 1859 English version. Again and again they return to how brief and fragile human plans are.

Here the image is snow on the desert. Our hopes either turn to ashes or come true, and either way they last only an hour or two before they're gone. The surprising part is that success and failure end up alike. Khayyam is not telling us to stop hoping. He is reminding us not to set our whole heart on outcomes, because nothing we win or lose will stay for long. What remains is how we live while it lasts.
prompt: Which ambition would matter less if you saw it as snow in the desert?

text: Myself when young did eagerly frequent / Doctor and Saint, and heard great Argument / About it and about: but evermore / Came out by the same Door as in I went.
context: Khayyam listened to the great scholars and preachers of his day and found he understood no more after than before. A humble note on the limits of argument.
about:
This quatrain is from Omar Khayyam's Rubáiát, in Edward FitzGerald's 1859 version. Khayyam was a learned man, an astronomer from Nishapur, yet here he looks back on his student days with a shrug.

As a young man he listened eagerly to great scholars and holy men arguing about the deepest questions, round and round. Each time he came out by the same door he went in: no wiser. The lines are funny and humble. They don't say that thinking is useless, only that some questions are not settled by debate, however brilliant. The next quatrain sums up his harvest: “I came like Water, and like Wind I go.”
prompt: Which big question have you argued about without getting any closer?

text: There was a Door to which I found no Key: / There was a Veil past which I could not see: / Some little Talk awhile of Me and Thee / There seem'd—and then no more of Thee and Me.
context: Some mysteries stay locked. Our lives are a brief conversation, and then they end.
about:
This quatrain is from Omar Khayyam's Rubáiát, in Edward FitzGerald's 1859 version. In the verse just before it, the speaker says he rose to the heavens and untied many knots on the way, “But not the Knot of Human Death and Fate.”

So he meets a door with no key and a veil he cannot see past. Our lives, he says, are a little talk of “me and thee”, and then it ends. Khayyam doesn't pretend to have answers he lacks, and that honesty is part of his appeal. The poem leaves us with two things at once: the mystery we cannot solve, and the brief conversation we do have. If the talk is short, it is worth having well.
prompt: What question have you made peace with not answering?

text: Ah, make the most of what we yet may spend, / Before we too into the Dust descend; / Dust into Dust, and under Dust, to lie, / Sans Wine, sans Song, sans Singer, and—sans End.
context: 'Sans' is French for 'without'. Since life ends, Khayyam urges us to use well what time we have.
about:
This quatrain is from Omar Khayyam's Rubáiát, in Edward FitzGerald's 1859 version. “Sans” is French for “without”. The verse before it remembers friends who have already gone, and says that we too must one day go down beneath the earth.

Then comes this urgent advice: make the most of what we may still spend, before we go to dust, without wine, song, singer, or end. The repeated “dust” and “sans” sound like a door closing. But the lines are not meant to frighten. Their message is one Khayyam returns to often: our time is limited, so use it well, and do not put off the good things in life for a future that may not come.
prompt: What would 'making the most' of the coming days look like?

text: Think, in this batter'd Caravanserai / Whose Doorways are alternate Night and Day, / How Sultan after Sultan with his Pomp / Abode his Hour or two, and went his way.
context: A caravanserai was a roadside inn for travellers. The world is such an inn: even the mightiest rulers only stayed a night.
about:
A caravanserai was a roadside inn where travellers and their animals stopped for the night, and Omar Khayyam uses one as his image in this quatrain from the Rubáiát, in Edward FitzGerald's 1859 version.

Khayyam pictures the world as such an inn, battered by age, with night and day as its two doors. Sultan after sultan has stayed here in all his pomp, for an hour or two, and gone his way. Even the most powerful are guests, not owners. The image is humbling, but also freeing. We need not cling to the room or dread leaving it. We can stay as good guests do: taking care of the place, and being kind to the other travellers.
prompt: If you are only staying a night, how do you want to spend it?

text: A Book of Verses underneath the Bough, / A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread—and Thou / Beside me singing in the Wilderness— / Oh, Wilderness were Paradise enow!
context: The most quoted lines of the Rubáiyát: a few simple pleasures and the person you love are enough to make any place a paradise.
about:
These are among the best-known lines of Omar Khayyam's Rubáiát. They come from Edward FitzGerald's fifth edition (1889): he kept revising his English version for thirty years after first publishing it in 1859.

The list is short: a book of poems under a tree, a jug of wine, a loaf of bread, and the one you love singing beside you. With that, even a wilderness would be paradise enough. The verse just before speaks of a strip of grass between the desert and the farmland, “Where name of Slave and Sultan is forgot.” Happiness, Khayyam suggests, needs little and nothing grand: presence, and someone to share it with.
prompt: What simple things make your wilderness a paradise?

text: Ah, fill the Cup:—what boots it to repeat / How Time is slipping underneath our Feet: / Unborn To-morrow, and dead Yesterday / Why fret about them if To-day be sweet!
context: 'What boots it' means 'what use is it'. Tomorrow isn't here and yesterday is gone; today is the only time we can enjoy.
about:
In Omar Khayyam's Rubáiát, in Edward FitzGerald's 1859 version, this quatrain follows one in which the poet watches a potter pounding wet clay, and imagines the clay murmuring, “Gently, Brother, gently, pray!” “What boots it” is old English for “what good does it do”.

The clay was once alive, the poem suggests, as we are now. So why spend today repeating how fast time is slipping away? Tomorrow is not yet born, and yesterday is dead. If today is sweet, enjoy it. This is not an argument against planning or remembering. It is a gentle rebuke to worry, which steals the present by living in a future or a past we cannot touch.
prompt: What sweetness in today are you missing by worrying?

text: Whoever has no patience has no wisdom.
context: For Sa'di, patience is not a separate virtue but part of being wise at all.
about:
This line comes at the very start of the third chapter of Sa'di's Gulistan, “On the Preciousness of Contentment”. A beggar in Aleppo tells the shopkeepers that if the rich were fair and the poor content, all begging would end. Sa'di follows with a few lines in praise of contentment and patience.

Whoever has no patience, he says, has no wisdom. For Sa'di, patience is not an extra virtue added on top of wisdom, but part of what wisdom is. A wise person sees further than the moment, and so can wait: for anger to cool, for a plan to ripen, for a situation to show what it really is. Impatience narrows our view to what we want right now. Patience widens it.
prompt: Where is impatience making you act unwisely?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: A vast and deep river is not rendered turbid by throwing into it a stone.
context: A deep river stays clear when a stone is thrown in; a deep person stays calm when insulted.
about:
In a story from Sa'di's Gulistan, a gang of rowdy men insult and beat a dervish, and he goes to his teacher to complain. The teacher reminds him that the patched cloak of a dervish is “the garment of resignation”: wearing it means learning to bear what comes.

Then the image: throw a stone into a deep river and its water stays clear. Only a shallow brook turns muddy. How much an insult disturbs us, Sa'di suggests, shows how deep we are. This is not a reason to accept mistreatment, but a picture of inner steadiness. A deep person can feel the stone and still not be clouded by it. And depth is something we can grow.
prompt: How deep is your river when someone throws a stone?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: The sheep are not intended for the service of the shepherd, but the shepherd is appointed to tend the sheep.
context: A clear statement, 750 years old, that leaders exist to serve the people, not the other way round.
about:
A dervish sits by the road as a king passes, and doesn't bother to look up, in this story from Sa'di's Gulistan, usually dated 1258. The offended king calls him rude, and a minister asks why he did not pay homage. The dervish replies that kings exist to protect the people, not the people to serve kings.

Then he gives this image: the sheep are not there for the shepherd; the shepherd is there for the sheep. It is a bold thing to say to a king's face, and a striking thing to find in a book more than 750 years old. Authority, in this view, is a duty, not a prize. Anyone with power over others, a manager, a teacher, a parent, holds it for those people's sake.
prompt: Who are you serving in your role, and who is serving you?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: A tyrant cannot govern a kingdom, for the duty of a shepherd is not expected from the wolf.
context: Those who exploit people can't be trusted to protect them.
about:
Sa'di was a Persian poet from Shiraz. His Gulistan (“Rose Garden”, usually dated 1258) mixes short prose stories with verse. This line comes from a story in the first chapter, “Of the Customs of Kings”, about a king who robbed his people until many of them fled and his treasury ran empty. His minister warns him with these words. The king throws him in prison, and soon loses his throne to rivals the scattered people support.

The idea is old but still sharp. Power rests on people's trust, and whoever preys on those they are meant to protect undermines their own position. It holds for bosses, teachers and parents as much as for kings.
prompt: When you have a little power over others, do you act more like the shepherd or the wolf?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: Esteem him not a friend who during your prosperity will brag of his love and brotherly affection.
context: Friends who appear in good times prove nothing. Hard times show who stays.
about:
In a long story from Sa'di's Gulistan, a poor friend wants a post at the king's court. When Sa'di warns him that court life is dangerous and advises contentment instead, the friend loses his temper and quotes this saying, along with another: real friends are those who help us in prison, while enemies can pretend friendship at our table.

The story then proves him right, though not as he expected. He gets his post and rises high, but later falls into disgrace, and his old friends stand aside. Fair-weather friendship is easy: anyone can be warm when things are going well. The test is who stays when they aren't. It is a good question to ask about our friends, and about ourselves.
prompt: Whose friendship has only ever been tested in good times?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: A peace-mingling falsehood is preferable to a mischief-stirring truth.
context: From the Gulistan's first story, where a minister softens a prisoner's curse to save his life. Sa'di's provocative point: truth told only to hurt can do more harm than a kind untruth.
about:
This is from the very first story of Sa'di's Gulistan. A captive about to be executed curses the king in a language the king does not understand. A kind minister translates it as a plea for mercy, and the king spares him. A rival minister then reveals the truth: the man had insulted the king.

The king replies that he prefers the first man's falsehood to this truth, because the falsehood aimed at peace and the truth at harm. It is a provocative lesson, and meant to be. Sa'di is not praising lying in general. He is asking why we speak. A truth told only to hurt someone can do more damage than a kind untruth that prevents harm. Honesty matters, and so does what we use it for.
prompt: When is truth used as a weapon rather than a gift?
translation: James Ross, revised edition (1900), lightly modernised

text: If you look at the contents you are wise; / If you look only at the vessel you are misguided.
context: Judge what is inside, not the container: a person's character, not their looks or status.
about:
This comes from Book VI, the last book of Rumi's Masnavi. Rumi compares people's bodies to pitchers with closed mouths: from the outside they look alike, but one may hold the water of life and another deadly poison.

So, he says, look at what is inside, not at the vessel. It is a familiar idea, but hard to live by. We judge people by looks, clothes, accent or status almost without noticing. Rumi applies the same rule to words: “The form misleads, but the inner meaning guides.” Whether we are meeting a person or reading a book, the invitation is the same: take the time to see what it holds.
prompt: Whose 'vessel' have you judged instead of what is inside?

text: Boil your pot by degrees and in a masterly way; / Food boiled in mad haste is spoiled.
context: Good things, like good food, need time and steady heat. Rushing spoils them.
about:
These lines come from Book VI of Rumi's Masnavi, in a passage about slow inner growth. A teacher tells an impatient student that he must climb to the summit step by step.

Then the kitchen image: a pot boiled slowly and with skill turns out well, while food boiled in a mad hurry is spoiled. Rumi adds other examples, such as the nine months it takes for a baby to form. Growth, in people as in cooking, has its own pace. We often want results now: a new habit, a changed character, a mastered skill. Rushing does not speed up real change; it spoils it. Steady heat, kept up over time, does the work.
prompt: What are you rushing that needs slow heat?

text: Not one of all these is good absolutely, / Nor is any one of them absolutely bad.
context: Rumi reminds us that most things in life are mixed: what seems bad may bring good, and the reverse.
about:
These lines come from Book VI of Rumi's Masnavi. In the story, a prince is urged to show kindness instead of punishing. He answers that kindness is good in its proper place, and uses chess to explain: put the king where the rook belongs, or the knight where the king belongs, and the game goes wrong.

So, he concludes, nothing is good or bad absolutely. Each thing helps or harms according to where and when it is used. Gentleness can heal or spoil; firmness can protect or wound. Wisdom lies less in having one rule for everything than in knowing what fits the situation. Justice, as the prince puts it, is putting each thing in its place.
prompt: What 'bad' thing in your life turned out to have good in it?

text: Pain is a treasure, for it contains mercies; / The kernel is soft when the rind is scraped off.
context: Like a nut whose hard shell must be broken, hardship can reveal something tender and valuable inside us.
about:
These lines come from Book II of Rumi's Masnavi, from a story about an old man who is ill. When an honoured guest comes to visit him, he thanks his sickness for bringing the visit. His pains, he adds, wake him at night and keep him from sleeping all night like cattle.

Rumi draws the lesson: pain can be a treasure, because it holds hidden gifts, as a soft kernel lies under a hard rind. He adds that spring is hidden in autumn. This is not a claim that suffering is good in itself. It is a claim that hardship can open us: it can bring people closer, show us what matters and make us gentler. The gift is not automatic, but it is often there to be found.
prompt: What has hardship softened or opened in you?

text: Saying this one is my enemy, and this one my foe, / While it is his own body which is his enemy and foe …
context: We look for enemies outside while our own cravings and habits do the most harm.
about:
In Book II of his Masnavi, Rumi has just retold the story of Pharaoh, who killed countless babies to stop Moses from being born, while Moses was growing up safely in Pharaoh's own house.

Rumi turns the story inward. Someone ruled by their cravings goes around saying this person is my enemy, that one my foe, while the real enemy lives in their own house: their own appetites and habits. It is a sharp and familiar picture. We often blame others for what our own impatience, greed or anger brings about. The first place to look for the trouble, Rumi suggests, is close to home.
prompt: Which 'enemy' in your life is really inside you?

text: The powers of the world endure for an hour, / But nought shall remain of their majesty.
context: Empires and fortunes rise and fall. Hafiz saw it happen in his own city, Shiraz, as rulers came and went.
about:
Hafiz lived in Shiraz in the 14th century, in turbulent times. According to Gertrude Bell, whose 1897 translation this is, scarcely a year passed there without civil war, and the city was conquered by Timur twice.

So when Hafiz writes that the powers of the world last only an hour, he is not speaking in the abstract. He had watched rulers come and go. The line is a warning to the proud and a comfort to everyone else: no power, however impressive, is permanent. The same poem tells us not to be too sure of our crown. Whatever we hold, influence, status or success, we hold for a while.
prompt: What power that seems permanent will pass?

text: No wisdom of ours has unlocked that gate, / And locked to our wisdom it still shall be.
context: Some mysteries, about life, death, and meaning, stay closed however clever we are.
about:
This poem, in Gertrude Bell's 1897 translation of Hafiz, begins as a love song: the poet would give the cities of Bukhara and Samarkand for the mole on his beloved's cheek.

In the middle of it, Hafiz turns to the big questions. Tell stories of singers and wine, he says; it is vain to seek the key to what is hidden. Some gates do not open to cleverness. That is not a rejection of thinking, but an honest admission of its limits. There are questions about life and death that people have asked for thousands of years without settling. Hafiz suggests we can still live well, love and enjoy beauty without having solved them.
prompt: What mystery have you stopped trying to solve?

text: Nothing is nearer to you than yourself, and if you know not yourself how can you know anything else?
source: Al-Ghazali, The Alchemy of Happiness, ch. I
context: Al-Ghazali's starting point echoes the Greek 'Know thyself': self-knowledge comes before all other knowledge.
about:
These are among the first words of The Alchemy of Happiness by Al-Ghazali (1058–1111), a famous teacher of theology in Baghdad. His book on living well begins with knowing oneself.

Nothing is nearer to you than yourself, he says, so if you do not know yourself, how can you know anything else? He means more than knowing our face and body, or that we eat when hungry and lash out when angry. He means knowing what we really are and what moves us. The thought echoes the old Greek saying “Know thyself”. Before we try to understand the world, it helps to understand the one who is looking at it.
