prompt: What do you understand least about yourself?

text: But if passion and resentment master reason, the ruin of the soul infallibly ensues.
source: Al-Ghazali, The Alchemy of Happiness, ch. I
context: When anger and craving take charge, judgment goes, and harm follows.
about:
Al-Ghazali (1058–1111) was a famous teacher in Baghdad who later gave up his post to search for a truer way of life. In The Alchemy of Happiness he pictures a person as a small kingdom, with reason as chief minister, and desire and anger as its officials.

Desire and anger are useful, he says, and must be kept in their place, not destroyed. But when they overrule reason, the whole person goes to ruin. Most of us know the moment: anger makes the decision before we have thought, or craving chooses before we have weighed it up. Al-Ghazali's line is not a call to feel less, but to keep the order right. Feelings can advise; reason should decide.
prompt: When did a strong feeling override your judgment?

text: Those things he takes most delight in are often the most injurious to him.
context: What feels best in the moment often hurts us in the long run.
about:
This line comes near the end of the first chapter of Al-Ghazali's The Alchemy of Happiness. Having praised what human beings can become, he turns to how fragile we are: subject to hunger, thirst, heat, cold and sorrow, and robbed of our ease by a wasp sting.

Among these weaknesses he lists this one: what we enjoy most is often what harms us most, while what is good for us usually takes toil and trouble. It is a plain observation, and still true. Too much food, too little sleep, the easy word instead of the honest one: pleasure tends to be quick, and benefit slow. Al-Ghazali is not against delight. He asks us to notice which delights serve us, and which quietly cost us.
prompt: Which delight is quietly harming you?

text: I was snow and melted away, so that the earth drank me up, / Till I became one mist of soul and mounted to the sky.
context: An image of transformation: the self melts, is absorbed, and rises as something lighter. Rumi wrote these poems after meeting his teacher Shams of Tabriz.
about:
Rumi wrote his lyric poems, collected as the Divani Shamsi Tabriz, after meeting Shams of Tabriz, a dervish who became his spiritual teacher; the collection bears Shams' name. The translator R. A. Nicholson quotes these lines in the introduction to his 1898 selection.

The image is of snow that melts, sinks into the earth, and rises again as mist. Something hard and separate becomes soft, disappears, and returns lighter. Real change can feel like this: like losing who we were, before it becomes a kind of freedom. We usually fear losing ourselves. The poem suggests that letting go of an old shape is sometimes how we rise.
prompt: What did you have to let melt away to become who you are?

text: Let vows bind all, ye cannot bind the free / And mountain-surging thunder of the Sea.
context: For Rumi, love is like the sea: no rule or promise can contain it.
about:
These lines come from the Divani Shamsi Tabriz, the lyric poems Rumi named after his teacher Shams of Tabriz. R. A. Nicholson quotes them in his 1898 introduction, just after another couplet: however fast penitence grows, love will uproot it in a moment.

Vows and promises can bind many things, Rumi says, but not the free, and not the thunder of the sea. Love, in these lines, is like that sea: too large and too alive to be held by rules. It is a bold thought, not a recipe for breaking promises. Rumi is describing how love feels from the inside: it does not wait for permission, and it can sweep away resolutions we thought were firm.
prompt: What in you refuses to be bound?

text: It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
context: Machiavelli (1469–1527), a Florentine diplomat, wrote The Prince after losing his post. His reasoning: people are fickle, so love can break, while fear holds. He adds that a ruler must never be hated.
about:
Chapter 17 of The Prince asks whether it is better for a ruler to be loved or feared. Machiavelli wrote the book in 1513, the year after the Medici returned to Florence and dismissed him from the post he had held since 1494. His answer rests on a bleak view of people: “as long as you succeed they are yours entirely”, but when danger comes close they turn against you.

Love, he argues, is a bond of obligation that people break whenever it suits them, while fear holds because the dread of punishment never fails. Yet he sets a limit: a ruler must avoid being hated. Few of us rule anyone, but the choice is familiar. Do we rely on goodwill, or only on what we can enforce?
prompt: Would you rather be feared or loved, and what would each cost you?

text: …men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand, because it belongs to everybody to see you, to few to come in touch with you. Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are …
context: Most people only see how you appear; few get close enough to know who you are. Machiavelli meant it as advice to rulers. Today it also reads as a warning about living for appearances.
about:
In chapter 18, Machiavelli lists the qualities a prince should seem to have, such as mercy, good faith and honesty. Seeming, he insists, matters more than being, because people judge by what they see. Only a few get close enough to know the truth, and “those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many”.

It is cold advice, written for rulers who need to keep power. Yet it describes something everyone knows. Most people meet only our surface: a face, a role, a reputation. Read the other way round, the line is also an invitation. It asks who the few are who really know us, and whether we let anyone come close enough to touch, and not just to see.
prompt: Who knows who you really are, and not just how you appear?

text: …in the beginning of the malady it is easy to cure but difficult to detect, but in the course of time, not having been either detected or treated in the beginning, it becomes easy to detect but difficult to cure.
context: Machiavelli borrows a saying from doctors: early on, an illness is easy to cure but hard to spot; later it is easy to spot but hard to cure. He meant trouble in a state. It fits habits and relationships too.
about:
Chapter 3 of The Prince explains how the Romans held new lands. They dealt with future troubles early, and Machiavelli praises them for it. To make the point, he borrows what doctors said of “hectic fever”. Then he applies it to the state: troubles foreseen early “can be quickly redressed”, but once everyone can see them, “there is no longer a remedy”.

The pattern is everywhere. A small resentment between friends, an unpaid bill, a habit that is starting to take hold: each is easy to fix while it is still hard to notice. By the time it is obvious, it costs far more. The lesson is attention. Looking closely at small things, before they demand it, is often the cheapest care we can give.
prompt: Which small problem are you noticing now that will be harder to fix later?

text: …there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things, because the innovator has for enemies all those who have done well under the old conditions, and lukewarm defenders in those who may do well under the new.
context: Change is hard to lead because the people it will hurt know it now, while those it will help cannot yet be sure. Five centuries later, anyone who has led change at work will recognise this.
about:
Chapter 6 of The Prince is about rulers who rise by their own ability, like Cyrus, Romulus and Theseus. They win power with difficulty, Machiavelli says, partly because they must bring in new rules and methods. Supporters stay cool, partly from fear of opponents and partly because people “do not readily believe in new things until they have had a long experience of them”.

The imbalance is the heart of it. Those who stand to lose know exactly what they will lose, and fight hard. Those who stand to gain cannot see it yet, so they help only half-heartedly. Anyone who has tried to change a workplace or a family habit will know the feeling. It helps to expect it, and to give new ways time to prove themselves.
prompt: If your idea succeeds, who loses, and how will they react?

text: …envy is ever joined with the comparing of a man's self; and where there is no comparison, no envy …
context: Francis Bacon (1561–1626), English statesman and philosopher, wrote short essays of practical wisdom. Envy needs a comparison: we only envy those we measure ourselves against. "A man's self" simply means oneself.
about:
Bacon's essay 'Of Envy' sorts people into those most apt to envy and those most likely to be envied. Relatives, colleagues and those raised together, he notes, envy one another most when one of them rises. People of real merit who are promoted are envied less, because their good fortune seems no more than their due: “no man envieth the payment of a debt”.

This line explains why. Envy needs a comparison, and we compare ourselves with those close to us. As Bacon goes on, “kings are not envied, but by kings”. We rarely envy a stranger's fame, yet a friend's success can sting. Knowing this helps. When envy appears, it shows who we are measuring ourselves against, and invites us to ask whether that measure is a fair one.
prompt: Who do you compare yourself with, and does it help you?

text: Reading makes a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
context: Reading fills the mind, conversation makes it quick, and writing makes it precise. In Bacon's English, "conference" meant conversation and "exact" meant precise. Each gives something the others cannot.
about:
Bacon's essay 'Of Studies' is about what learning does for us, and how to use it. It holds his famous advice that “Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested”. Right after this line, he spells out the trade-offs: whoever writes little needs a great memory, and whoever talks little with others needs a quick wit.

Each habit trains a different part of the mind. Reading fills it with material. Conversation makes us ready to think on our feet, because others push back. Writing forces precision, since vague ideas fall apart on the page. Bacon also warns against reading only to contradict, or only to believe. We should read, he says, “to weigh and consider”. The three habits work best together.
prompt: Which do you do least: reading, talking, or writing?

text: "I also know," said Candide, "that we must cultivate our garden."
context: Near the end of Candide (1759), Voltaire's comic novel. Through war, shipwreck, and earthquake, Candide's teacher insists all is for the best. Settled at last on a small farm, Candide stops arguing: tend to what is within reach, and work at it.
about:
Candide is Voltaire's comic attack on easy optimism. Its young hero is taught by his tutor Pangloss that all is for the best, then lives through war, shipwreck, an earthquake and worse. In the last chapter, the friends meet an old farmer near Constantinople who works his twenty acres with his children. Work, the old man says, keeps away three great evils: boredom, vice and need.

When Pangloss starts listing kings who came to bad ends, Candide cuts him short with this line. Instead of arguing about the best of all possible worlds, the little group gets to work. The book ends with Candide saying it once more, in reply to Pangloss. The garden can be read in many ways: a plot of land, a job, a mind. Whatever it is, it needs tending.
prompt: What is your garden: the small thing within reach that deserves your care?

text: Friendship is the marriage of the soul, and this marriage is open to divorce.
context: Voltaire (1694–1778), the great wit of the French Enlightenment, wrote this in his Philosophical Dictionary. Friendship is freely chosen, so it can also end, which is part of what makes it precious.
about:
Voltaire's article on friendship appeared in his Philosophical Dictionary in 1764, and this line was then its opening. The joke that now comes first was added in 1770: people have long spoken of the temple of Friendship, and everyone knows it has had few visitors. Friendship, he adds, cannot be ordered, any more than love or esteem.

Right after this line, he calls friendship an unspoken contract between two people who are sensitive and good. The wicked have only accomplices, he says, pleasure-seekers have companions, the self-interested have partners; only the virtuous have friends. Because friendship is freely chosen, it can also end. That is not a flaw. It means that every day a friendship lasts, both people are choosing it again.
prompt: Which friendship needs some care before it quietly fades?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: What is tolerance? It is the mark of our humanity. We are all made of weakness and error; let us forgive one another our foolishness: that is the first law of nature.
context: Voltaire spent years campaigning against persecution. His answer here is simple: since everyone is weak and makes mistakes, forgiving one another is the most natural rule there is.
about:
This line opens the second section of Voltaire's article on tolerance in the Philosophical Dictionary. The first section ends by recalling how long blood flowed across Europe over arguments of doctrine, until tolerance alone could stop it. Right after this line, he pictures the exchanges of Amsterdam and London, where traders of many faiths do business side by side in peace.

His argument is short. We are all made of weakness and error, so none of us is in a position to punish others for theirs. Forgiving one another's foolishness is not a generous extra; it is the first law of nature, the rule that follows from what we are. It applies at work and at home too, where it is easy to count other people's mistakes and forget our own.
prompt: Whose foolishness could you forgive today, remembering your own?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Prejudice is an opinion without judgement. All over the world, children are taught whatever opinions people like, before they are able to judge.
context: In French the wordplay is plain: préjugé means "pre-judged". A prejudice is a verdict reached before any judging, often handed to us as children, before we could think for ourselves.
about:
In the Philosophical Dictionary, Voltaire's short article on prejudice opens with this definition, then makes a surprising turn: some prejudices are good. Everywhere, he notes, children are taught to love their parents and to see theft as a crime before they can know what a vice or a virtue is. Good prejudices are the ones our judgement confirms once we reason.

The trouble is the rest. He imagines a child taught to bow before a man in certain clothes who walks and speaks gravely. Grown up, the child sees a charlatan full of pride, and the prejudice gives way to judgement. Much of what we believe reached us before we could check it. The task is not to throw it all out, but to test it and keep what holds up.
prompt: Which opinion did you receive as a child and never examine?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: It is better to risk saving a guilty person than to condemn an innocent one.
context: From Zadig (1747), one of Voltaire's tales. Punishing an innocent person is worse than letting a guilty one go free. The English judge William Blackstone made the same point in 1769.
about:
In chapter 6 of Zadig, the young hero becomes first minister of Babylon. Voltaire paints him as a model judge: when he judged a case, it was not he who judged but the law, and when the law was too severe, he softened it. Nations owe this great principle to Zadig, Voltaire says with a wink.

The idea is simple: punishing an innocent person is a deeper wrong than letting a guilty one go. It asks something hard of us, which is to accept that some guilty people will go free. It also reaches beyond the courtroom. Before we condemn someone on thin evidence, at work or among friends, it is worth asking which mistake we would rather make.
prompt: When have you judged someone before you knew the whole story?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Such is the human condition that to wish for your country's greatness is to wish harm on your neighbours. Whoever wanted their homeland never to be bigger or smaller, richer or poorer, would be a citizen of the universe.
context: Voltaire points to an uncomfortable truth: wanting your country to be great often means wanting others to lose. His alternative is the old ideal of the citizen of the world, loyal to people everywhere.
about:
The Philosophical Dictionary's article on the homeland ranges widely, from the first republics to forms of government. Near the end it turns darker. It is sad, he writes, that being a good patriot so often means being the enemy of the rest of humanity. He recalls Cato the Elder, who always added, when giving his view in the Roman senate, that Carthage should be destroyed.

His reasoning is plain. A good patriot wants their city rich through trade and strong in arms, but one country cannot gain without another losing. His way out is not to stop caring, but to care for everyone alike. It is a demanding ideal. It asks whether loyalty to our own can live alongside goodwill to all.
prompt: Where does loyalty to your own group cost someone else?

text: As soon as anyone says of public affairs, "What does it matter to me?", the state should be counted as lost.
source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, Book III, ch. 15
context: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778), born in Geneva, believed freedom depends on citizens taking part. Once people stop caring about shared affairs, others start deciding for them.
about:
Book III, chapter 15 of The Social Contract deals with deputies, the representatives of the people, and Rousseau distrusts them. In a well-run city, he writes, everyone hurries to the assemblies. Under bad government no one will take a step to attend, because no one expects the common will to win and private cares absorb everything. He also warns against paying others to do our civic duties: give money, and soon you will have chains.

This line marks the turning point. Once citizens shrug at public affairs, others begin deciding for them, and freedom slips away quietly. The warning holds for any shared life, from a nation to a neighbourhood or a family. What nobody cares for falls to whoever is still paying attention, and their interests may not be ours.
prompt: Which shared matter have you left for others to decide?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: The person who has lived the most is not the one who has counted the most years, but the one who has most felt life.
context: From Emile (1762), Rousseau's book on education. A long life and a full one are not the same; what counts is how deeply we feel the life we have. Montaigne made a similar point two centuries earlier.
about:
Book I of Emile, Rousseau's long work on education, criticises parents who raise children as if they would never leave their rooms. He wants children taught to bear the blows of fortune, even in the ice of Iceland or on the burning rock of Malta. The point, he says, is less to stop a child from dying than to make them live.

Living, he writes just before this line, is not breathing but acting: using our senses, our faculties and every part of ourselves that gives us the feeling of existing. Just after it comes a sharp image: someone buried at a hundred may have died at birth. A life is measured less in years than in how fully we are present in it.
prompt: When did you last feel fully alive?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Everything changes around us. We ourselves change, and no one can be sure they will love tomorrow what they love today.
source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Reveries of the Solitary Walker, Ninth Walk
context: Written in Rousseau's last years, during long walks alone. Even our tastes and loves change, so a happiness that depends on things staying the same cannot last.
about:
The Reveries of the Solitary Walker was Rousseau's last work: ten walks, the tenth written less than three months before his death and left unfinished. The Ninth Walk opens with this reflection, which follows a bleak premise: happiness is a lasting state that does not seem made for us here, since everything on earth is in constant flux.

From this he draws a gentle lesson. Our plans for lasting happiness are fantasies, so we should enjoy contentment when it comes, take care not to drive it away, and not try to chain it down. Knowing that what we love may change does not make it worth less. It makes today worth noticing.
prompt: What do you love today that you did not love five years ago?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: I have never believed that human freedom lies in doing what we want, but rather in never doing what we do not want.
source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Reveries of the Solitary Walker, Sixth Walk
context: Rousseau's idea of freedom is a quiet one: not getting everything we want, but never being made to do what we don't want.
about:
In the Sixth Walk of the Reveries, Rousseau asks why he never fitted into society, where everything is constraint, obligation and duty. When he acts freely, he says, he is good; as soon as he feels the yoke of necessity or of other people, he turns stubborn. His strength is all negative: his faults are faults of leaving things undone, rarely of doing harm.

This line is his definition of freedom. It is not the power to do whatever we like, but never being made to do what we do not want. He contrasts it with ambitious people, who spend their lives doing what they dislike so that they can command others. How much of what we do each day goes against our own will?
prompt: What are you doing right now that you do not really want to do?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: People are born free, and everywhere they are in chains. Some think they are the masters of others, yet are more enslaved than those others.
source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, Book I, ch. 1
context: The famous opening of The Social Contract (1762), usually quoted as "Man is born free". Rousseau asks what could make power over others fair, and notes that those who rule are bound too.
about:
The Social Contract opens Book I with these lines. Just before, Rousseau explains why he writes about politics: born a citizen of a free state, he says, his right to vote, however small its weight, obliges him to study public affairs. He admits next that he does not know how this change came about; what he can answer is what could make it legitimate.

His answer, built up across the book, is that rightful power rests on agreements, not on force. Force alone gives no right, he argues: a people forced to obey does well to obey, but does better still to shake off the yoke when it can. The second sentence adds the sting. Those who think they rule others are bound as well, and often more tightly.
prompt: Which chains do you carry that you have stopped noticing?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: …you are lost if you forget that the fruits belong to all, and the earth to no one!
source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Discourse on Inequality, Part Two
context: From the Discourse on Inequality (1755). Rousseau imagines the first person who fenced off land and said "This is mine", and someone who should have pulled up the stakes and cried this out.
about:
The second part of Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality opens with a famous scene. The first person who fenced off a piece of land, thought of saying 'This is mine', and found people simple enough to believe it, was the true founder of civil society. Rousseau then imagines someone pulling up the stakes or filling in the ditch, and warning everyone not to listen to this impostor.

How many crimes, wars and miseries, he asks, that person would have spared humanity. This line is the cry itself. Rousseau admits that the idea of property grew slowly, and that by then things could probably not have stayed as they were. Still, the cry asks us to remember what is shared: the earth was here before any of us.
prompt: What do you treat as yours that might belong to everyone?
