text: Leisure is the mother of Philosophy; and Common-wealth, the mother of Peace, and Leisure.
context: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) lived through England's civil wars. By "common-wealth" he means an organised state, not today's Commonwealth of Nations. Only where a state keeps the peace do people have time to think.
about:
Chapter 46 of Leviathan is an attack on what Hobbes calls vain philosophy, and here he looks back at how philosophy began. True and useful ideas existed from the start, he says, like corn and vines growing wild before anyone planted them. But people lacked the time to cultivate them, busy with the necessities of life and with defending themselves against their neighbours.

Only great states changed that. “Where first were great and flourishing Cities, there was first the study of Philosophy”, Hobbes writes. Thinking needs safety. People struggling to survive, or living in fear, have no time to wonder about anything else. Peace and free time are not luxuries for thought but its ground. It is worth remembering on busy days.
prompt: What gives you the calm and free time to think, and who helps make it possible?

text: …new opinions are always suspected, and usually opposed, without any other reason but because they are not already common. But truth, like gold, is not the less so for being newly brought out of the mine.
source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Epistle Dedicatory
context: John Locke (1632–1704), English philosopher, wrote this while presenting his own new ideas. New thinking is often rejected only because it is new, but a truth is no less true for being recently found.
about:
An Essay Concerning Human Understanding opens with a letter dedicating the book to Thomas, Earl of Pembroke and Montgomery. Locke knows his ideas are new and expects resistance. “The imputation of Novelty is a terrible charge”, he writes, among those who judge “of men’s heads, as they do of their perukes, by the fashion”, that is, like their wigs.

The image of gold carries the argument. It is “trial and examination” that must give truth its value, he goes on, not any antique fashion. A new idea is not right because it is new, and not wrong either. It has to be tested. When we dismiss an idea, is it because we have weighed it, or only because we have not heard it before?
prompt: Which idea do you resist mainly because it is unfamiliar?

text: …the end of law is not to abolish or restrain, but to preserve and enlarge freedom: for in all the states of created beings capable of laws, where there is no law, there is no freedom …
source: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, ch. 6, sect. 57
context: Just before this, Locke says a fence that keeps us from bogs and cliffs hardly deserves to be called a prison. Good laws do not shrink our freedom; they protect it from other people's force.
about:
Chapter 6 of Locke's Second Treatise of Government is about the power of parents over their children. Children are not born able to reason, Locke argues, so they are not yet fully free, and guidance helps them grow into freedom. Law, he writes, is “not so much the limitation as the direction of a free and intelligent agent to his proper interest”.

Then comes his image: “that ill deserves the name of confinement which hedges us in only from bogs and precipices”. Freedom, he goes on, is not doing whatever we please, “for who could be free, when every other man’s humour might domineer over him?” It means not living under another person's arbitrary will. The right rules do not shrink our room to act; they protect it.
prompt: Which rule in your life gives you more freedom, not less?

text: There are only three events in a person's life: being born, living, and dying. We do not feel ourselves being born, we suffer in dying, and we forget to live.
source: Jean de La Bruyère, The Characters, 'Of Man', 48
context: Jean de La Bruyère (1645–1696) wrote The Characters, sharp portraits of people at the French court. Of life's three events, only the middle one is in our hands, and it is the one we forget.
about:
The Characters, first published in 1688, gathers La Bruyère's remarks and portraits of the people of his time, printed with his translation of the Greek writer Theophrastus. This remark sits in the chapter 'Of Man', in a run of thoughts on time and death. Just before it, he compares life to a sleep from which the old only begin to wake when it is time to die.

His point is sharp and a little sad. Of life's three events, we do not feel the first and we suffer the last, while the middle one, the only one we can do anything with, slips by unnoticed. We spend so much thought on beginnings and endings that we neglect the living in between. The line is a quiet nudge to pay attention to it.
prompt: What would "not forgetting to live" look like for you this week?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Children have no past and no future, and, something we rarely manage, they enjoy the present.
source: Jean de La Bruyère, The Characters, 'Of Man', 51
context: Children live in the present without trying. Adults spend much of their time in regret or worry, and have to learn again what children have never forgotten.
about:
This remark in the chapter 'Of Man' of La Bruyère's Characters comes right after a far less flattering one. There he lists children's faults: they are proud, envious, idle, fickle and quick-tempered, laughing and crying easily over very small things. They are, he concludes, already adults.

Then comes this gentler observation. Children carry no regrets and fret over no plans, so they can simply enjoy the moment. La Bruyère admits, in passing, that this rarely happens to us. Adults live much of the time somewhere else, going over the past or worrying about what comes next. We cannot become children again. We can, now and then, give the present our whole attention.
prompt: When did you last enjoy a moment without thinking of before or after?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: It is a great misfortune to have neither enough wit to speak well nor enough judgement to keep quiet.
source: Jean de La Bruyère, The Characters, 'Of Society and Conversation', 18
context: Speaking well and knowing when to stay quiet are two different skills. Lacking both, La Bruyère adds, is where all rudeness begins.
about:
In the chapter 'Of Society and Conversation', La Bruyère sketches the people who spoil talk: those who speak before they think, and those who weigh every word so carefully that listening to them becomes hard work. Just before this remark, he warns that conversation should rest on good sense and judgement rather than on too much imagination.

Speaking well and keeping quiet are separate gifts, and missing both, he adds, is the source of all tactless talk. Most of us have at least one of them. Some people speak brilliantly but never know when to stop; others say little, but at the right moment. The line invites a little self-knowledge: which gift do we have, and which one could we practise?
prompt: When would silence have served you better than words?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: The art of conversation lies much less in showing your own wit than in helping others find theirs: whoever leaves a conversation with you pleased with themselves and their own cleverness is perfectly pleased with you.
source: Jean de La Bruyère, The Characters, 'Of Society and Conversation', 16
context: People leave a good conversation pleased with themselves, not with you, and that is exactly why they like you. The best talkers help others shine.
about:
This remark from 'Of Society and Conversation' follows La Bruyère's portrait of careful talkers who never risk a word and speak correctly and boringly. In the same remark, he explains why this works: people do not want to admire you, they want to please. They seek less to be taught, or even entertained, than to be appreciated and applauded.

His conclusion is that the most delicate pleasure is giving pleasure to others. Good conversation is not a stage for our own cleverness. It works best when we ask, listen and leave room for the other person's ideas. The result looks odd but is true: people leave pleased with themselves, and so with us. Generous attention often wins more than brilliance.
prompt: In your last conversation, who did more of the shining?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: The most wasted of all days is the one on which we have not laughed.
context: Nicolas Chamfort (1741–1794), a playwright and famous wit of the Paris salons, left notes of maxims published after his death. Laughter, for him, is no luxury: a day without it is a day lost.
about:
Chamfort's Maxims and Thoughts fill part of the first volume of his Complete Works, printed in Paris in 1824. This one sits in the opening chapter of general maxims, which begins by teasing maxims themselves as shortcuts for lazy minds. Nearby, he compares the philosopher who wants to put out his passions to a chemist who wants to put out his fire.

Just before this maxim, Chamfort, himself the author of a tragedy, notes that tragic theatre gives too much importance to life and death. Laughter is the counterweight. A day with laughter is one in which something absurd or delightful reached us and we let it in. The editor's notice speaks of Chamfort's bitterness, which makes the line more striking: even he counted a day without laughter as lost.
prompt: What made you laugh today, or who could?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Great thoughts come from the heart.
context: Vauvenargues (1715–1747) was a French soldier who died at 31, much admired by Voltaire. In an age that prized cool reason, he argued that our best ideas begin with feeling.
about:
This maxim, number 127 in this edition of Vauvenargues' Reflections and Maxims, sits in a run of thoughts on reason and feeling. A few maxims earlier, he writes that reason deceives us more often than nature, and that reason does not know the interests of the heart. Just after it, he adds that good instinct has no need of reason, but gives it.

In his notes, the editor explains that by the heart Vauvenargues means feeling and instinct, and calls this the famous maxim that everyone admires and no one disputes. The idea is not that thinking is useless. It is that our deepest ideas begin with something we care about, and that reason follows and shapes them. Great thoughts often start as a feeling taken seriously.
prompt: Which of your best ideas began as a feeling?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: The thought of death deceives us, for it makes us forget to live.
context: Thinking about death can be useful, but too much of it steals the life we still have. Spinoza said something similar: the wise think of life, not death.
about:
This is maxim 143 of Vauvenargues' Reflections and Maxims, and it comes right after another about death: to do great things, he writes, we must live as if we were never going to die. The maxim after it is a wry confession. He sometimes tells himself life is too short to be worth worrying about, yet if a bore keeps him from going out, he cannot bear half an hour of it.

The line warns against a certain kind of gloom. Thinking of death can teach us what matters, but brooding on it draws attention away from the life still in front of us. For Vauvenargues, the remedy is more life, not less.
prompt: Which fear about an ending is taking room from enjoying something now?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Patience is the art of hoping.
context: Patience is not passive waiting. For Vauvenargues it is a skill: keeping hope alive while things take their time.
about:
Maxim 251 of Vauvenargues' Reflections and Maxims sits among his thoughts on misfortune. Just before it, he notes that necessity eases more sorrows than reason does, and that the favourites of fortune, however unhappy they look to us, never cure us of ambition. Just after it, he adds that despair adds not only to our misery but to our weakness.

Set beside despair, patience looks different. It is not passive waiting, and it is not giving up. It is hope that has learned to last: the skill of keeping a good outcome in view while time does its work. Despair weakens us; patience keeps our strength for when it is needed. It is a line worth remembering on slow days, when results take longer than we would like.
prompt: What are you waiting for, and how do you keep your hope alive?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: …only the passions, and great passions, can raise the soul to great things.
context: Denis Diderot (1713–1784), editor of the great French Encyclopédie, opens his Philosophical Thoughts (1746) by defending the passions. Without strong feeling, he says, there is no great art and no great courage.
about:
Diderot's Philosophical Thoughts open with this defence of the passions. People rail against them endlessly, he complains, blaming them for all human pain and forgetting that they are also the source of all our pleasures. What annoys him is that they are only ever seen from their bad side, as if a word in their favour were an insult to reason.

Without the passions, he goes on, nothing is sublime, in conduct or in works; the fine arts return to childhood and virtue becomes petty. The next thought adds that sober passions make ordinary people. Diderot is not praising every impulse. He is saying that strong feeling gives us the energy to love, create and act bravely. Reason can steer, but it needs something to steer.
prompt: Which passion has pushed you to do something difficult?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: I was the absolute master of my old dressing gown; I have become the slave of the new one.
source: Denis Diderot, Regrets on My Old Dressing Gown
context: Diderot swapped his worn old dressing gown for a beautiful new one. Next to it, his study suddenly looked shabby, so he replaced it piece by piece: a fine desk, a clock, paintings. Today this chain of new wants is called the Diderot effect.
about:
Diderot's playful essay Regrets on My Old Dressing Gown carries a subtitle: advice to those who have more taste than fortune. His old gown, he writes, was made for him and he for it. He used it to wipe dusty books and spare ink from his pen, and its long black stains marked a man who works. In the new one, he looks like an idle rich man.

The new scarlet gown changed everything. Beside it, his straw chair, wooden table and cheap prints looked wrong, so one by one they gave way: a leather armchair, damask hangings, an inlaid cabinet, a mirror, a fine desk, a clock. Today this chain of new wants is often called the Diderot effect, a name given long after him. His line names the cost: what we own can end up owning us.
prompt: Which thing you own has made you want more things?
translation: Translated from the French by The Thinking Place

text: Act only on that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
context: Kant's 'categorical imperative', the test at the heart of his ethics: could you want everyone to do what you are about to do?
prompt: What would happen if everyone did what you are tempted to do today?

text: I need to discover a Truth which is a Truth for me; I need to find the idea for which I can live and die.
context: Written at twenty-two, on a summer stay by the sea. Kierkegaard, often called the first existentialist, wanted not a system to admire but a truth he could live by.
prompt: What idea would you be willing to build your life around?

text: Teaism is a cult founded on the adoration of the beautiful among the sordid facts of everyday existence. It inculcates purity and harmony, the mystery of mutual charity, the romanticism of the social order. It is essentially a worship of the Imperfect, as it is a tender attempt to accomplish something possible in this impossible thing we know as life.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura's definition of the tea ceremony's spirit: finding beauty in ordinary life, and honouring what is imperfect.
prompt: Where could you find beauty in the ordinary today?

text: The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness.
context: The founding principle of utilitarianism, developed by Jeremy Bentham and refined by Mill: judge actions by how much happiness and suffering they bring.
prompt: Whose happiness will your choices touch today?

text:
It is sweet, when, down the mighty main, the winds
Roll up its waste of waters, from the land
To watch another's labouring anguish far,
Not that we joyously delight that man
Should thus be smitten, but because it is sweet
To mark what evils we ourselves be spared;
It is sweet, again, to view the mighty strife
Of armies embattled yonder o'er the plains,
Ourselves no sharers in the peril; but nothing
There is more goodly than to hold the high
Serene plateaus, well fortressed by the wise,
Whence you may look below on other men
And see them everywhere wandering, all dispersed
In their lone seeking for the road of life.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius, a Roman poet, set Epicurus' philosophy to verse. Here he describes the calm of a mind that has found its footing, looking out on a restless world.
prompt: Where is your 'serene plateau' when life gets stormy?

text: Like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light, as a thing which has its whole value in itself.
context: Even if a good intention fails completely, says Kant, its worth is untouched. Its value doesn't depend on results.
prompt: Which of your efforts failed, yet still shone by its own light?

text: The virtues therefore are engendered in us neither by nature nor yet in violation of nature; nature gives us the capacity to receive them, and this capacity is brought to maturity by habit.
context: We have a natural capacity for goodness, but it only becomes real through practice, the way a seed needs tending.
prompt: Which of your good capacities is waiting for practice?

text: He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"—in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease. "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"—in those who do not harbour such thoughts hatred will cease."
context: Two nearly identical verses that differ by a single word. Hatred lives on in the stories we rehearse about the wrongs done to us.
prompt: Which old grievance do you still replay, and what would happen if you stopped?

text: Accustom yourself to believe that death is nothing to us, for good and evil imply sentience, and death is the privation of all sentience; therefore a right understanding that death is nothing to us makes the mortality of life enjoyable, not by adding to life an illimitable time, but by taking away the yearning after immortality.
context: The goal is not to make life longer but to make mortal life enjoyable, by letting go of the craving to live forever.
prompt: How would you live if you made peace with being mortal?

text: In the kingdom of ends everything has either value or dignity. Whatever has a value can be replaced by something else which is equivalent; whatever, on the other hand, is above all value, and therefore admits of no equivalent, has a dignity.
context: Things have a price and can be swapped. People have dignity: they cannot be replaced by anything 'equivalent'.
prompt: Where have you been putting a price on something that has dignity?

text: Be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
context: Socrates' words to the jurors who voted to acquit him. A good person's integrity cannot be taken from them by anything that happens.
prompt: What in you can no misfortune touch?

text: Take away your opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
context: A compressed version of the Stoic method: the injury we feel is bound up with the judgment that we have been injured.
prompt: Which 'I have been harmed' could you set down today?

text: Duty is the necessity of acting from respect for the law.
context: For Kant, duty isn't blind obedience. It means acting from respect for a principle you recognise as right.
prompt: Which principle do you keep even when nobody is watching?

text: It is therefore not of small moment whether we are trained from childhood in one set of habits or another; on the contrary it is of very great, or rather of supreme, importance.
context: Habits formed early shape the person we become. The same is true of the habits we form now.
prompt: Which habit from your childhood still shapes you, for better or worse?

text: Should I be content that my maxim (to extricate myself from difficulty by a false promise) should hold good as a universal law, for myself as well as for others?
context: Kant's test for a lie told to escape a difficulty: would you accept a world where everyone lied whenever it suited them?
prompt: What small untruth would fail this test?

text: The hour of departure has arrived, and we go our ways—I to die, and you to live.
context: The final words of Socrates' defence, spoken with calm to the court that has condemned him.
prompt: How would you want to speak if these were your last words?

text: What I need is the power to live a complete human life, and not merely a life of knowledge; lest I come to base my thought upon something so-called objective, in any case something not my own.
context: Written at twenty-two, in a journal kept during a summer by the sea. Kierkegaard warns that knowing about life is not the same as living it, and that borrowed ideas cannot carry a life.
prompt: Where are you collecting knowledge about life instead of living it?

text: If the proper object of nature were its conservation, its welfare, in a word, its happiness, then nature would have hit upon a very bad arrangement in selecting the reason of the creature to carry out this purpose.
context: If we existed only to be happy, Kant argues, instinct would have served us better than reason. So reason must have a higher purpose: to make our will good.
prompt: What is your reason for, if not only your comfort?

text: Next to selfishness, the principal cause which makes life unsatisfactory, is want of mental cultivation. A cultivated mind—I do not mean that of a philosopher, but any mind to which the fountains of knowledge have been opened, and which has been taught, in any tolerable degree, to exercise its faculties—finds sources of inexhaustible interest in all that surrounds it.
context: A cultivated mind, Mill insists, doesn't need to be a philosopher's: just one that has been opened to learning and finds endless interest in the world.
prompt: What have you become curious about lately?

text: But a man is not a thing, that is to say, something which can be used merely as means, but must in all his actions be always considered as an end in himself.
context: Every person is an end in themselves, never merely an object to be used, not even by themselves.
prompt: Where are you treating yourself as a thing to be used?

text: For I do nothing but go about persuading you all, old and young alike, not to take thought for your persons or your properties, but first and chiefly to care about the greatest improvement of the soul. I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue comes money and every other good of man, public as well as private.
context: Socrates describes the message he has spent his life repeating to the people of Athens: care first for your soul.
prompt: How much of your care goes to your soul, compared with your possessions?

text: The perfect form of friendship is that between the good, and those who resemble each other in virtue. For these friends wish each alike the other’s good in respect of their goodness, and they are good in themselves; but it is those who wish the good of their friends for their friends’ sake who are friends in the fullest sense.
context: Aristotle distinguishes friendships of usefulness, of pleasure, and of goodness. Only the last lasts, because it loves the person, not what they provide.
prompt: Which of your friendships rest on usefulness, pleasure, or goodness?

text: We regard independence of outward things as a great good, not so as in all cases to use little, but so as to be contented with little if we have not much, being honestly persuaded that they have the sweetest enjoyment of luxury who stand least in need of it, and that whatever is natural is easily procured and only the vain and worthless hard to win.
context: The point is not to live with little, but to be able to be content with little, which makes us freer whatever we have.
prompt: What could you happily do without?

text: To be beneficent when we can is a duty; and besides this, there are many minds so sympathetically constituted that, without any other motive of vanity or self-interest, they find a pleasure in spreading joy around them and can take delight in the satisfaction of others so far as it is their own work.
context: Kant admires naturally kind people, but makes a surprising claim: kindness that comes only from temperament has less moral worth than kindness done from principle, when it is hard.
prompt: Where is kindness easy for you, and where would it take principle?

text: Nobody ever grudges a moment of time; but is that altogether wise of him, or foolish? A single farthing is a mere nothing to a silly idle man, but yet when farthings accumulate they make the poor grow rich; and it is for this reason that a merchant is careful and anxious about each separate coin. An instant of time is barely realized, yet they continue to pass by with never a pause, and life's end comes all too suddenly.
context: Like a merchant careful with each coin, Kenkō asks us to value each moment, since moments are what a life is made of.
prompt: Which moments are you spending without noticing?

text: Capacity for the nobler feelings is in most natures a very tender plant, easily killed, not only by hostile influences, but by mere want of sustenance.
context: Our finer capacities don't die only from hostility; they wither from neglect.
prompt: Which of your finer capacities needs some nourishment?

text: A good will appears to constitute the indispensable condition even of being worthy of happiness.
context: We don't enjoy seeing a bad person flourish. Kant takes this as a sign that goodness is what makes us deserve happiness.
prompt: What would make you feel you had earned your happiness?

text: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;—for there is nothing so effectual for which it can be changed. Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
context: Water wears down stone. Everyone knows that softness can win, says Laozi, yet hardly anyone lives by it.
prompt: Where could softness achieve what force has not?

text: A man is temperate if he abstains from bodily pleasures and finds this abstinence itself enjoyable, profligate if he feels it irksome.
context: The test of a real virtue is pleasure in acting well. If doing the right thing still feels like a grim effort, the habit is not yet formed.
prompt: Which good habit has started to feel natural, and which still feels forced?

text: Duty! Sublime and mighty name that embraces nothing charming or insinuating, but requires submission, and yet seeks not to move the will by threatening anything that would arouse natural aversion or terror, but merely holds forth a law which of itself finds entrance into the mind, and yet gains reluctant reverence.
context: A rare burst of lyricism from Kant. Duty doesn't charm or threaten us; it simply asks, and we can't help respecting it.
prompt: Which duty do you respect, even when you don't feel like doing it?

text: My misfortune is that I am interested in too many things, and not decisively committed to any one thing, to which I might subordinate everything else.
context: Kierkegaard at twenty-two, torn between law, theatre, science and theology. He later described the dizziness of facing too many possibilities as anxiety, the feeling that comes with freedom.
prompt: Which of your many interests deserves to come first?

text: The beginning is admittedly more than half of the whole.
context: Getting the starting point right shapes everything that follows.
prompt: What are you starting now, and is the starting point right?

text: Wherefore prudence is a more precious thing even than philosophy; from it spring all the other virtues, for it teaches that we cannot lead a life of pleasure which is not also a life of prudence, honour, and justice; nor lead a life of prudence, honour, and justice, which is not also a life of pleasure. For the virtues have grown into one with a pleasant life, and a pleasant life is inseparable from them.
context: For Epicurus, a pleasant life and a good life are the same thing: you cannot have one without the other.
prompt: Where do pleasure and goodness meet in your life?

text: He judges, therefore, that he can do a certain thing because he is conscious that he ought, and he recognizes that he is free…
context: Often summed up as 'ought implies can'. Knowing what we ought to do is how we discover that we are free to do it.
prompt: What do you know you ought to do, and so know you can?

text: The main constituents of a satisfied life appear to be two, either of which by itself is often found sufficient for the purpose: tranquillity, and excitement. With much tranquillity, many find that they can be content with very little pleasure: with much excitement, many can reconcile themselves to a considerable quantity of pain.
context: Calm and stimulation: Mill thought most people need some balance of both to be content.
prompt: Does your life need more tranquillity, or more excitement, right now?

text: Every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others.
context: A puzzled observation from the last book of the Meditations: we care most about ourselves, yet trust others' view of us more than our own.
prompt: Whose opinion of you counts for more than your own, and why?

text: These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me," with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?"
context: A reflection on possession: we say 'mine' about people and things, yet we do not even fully own ourselves.
prompt: What do you call 'mine' that you might hold more loosely?

text: Death is nothing to us; for the body, when it has been resolved into its elements, has no feeling, and that which has no feeling is nothing to us.
context: The second of Epicurus' forty core teachings, memorised by his followers. Death cannot harm one who no longer feels.
prompt: What fear might shrink if you looked at it this plainly?

text: Fontenelle says, "I bow before a great man, but my mind does not bow." I would add, before an humble plain man, in whom I perceive uprightness of character in a higher degree than I am conscious of in myself,- my mind bows whether I choose it or not, and though I bear my head never so high that he may not forget my superior rank.
context: Rank and talent may impress us, but only good character commands real inner respect.
prompt: Whose quiet goodness do you respect most?

text: Every man lives only this present time, which is an indivisible point, and that all the rest of his life is either past or it is uncertain.
context: The past is gone and the future unknown; the only life anyone actually lives is the present moment.
prompt: What would change if you gave this moment your whole attention?

text: It is not easy to define in what manner and with whom and on what grounds and how long one ought to be angry, and up to what point one does right in so doing and where error begins.
context: No rulebook can say exactly when anger is justified. That judgement has to be developed through experience.
prompt: When was your anger last right, and when was it not?

text: Because his example exhibits to me a law that humbles my self-conceit when I compare it with my conduct: a law, the practicability of obedience to which I see proved by fact before my eyes.
context: A good person's example humbles us because it proves that goodness is possible.
prompt: Whose example shows you what is possible?

text: Continuous pain does not last long in the flesh; on the contrary, pain, if extreme, is present a very short time, and even that degree of pain which barely outweighs pleasure in the flesh does not last for many days together.
context: Epicurus himself suffered from painful illness. His teaching was that severe pain is brief and long pain is bearable.
prompt: What pain have you endured that turned out more bearable than you feared?

text: Let us, then, take the argument as our guide, which has revealed to us that the best way of life is to practise justice and every virtue in life and death.
context: The closing words of the Gorgias. After a long and heated argument, Socrates concludes simply: practise justice and every virtue.
prompt: What would it mean to follow the argument wherever it leads?

text: From this moment my burden grew lighter. The oppression of the thought that all feeling was dead within me was gone. I was no longer hopeless: I was not a stock or a stone. I had still, it seemed, some of the material out of which all worth of character, and all capacity for happiness, are made.
context: Mill describes the moment his depression began to lift: reading a moving story, he cried, and realised he could still feel.
prompt: When did you last feel something deeply, and what did it tell you?

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
context: The Stoics saw humans as social by nature. When others fall short, there are only two fitting responses: help them see, or be patient.
prompt: Is there someone you could teach, or someone you need to bear with?

text: Ask him, however- if his sovereign ordered him, on pain of the same immediate execution, to bear false witness against an honourable man, whom the prince might wish to destroy under a plausible pretext, would he consider it possible in that case to overcome his love of life, however great it may be.
context: Kant's thought experiment: ordered on pain of death to bear false witness against an innocent person, could you refuse? You may not know whether you would, but you know you could.
prompt: What would you refuse to do, whatever it cost?

text: The happiness which forms the utilitarian standard of what is right in conduct, is not the agent's own happiness, but that of all concerned. As between his own happiness and that of others, utilitarianism requires him to be as strictly impartial as a disinterested and benevolent spectator.
context: Utilitarianism counts everyone's happiness equally, your own included but no more than anyone else's.
prompt: How would you decide if your own happiness counted no more than another's?

text: In a particular flower I may train myself to see the whole world; or I may listen to the many hints and suggestions which Nature offers with respect to human life.
context: The young Kierkegaard decides he does not need to master science to learn from nature. One flower, looked at closely, can teach a great deal.
prompt: What small thing near you could you look at long enough to learn from?

text: Persons who wish another good for his own sake, if the feeling is not reciprocated, are merely said to feel goodwill for him: only when mutual is such goodwill termed friendship. And perhaps we should also add the qualification that the feeling of goodwill must be known to its object.
context: Goodwill isn't enough for friendship; it has to be mutual, and both people have to know it.
prompt: Who might not know how much goodwill you feel toward them?

text: This is virtue, and virtue, at least as a naturally acquired faculty, can never be perfect.
context: Virtue, for Kant, is steady progress rather than a finished state.
prompt: Where are you making steady progress, even if you're not perfect?

text: A person whose desires and impulses are his own—are the expression of his own nature, as it has been developed and modified by his own culture—is said to have a character. One whose desires and impulses are not his own, has no character, no more than a steam-engine has a character.
context: Character, for Mill, means desires that are genuinely your own, developed by your own reflection.
prompt: Which of your desires are truly your own?

text: Fortune but seldom interferes with the wise man; his greatest and highest interests have been, are, and will be, directed by reason throughout the course of his life.
context: Luck affects the outer edges of a life. What matters most is guided by our own reasoning.
prompt: What part of your life is governed by reason rather than luck?

text: In them I seemed to draw from a source of inward joy, of sympathetic and imaginative pleasure, which could be shared in by all human beings.
context: Wordsworth's poems helped heal Mill. In them he found a joy that excluded no one.
prompt: What gives you a joy that anyone could share?

text: Since it is possible that you may depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly.
context: Not a counsel of fear, but of seriousness: live as one who knows life is not guaranteed.
prompt: Which of today's acts would you do differently in that light?

text: A man must first appreciate the importance of what we call duty, the authority of the moral law, and the immediate dignity which the following of it gives to the person in his own eyes.
context: The satisfaction of doing right only comes once we've recognised for ourselves why it matters.
prompt: Which duty brings you a quiet sense of dignity?

text: Few human creatures would consent to be changed into any of the lower animals, for a promise of the fullest allowance of a beast's pleasures.
context: Mill's argument for higher pleasures: almost nobody would trade a human life for an animal's, however comfortable.
prompt: What makes your life worth more to you than comfort?

text: Unlimited time and limited time afford an equal amount of pleasure, if we measure the limits of that pleasure by reason.
context: A complete life is not measured by its length. Understood rightly, a finite life can be whole.
prompt: What would make your life feel complete, regardless of its length?

text: Put the case that the mind of that philanthropist were clouded by sorrow of his own, extinguishing all sympathy with the lot of others, and that, while he still has the power to benefit others in distress, he is not touched by their trouble because he is absorbed with his own; and now suppose that he tears himself out of this dead insensibility, and performs the action without any inclination to it, but simply from duty, then first has his action its genuine moral worth.
context: Kant imagines a kind person whose own grief has numbed their sympathy, yet who helps others anyway. That, he says, is where moral worth truly shows.
prompt: Who could you help today even if you don't feel like it?

text: The power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already; and that just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being.
context: Education, for Plato, is not pouring knowledge into an empty vessel but turning the whole soul toward the light.
prompt: What understanding is already in you, waiting to be turned toward?

text: He who understands the limits of life knows how easy it is to procure enough to remove the pain of want and make the whole of life complete and perfect. Hence he has no longer any need of things which are not to be won save by labour and conflict.
context: Knowing how little we truly need frees us from struggles that were never necessary.
prompt: Which of your struggles is for something you don't really need?

text: For love, as an affection, cannot be commanded, but beneficence for duty's sake may; even though we are not impelled to it by any inclination- nay, are even repelled by a natural and unconquerable aversion. This is practical love and not pathological- a love which is seated in the will, and not in the propensions of sense- in principles of action and not of tender sympathy; and it is this love alone which can be commanded.
context: Feelings can't be ordered, says Kant, but kindness can. 'Practical love' lives in what we choose to do, not in what we happen to feel.
prompt: Who could you treat with love today, even without feeling it?

text: Its most appropriate appellation is a sense of dignity, which all human beings possess in one form or other.
context: Why would anyone prefer a harder, nobler life? Mill's answer: a sense of dignity that every human being has in some form.
prompt: What would you never do because of your own sense of dignity?

text: What is a poet? A poet is an unhappy creature; his heart is torn by secret sufferings, but his lips are so formed that when the cries and the sighs escape them, they create a sound of beautiful music.
context: The opening aphorism of Either/Or (1843), in the voice of a young aesthete. Beautiful art can hide real pain, and admirers rarely ask what it costs.
prompt: Whose cheerful surface might be hiding something you haven't asked about?

text: All such desires as lead to no pain when they remain ungratified are unnecessary, and the longing is easily got rid of, when the thing desired is difficult to procure or when the desires seem likely to produce harm.
context: A test for any desire: would going without it actually hurt? If not, it can be let go.
prompt: Which desire would cost you nothing to give up?

text: That which is best and most pleasant for each creature is that which is proper to the nature of each; accordingly the life of the intellect is the best and the pleasantest life for man, inasmuch as the intellect more than anything else is man; therefore this life will be the happiest.
context: Each creature flourishes by doing what is most its own. For humans, Aristotle thought, that means a life of thought and understanding.
prompt: What activity makes you feel most yourself?

text: The maintenance of a due balance among the faculties now seemed to be of primary importance. The cultivation of the feelings became one of the cardinal points in my ethical and philosophical creed.
context: After his crisis, Mill decided that reason alone was not enough; feelings needed cultivating too, through poetry, art and nature.
prompt: Which side of you, thinking or feeling, needs more attention?

text: If we look closer at them we everywhere come upon the dear self which is always prominent, and it is this they have in view and not the strict command of duty which would often require self-denial.
context: Kant admits that most of our good actions are mixed with self-interest. 'The dear self' is always somewhere nearby.
prompt: Where is the dear self hiding in your good deeds?

text: Many are the things on which we should place no reliance; for it is because he had had such complete confidence in them that a foolish man feels angry and resentful (when they fail him). Have you power and authority? trust not in them; even the most dread personage may be overthrown. Have you riches? trust not in them; in an instant of time they may all be lost.
context: Kenkō lists the things we lean on (power, wealth, cleverness) and reminds us how quickly each can fail.
prompt: What are you relying on that could change in an instant?

text: “This, my dear Socrates,” said the stranger of Mantineia, “is that life above all others which man should live, in the contemplation of beauty absolute.”
context: The priestess Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from beautiful bodies to beautiful souls, ideas, and finally beauty itself.
prompt: Where did you notice beauty today?

text: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty. It is not possible then for him to follow that which seems right to you, but that which seems right to himself. … you will be mild in temper to him who reviles you; for say on each occasion, It seemed so to him.
context: People act on what seems right to them. Remembering this softens anger without excusing the act.
prompt: Who has acted on how things seemed to them, and can you see it from there?

text: Everything in nature works according to laws. Rational beings alone have the faculty of acting according to the conception of laws, that is according to principles, i.e., have a will.
context: Stones fall and rivers flow by law. People alone can act according to principles they understand, and that is what it means to have a will.
prompt: Which principle do you choose to live by?

text: For wisdom is a most beautiful thing, and Love is of the beautiful; and therefore Love is also a philosopher or lover of wisdom, and being a lover of wisdom is in a mean between the wise and the ignorant.
context: Love, in Diotima's account, is neither wise nor ignorant but always reaching: the very definition of a philosopher.
prompt: What are you reaching for that you don't yet have?

text:
And in fee-simple life is given to none,
But to all mere usufruct. Look back:
Nothing to us was all fore-passed eld
Of time the eternal, ere we had a birth.
And Nature holds this like a mirror up
Of time-to-be when we are dead and gone.
And what is there so horrible appears?
Now what is there so sad about it all?
Is it not serener far than any sleep?
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Life is lent, not owned. And the eternity after death, Lucretius argues, is no more frightening than the eternity before birth.
prompt: If life is on loan, how do you want to use it?

text: Tell him the history of an honest man whom men want to persuade to join the calumniators of an innocent and powerless person (say Anne Boleyn, accused by Henry VIII of England). He is offered advantages, great gifts, or high rank; he rejects them.
context: Kant suggests teaching ethics to children through stories like this one, where an honest man refuses bribes to join in slandering an innocent person.
prompt: Which story of honesty has stayed with you?

text: Give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one. May I reckon the wise to be the wealthy, and may I have such a quantity of gold as a temperate man and he only can bear and carry.
context: Socrates' prayer at the end of the Phaedrus: inner beauty, harmony between inner and outer life, and only as much wealth as a temperate person can carry.
prompt: How could your outward life better match your inward one?

text: We smile at the life of the cloister, and yet no hermit ever lived so unreal a life as is common today, for the hermit did indeed abstract from the whole world, but he did not abstract from himself.
context: Kierkegaard mocks thinkers who build grand systems and forget that they are living people too. The hermit leaves the world; the pure thinker leaves himself.
prompt: Where do you think about life in a way that leaves you out of it?

text: There is a state of mind in which a man may do these various acts with the result that he really is a good man: I mean when he does them from choice, and for the sake of the acts themselves.
context: Doing the right thing for the wrong reason isn't quite virtue. Goodness includes choosing the good for its own sake.
prompt: What good thing are you doing, and why are you really doing it?

text:
The man who sickens of his home goes out,
Forth from his splendid halls, and straight—returns,
Feeling i'faith no better off abroad.
He races, driving his Gallic ponies along,
Down to his villa, madly,—as in haste
To hurry help to a house afire.—At once
He yawns, as soon as foot has touched the threshold,
Or drowsily goes off in sleep and seeks
Forgetfulness, or maybe bustles about
And makes for town again. In such a way
Each human flees himself—a self in sooth,
As happens, he by no means can escape;
And willy-nilly he cleaves to it and loathes,
Sick, sick, and guessing not the cause of ail.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: A strikingly modern portrait of restlessness: the rich man rushing to his country house, bored on arrival, rushing back to town, always fleeing himself.
prompt: What are you running from by keeping busy?

text: It is hygiene, for it enforces cleanliness; it is economics, for it shows comfort in simplicity rather than in the complex and costly; it is moral geometry, inasmuch as it defines our sense of proportion to the universe.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura describes the tea ceremony as a whole way of life: cleanliness, simplicity, and a sense of our place in things.
prompt: Where could you choose the simple over the complex and costly?

text: The utilitarian morality does recognise in human beings the power of sacrificing their own greatest good for the good of others. It only refuses to admit that the sacrifice is itself a good.
context: Mill honours self-sacrifice, but only when it actually helps someone. Suffering for its own sake, he says, is wasted.
prompt: Is a sacrifice you're making actually helping anyone?

text: Hence the importance, as Plato points out, of having been definitely trained from childhood to like and dislike the proper things; this is what good education means.
context: Aristotle quotes his teacher Plato: a good education teaches us to enjoy the right things, not just to know them.
prompt: Which good things have you learned to enjoy?

text: When an upright man is in the greatest distress, which he might have avoided if he could only have disregarded duty, is he not sustained by the consciousness that he has maintained humanity in its proper dignity in his own person and honoured it, that he has no reason to be ashamed of himself in his own sight, or to dread the inward glance of self-examination?
context: Doing right may cost us dearly. What remains is the dignity of being able to look at ourselves honestly.
prompt: What would let you face your own honest gaze tonight?

text: Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 2
context: Seneca's whole argument in one line: the problem is not the length of life but how we spend it.
prompt: What would 'using it well' look like this week?

text: Pleasures and pains are the things with which moral virtue is concerned. For pleasure causes us to do base actions and pain causes us to abstain from doing noble actions.
context: Most of our failures come from chasing pleasure or avoiding discomfort. That's why virtue is mainly about training our likes and dislikes.
prompt: Which discomfort are you avoiding at the cost of doing right?

text:
O wretched minds of men! O blinded hearts!
In how great perils, in what darks of life
Are spent the human years, however brief!—
O not to see that nature for herself
Barks after nothing, save that pain keep off,
Disjoined from the body, and that mind enjoy
Delightsome feeling, far from care and fear!
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius laments how people waste their short lives striving for power, when nature asks only for freedom from pain and a mind at ease.
prompt: What does your nature actually ask of you today?

text: This word is self-contentment which in its proper signification always designates only a negative satisfaction in one's existence, in which one is conscious of needing nothing.
context: Kant's word for the quiet satisfaction of a good conscience: not pleasure, but the sense of needing nothing more.
prompt: When did you last feel that you needed nothing more?

text: The demand that all other people shall resemble ourselves, grows by what it feeds on.
context: The urge to make others like us never stops on its own; every concession feeds it.
prompt: Where are you asking someone to be more like you?

text: The pleasure perfects the activity, not as the fixed disposition does, by being already present in the agent, but as a supervening perfection, like the bloom of health in the young and vigorous.
context: For Aristotle, pleasure is not opposed to good activity; it is what completes it and makes it whole.
prompt: Which of your good activities also bring you pleasure?

text: Through zeal knowledge is gotten, through lack of zeal knowledge is lost; let a man who knows this double path of gain and loss thus place himself that knowledge may grow.
context: Knowledge grows with effort and fades without it. The wise place themselves where it can grow.
prompt: Where could you put yourself so that your understanding grows?

text: Even the moral law itself in its solemn majesty is exposed to this endeavour to save oneself from yielding it respect.
context: We often look for a flaw in good people, and even in the moral law, so we don't have to feel humbled by them.
prompt: Whose goodness do you try to explain away?

text: The tea-room is unimpressive in appearance. It is smaller than the smallest of Japanese houses, while the materials used in its construction are intended to give the suggestion of refined poverty.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: The tea room is deliberately tiny and plain, built to suggest 'refined poverty', and every humble detail is carefully chosen.
prompt: Where could plainness be a kind of refinement in your life?

text: Lest we become misologists, he replied, no worse thing can happen to a man than this. For as there are misanthropists or haters of men, there are also misologists or haters of ideas, and both spring from the same cause, which is ignorance of the world.
context: After an argument collapses, Socrates warns against giving up on reasoning altogether, just as disappointment can turn people against humanity.
prompt: Where has disappointment made you cynical?

text: Although he will sometimes fear even terrors not beyond man’s endurance, he will do so in the right way, and he will endure them as principle dictates, for the sake of what is noble; for that is the end at which virtue aims.
context: The brave person isn't fearless. They feel fear and act well anyway, for the sake of what is right.
prompt: What are you afraid of that is still worth facing?

text:
But rather this:
To look on all things with a master eye
And mind at peace.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things V
context: Lucretius contrasts anxious rituals with what he sees as true reverence: looking on the world with calm and clarity.
prompt: What would you see differently if you looked with a mind at peace?

text: Of all the men of his time whom I have known, he was the wisest and justest and best.
context: The last line of the Phaedo, Phaedo's tribute to Socrates after his death.
prompt: What would you want those who knew you to say?

text: The only unfailing and permanent source of improvement is liberty, since by it there are as many possible independent centres of improvement as there are individuals.
context: Freedom multiplies the places where new ideas can start: one for every person.
prompt: What could you improve if you felt free to try?

text: What you have vainly sought for in books is suddenly illuminated for you while listening to a servant-girl as she talks with another servant-girl. An expression that you have vainly attempted to torture out of your own head, you hear in passing; a soldierboy says it, and he does not dream how rich he is.
source: Søren Kierkegaard, Stages on Life's Way
context: Kierkegaard spent his afternoons walking Copenhagen and talking with anyone he met. Some of his best words, he says, came from overhearing ordinary people.
prompt: What could you learn today by listening to someone you would usually pass by?
